articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1686: Sanctioned tankers carried fuel from South Korea to Russia
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Ukrainian units hit record number of Russian air defense systems and radars in September, one of them 552 kilometers away. Every result is recorded on video in the Delta battlefield system.
At ruined Donetsk’s airport, three Russians snap selfies and ready jet-powered Geran-4. Ukrainian drone slips in unseen and rams their launcher. The pickup truck was converted to launch Russian drones.
Ukraine’s drone pilots hit 76.5% more Russian infantry than two months ago: 2,699 in first five days of October. Commander Robert Brovdi says the pilots count only losses verified in the military's Delta system, so the real toll is higher.
Ukraine’s battlefield gains may be pushing Putin to shift focus to early winter strikes, ISW says. Russia is likely starting its recurring winter campaign earlier than usual while Ukraine is still developing defenses against the ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones being used in increasingly large strike packages.
The tanks that fuel Moscow’s airliners are reported burning after Ukraine’s latest drone raid on the capital region. Footage geolocated by OSINT analysts placed the blaze at the Volodarskaya station, part of Russia's state pipeline network.
Intelligence and technology
Ukraine’s war leadership sets new electronic warfare tasks as Russia’s jet-powered drones slip past nearly half of its air defenses. Zelenskyy said the main criterion is that Ukraine must be able to respond in kind to Russian strikes.
Ukraine is third in world for cyberattacks after US and Israel, and first in Europe. Machine-speed assaults run continuously and without fatigue. Malware accounts for 33% of incidents in the first half of 2026, and system compromises for 4.5%.
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry says some suppliers cannot build weapons ordered, and drops contracts to free $346 million for front. Technology and tactics change quickly, the ministry says, and some weapons no longer match combat tasks.
Proven on Ukraine’s front line, now made in Germany. National Guard signs for the Linza and Zoom drones. The German-Ukrainian venture Quantum Frontline Industries will build both systems and is scaling up as its first production year wraps up.
Türkiye’s Korkut guns now shoot down Russian drones over Ukraine. Almost half of the jet-powered Shaheds still get through. Russia launched about as many of the fast ones as slow ones in September, by one analyst's count, and its winter assault on the power grid is still ahead.
International
Seoul backs Ukraine, but sanctioned tankers carried fuel from South Korea to Russia. The trade could cast Seoul as a gap in the West's effort to squeeze Moscow, the Guardian said.
Russia is out to break Ukraine’s economy this winter, Jetten says—and the Netherlands will help keep Ukraine’s drone-hunting F-16s in the air. Ukraine is finding ammunition for its F-16s “virtually all over the world,” Zelenskyy said on 5 October.
Humanitarian and social impact
Three ambulances hit, a woman killed at home: 25 minutes of Russian drone attacks on Kramatorsk. The strikes on medical vehicles and a high-rise are now under investigation as war crimes.
Ukraine’s civilian casualties 55% higher in first eight months than in the same period in 2025, UN says. Strikes on energy facilities and businesses have surged, while damage to power plants is causing outages as winter approaches.
Political and legal developments
Ukraine cuts more than 4,000 vacant government posts and trims deputy ministers by about 20% in the first stage of civil service reform. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi says the number of deputies will be tied to how much work each office carries.
New developments
Germany accuses Russia of a drone bomb attempt at Leipzig. Now its eight biggest airports get drone detection. The air traffic controller's system spots drones in approach and departure paths and alerts the police, who remain responsible for stopping them.
Two ships sunk and a third set ablaze off NATO coasts in two days, and neither Bucharest nor Sofia will say “Russia”. Romania and Bulgaria have described the attacks only as drone strikes, without saying where the drones came from.

articles.title: Russia Continues to Develop Cheap Cruise Missile Substitutes
articles.body:
An Oct. 5 report by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) says Russia is increasingly turning to cheaper, maneuverable “quasi-cruise” missiles to supplement its conventional strike capabilities, a tactic that is pressuring Ukraine’s already overstretched air defenses.
Building on the relative success of the jet-powered variants of the Iranian-designed Shahed/Geran kamikaze drones, Russia has been introducing the so-called Banderol and Dan-T weapons and is believed to be developing other variants, increasing production and testing new launch platforms.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Mass attacks combining these new weapons with ballistic and conventional cruise missiles and jet-powered drones are exacerbating Ukrainian interceptor missile shortages.
While Ukraine is developing countermeasures including faster interceptors, electronic warfare and artificial intelligence-enhanced automatic gun towers, these will, as President Volodymyr Zelensky has admitted, take time to develop and bring into service. Meanwhile, Kyiv will struggle to protect itself from the onslaught these weapons will unleash.
The Banderol
Russia’s S8000 “Banderol” (meaning a small parcel in Russian) is a jet-powered medium-size cruise missile analog manufactured by the Kronshtadt Group.
It uses the Chinese Swiwin SW800Pro-A95 turbojet engine, giving it a range of up to 500 kilometers (312 miles) at speeds up to 650 kph (400 mph) and a 150-kilogram (330-pound) warhead.
Power Cuts Return After Russian Strikes Damage Grid
The Ukrainian Air Force describes it as a “hybrid of a drone, an aerial bomb, and a missile.”
It first appeared during a strike on the Odesa region in early 2025 before taking part in 40 separate strikes between May and September this year, while Ukraine’s Main Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR) reported in July that Russia had completed testing and the weapon had entered mass production.
They have been used in attacks targeting ports, logistics hubs, terminals, food warehouses and infrastructure in Kharkiv, Odesa, Zhytomyr and Kyiv.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Kyiv’s presidential commissioner for sanctions policy, said in July that Banderols had been used in 80% of Russian strikes on the Odesa City port.
The Dan-T
Russia unveiled its Dan-T at the El-Alamein airshow in Egypt in September. It is based on the 1990s Dan-M target aircraft, which was designed to simulate US Tomahawk cruise missiles for air-defense training.
According to the ISW report, Russia’s state-owned arms conglomerate Rostec, which makes the missiles, converted Dan-M stockpiles into air-launched loitering munitions by adding 135-kilogram (300-pound) warheads. It has an all-up weight of 270 kilograms (600 pounds) and a 500-kilometer (312-mile) range.
ISW assesses that construction of Dan-Ts has not yet reached scale but is another indication of Moscow’s efforts to repurpose existing technology into strike weapons. As an example, Soviet-era RM-48U missiles – originally designed for S-400 air defense training – have been converted into ballistic missiles for ground attacks on Ukraine.
The extent of Dan-T use is unclear. While Rostec and some Russian milbloggers claim hundreds have been successfully used in strikes on Ukraine, it was not until Sept. 13 that Ukraine began to differentiate between Banderols and Dan-Ts.
Launch platforms
Banderols and Dan-T were initially designed to be air-launched from Orion drones, helicopters and tactical aircraft – which some estimates say would potentially double their range.
HUR has reported ground launches from occupied Crimea, with Ukrainian analysts suggesting Dan-T could eventually launch from ground and naval systems.
Cost versus performance
These “quasi-cruise” missiles have inferior performance to conventional missiles, but their cost allows more to be manufactured and used, while their capabilities are more than sufficient for Russia’s purposes.
Compared to the Kh-101 cruise missile’s 2,500-kilometer (1,560-mile) range, 1,000 kph (625 mph) speed, and 480-kilogram (1,050-pound) warhead, the Banderol has a 500-kilometer (312-mile) range, speed of up to 650 kph (400 mph), and a 150-kilogram (330-pound) warhead.
The cost differential is even more stark. A Ukrainian aviation expert estimates that each Banderol costs less than 10% of the approximately $2million cost of a domestically produced Kh-101 cruise missile.
Banderols present especially difficult targets when used in attacks that combine them with Geran/Shahed drones and conventional missiles. They are maneuverable and have a smaller turning radius, which complicates tracking and interception.
Russian mass production
The report claims that Russia has prioritized production of jet-powered drones and quasi-cruise missiles in order to increase its strike capability at an affordable cost.
In September, Zelensky claimed that Russia would spend $12 billion on the weapons, with Ukrainian defense analyst Serhiy “Flash” Beskrestnov saying that Russia not only aims to increase the numbers of Banderol, Dan-T, Dan-M and jet-powered drones, but also aims to boost speeds to 750 kph (470 mph) while improving low-altitude flight and maneuverability.
HUR estimated in August that Russia was producing about 80 Banderols a month, with Beskrestnov setting the target at 120 and Ukrainian sources estimating Dan-T production at 14,000 in 2027.
Ukrainian countermeasures
Ukrainian developers recently unveiled upgraded interceptors, such as the LITAVR+ and Sting 2.0, capable of taking on jet-powered Geran/Shaheds flying at speeds over 400 kph (250 mph).
Beskrestnov said up to five such interceptors are in development and still require testing. Ukrainian developers have also reportedly deployed unspecified Banderol countermeasures and are scaling production.
Electronic warfare could reportedly play a role, as both Banderol and Dan-T reportedly rely on satellite and inertial navigation for guidance.

articles.title: Zelensky Warns of Massive Russian Strike as 3 Tu-160 Bombers Take Off
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky has urged Ukrainian citizens to take shelter when air raid alerts sound, citing updated intelligence reports about a massive strike planned by Moscow.
Ukrainian emergency services and the Air Force are ready to respond, Zelensky said in his evening address on Tuesday, Oct. 6, but the scale of their response depends on the air defense capabilities available to the country.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“A lot depends on our partners – every leader and every country in the world that has the defensive capabilities we need and can provide them to us,” Zelensky said, urging allies to continue supplying Kyiv as the war nears its fifth winter.
Bombers took off from Siberia
Hours later, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) reported that three Russian Tu-160 strategic bombers had taken off from Belaya airbase in Russia’s Siberian Irkutsk region.
In case the aircraft fire cruise missiles, the missiles could likely cross into Ukrainian airspace sometime after 3 a.m. local time, the Air Force said, urging citizens not to ignore air raid alerts and to stay in shelters.
Earlier warning
The evening address followed an initial warning Zelensky issued on Tuesday afternoon.
He announced the warning after a coordination meeting with government officials, military commanders and emergency services. According to the president, Kyiv was also preparing countermeasures.
At that meeting, the defense minister and the Air Force commander briefed the president on how air defense assets were being distributed and how protection was organized around key facilities.
Lithuania Moves Closer Toward Scrapping Nuclear Weapons Ban
Zelensky said the government and regional authorities had also prepared additional logistics measures in response to what he called a Russian operation against Ukraine’s logistics. Deadlines were set for many of the tasks, and the most urgent ones were already underway.
Separately on Tuesday, Zelensky chaired a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief.
According to the president, electronic warfare systems neutralize a significant share of Russia’s Shahed drones, and the most effective approaches will be scaled up.
The meeting also set priorities for supplying Ukrainian forces with long-range drones next year, with the main goal of giving Ukraine the ability to respond in kind to Russian strikes.

articles.title: Lithuania Moves Closer Toward Scrapping Nuclear Weapons Ban
articles.body:
Lithuania moved closer toward lifting its long-standing nuclear weapons ban on Tuesday, Oct. 6, after the amendment passed its first reading with 106-18 votes in favor.
The country’s Constitution currently prohibits weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases, including NATO’s, to be stationed on its territory. However, a final vote – scheduled for Jan. 12, 2027 – could remove that provision.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to Lithuanian news outlet LRT, Lithuania’s Constitution can only be changed through two votes held at least three months apart, each requiring a qualified majority of 94 in the 141-seat chamber.
“We will ensure stronger support that could be available to us,” Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said. “By addressing the legal exceptions that Lithuania had compared with other EU and NATO countries, they will be gone and we will be equal.”
The resistance was led by a populist party Nemunas Dawn, with 14 of its members voting no and two abstaining.
The remaining opposition votes came from three members of the mixed parliamentary group and one lawmaker from the Farmers and Greens Union and Christian Families Alliance.
Moscow responds with escalation warning
The Kremlin promptly responded to the move.
Asked about the vote alongside reports that Washington is weighing a permanent US base in Lithuania, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow would treat either development as escalatory.
Ukraine Rejects Permanent EU Limits on Its Farm Exports After Accession
“A military base is part of military infrastructure. If someone’s military infrastructure – in fact, that of a major NATO member – is approaching our borders, of course, this can only be viewed as a step toward escalation,” he said, according to LRT.
“The same applies to the deployment of nuclear weapons on the territory of a neighboring country.”
Peskov’s remarks appeared to be milder than earlier warnings by Russian authorities, although he reiterated previous threats that Russia will have to take “all necessary measures to guarantee its security.”
Russia’s former President and current Deputy Chairman of the Russian Security Council, Dmitry Medvedev, previously threatened Lithuania by saying the country would “disappear from the map of the world” should it lift its nuclear weapons ban.
“If God forbid, something like this happens and we have to react to their actions, no one will step in for them,” Medvedev said, adding that NATO would not invoke Article 5 as this would mean “a global catastrophe.”
Medvedev made the remarks on Sept. 11, after Peskov had already threatened Vilnius with nuclear weapons earlier on that same day.
Why Vilnius wants the provision gone
Article 137, part of the Constitution approved by referendum in 1992, rules out both weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases on Lithuanian soil.
The lifting of the ban would essentially allow NATO, of which Lithuania has been a member of since 2004, to deploy nuclear forces on its territory.
Although Lithuanian authorities insist no nuclear weapons are headed to its territory for now, they point to the need to change the constitution due to uncertain geopolitical circumstances.
The discussions over the possible ban gained traction in July. “The geopolitical situation is getting worse… Our constitution was written when geopolitical circumstances were totally different,” Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said.
Lithuania – among Ukraine’s strongest allies in Europe – borders both Russia’s exclave of Kaliningrad and the Kremlin’s ally Belarus.
Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas pointed to both countries on Tuesday again. “We are responding to Russia’s aggression,” he said. “If Russia had not started the war in Ukraine, we probably would not be having the discussions we are having today.”
In June 2023, Russia began deploying nuclear weapons to previously non-nuclear Belarus. Russia also deployed its nuclear-capable Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile (IRBM) to the country, whose combat use in Ukraine marked the first combat use of its kind in history.
Russia and Belarus conducted a joint nuclear war drill in May, 2026.
On Oct. 3, Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko reaffirmed Minsk’s alignment with Moscow, pledging that his country will execute Kremlin decisions and preserve a unified fatherland from Brest to Vladivostok.
He also joked that he and Russian President Vladimir Putin often debate who is the greater “co-aggressor” in Ukraine, despite Belarus aiming to portray itself as neutral in the war.
Meanwhile, Russia deployed its Iskander tactical missiles to Kaliningrad – its only ice-free port on the Baltic, which happens to host the headquarters of the Russian Baltic Fleet.
NATO has long been concerned that Russia could station non-strategic nuclear weapons in the exclave, and the latest Kremlin’s escalatory rhetoric had raised additional fears that Moscow could be searching for a justification for a direct attack on the Baltic States.
Although NATO did not provoke Russia, the Kremlin said it was ready to use its entire arsenal of weapons to defend Kaliningrad should the alliance try to block the region.
Around the same time, Russia has also accused the alliance of a reckless course carrying a high risk of direct armed conflict and threatened to strike “decision-making centers” in member countries.

articles.title: France's Macron observes test of new nuclear-capable missile without warhead
articles.body:
Macron observes test of new nuclear-capable missile without warhead
French President Emmanuel Macron on Tuesday observed the test firing of a new nuclear-capable missile without a warhead, according to the Elysée Palace and the Ministry of Defence.
France on Tuesday test-fired for the first time its new M51.3 nuclear-capable ballistic missile from a nuclear-powered submarine, the defence ministry said. It was not carrying a warhead.
The missile, a variant of France's M51 missile, was fired from the Le Vigilant submarine off Brittany and impacted "in the North Atlantic, hundreds of kilometres from any coastline", it said. President Emmanuel Macron witnessed the firing from a French warship, an official told AFP.
It said the launch was conducted without a payload and in strict compliance with international obligations.
While the announcement made no mention of Russia, the test comes after President Vladimir Putin warned the West last week not to escalate a standoff over Ukraine by threatening the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which is wedged between EU members Poland and Lithuania and which Moscow has made clear it would defend with nuclear weapons if necessary.
Macron hails clear message
NATO has said none of its "exercises or activities pose a threat to the territory of the Russian Federation". Putin also said Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to coexist peacefully.
"Today we are stronger. The message has been sent loud and clear for wherever it must be received,” Macron said in a video on X showing him watching the launch.
Macron said in March France would expand its nuclear arsenal and launched an initiative offering European partners joint exercises, the possible short-term deployment of nuclear-capable assets on allied territory and deeper consultation.
Since then, the message of being prepared to bear the costs of defending France's values and security has been a constant theme.
France spends roughly €5.6 billion ($6.04 billion) a year to maintain its stockpile of 290 submarine- and air-launched weapons — the world's fourth-largest arsenal. Britain has 225 nuclear warheads. Russia and the United States have more than 5,000 each.
The M51.3 is the latest version of the missile that entered service in October 2025 as part of the modernisation of France's nuclear deterrent.
Paris does not disclose the range of the M51.3. Publicly available estimates for the M51 family generally place its range at around 9,000 km (5,600 miles) or more, while French officials have said the new version can travel further.
France maintains a nuclear arsenal based on air- and sea-launched weapons, with four ballistic missile submarines forming the backbone of its ocean deterrent.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Sweden to deploy Patriot air defence systems to Poland
articles.body:

Sweden has announced that it will deploy Patriot air defence systems and around 100 accompanying military personnel to Poland later this year to protect the NATO logistics hub in the city of Rzeszów, which is the main conduit for aid to Ukraine.
The decision follows a number of other recent moves to strengthen defence ties between Stockholm and Warsaw, with Poland’s defence minister today hailing Sweden as an “excellent, proven ally”.
Sweden is deploying the Patriot air defence system to Poland to strengthen the protection of @NATO’s eastern flank. The Swedish forces will protect the logistics hub in south-eastern Poland that plays a key role in providing military and civilian support to Ukraine 🇺🇦. pic.twitter.com/EjGFYFLGnN
— Försvarsmakten (@Forsvarsmakten) October 6, 2026
The Patriot deployment was announced on Tuesday by Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, days after Sweden had also revealed that its Gripen fighter aircraft would patrol Polish airspace from October.
“The task for both the Gripen operation and Patriot [system] is to protect NATO’s logistics hub in Poland at the airport [in Rzeszów],” said Kristersson at a press conference alongside foreign minister Maria Malmer and defence minister Pål Jonson
“[We will] thus ensure that important equipment comes to Ukraine from all the countries that support Ukraine in its defence against Russia,” he added. “This all strengthens NATO, strengthens Europe and strengthens Sweden.”
Jonson added that “repeated violations of allied airspace and Russian attempts to influence support for Ukraine show the importance of protecting the logistics hub in Poland”.
Malmer, meanwhile, made clear that the deployment was intended not only to protect supply lines to Ukraine, but “is also part of our contribution to NATO’s deterrence and defence”.
Sweden will deploy its Patriots to Rzeszów in December and plans for them to remain there until the middle of next year. It will take over the mission from the Netherlands, which has had two of its Patriot batteries in Poland since last December.
Colonel Sofia Westermark, the commander of Sweden’s air defence regiment, told broadcaster SVT that the deployment would be “the most complex operation that Sweden has undertaken as a NATO ally”. The country joined the alliance in 2024.
Sweden will deploy Gripen aircraft to Poland to strengthen NATO’s eastern flank. Poland is a close ally and a vital hub for support to Ukraine. Swedish security is built together with our allies in NATO, and by taking responsibility together. (1/3) pic.twitter.com/4WaSp2UqYD
— Pål Jonson (@PlJonson) September 30, 2026
Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, thanked both Sweden and the Netherlands for their role in defending Polish airspace and NATO’s eastern flank.
“The continuity of this mission is an expression of allied solidarity and shared responsibility for the region’s security in the face of the threat from Russia. Together we are stronger,” he wrote on social media.
His deputy minister, Paweł Zalewski, told broadcaster TVN that Patriot systems “are currently the only ones effective against ballistic missiles”, making them vital for protecting Rzeszów. He noted that around 90% of international aid for Ukraine goes through the hub.
Poland has also been taking delivery of its own Patriot systems from the United States. The first were deployed at Warsaw Babice airport in 2023. Last year, Poland announced full operational readiness of its US-supplied Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS), an air-defence network that includes Patriot missile batteries.
Dziękuję rządowi Szwecji za podjęcie decyzji o wysłaniu do Polski systemów Patriot. Szwedzi przejmą ochronę hubu logistycznego NATO w Rzeszowie.
Dziękuję także Holandii 🇳🇱 za dotychczasowe wsparcie Polski i  wschodniej flanki NATO. Ciągłość tej misji to wyraz sojuszniczej…
— Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) October 6, 2026
Earlier this year, Poland’s airspace was violated by a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, which landed in a field. On one night last year, around 20 Russian drones crossed the country’s eastern borders, and last month a Russian military helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace from Kaliningrad.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental.
The growing threat from Russia has pushed Poland to forge closer military ties with other countries around the Baltic Sea, and above all with Sweden. In 2024, the two countries signed a strategic partnership to enhance cooperation on defence and economic development.
Since then, they have held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic; Poland has ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab; and Sweden bought €274 million worth of Piorun man-portable air-defence systems from Polish firm Mesko.

articles.title: Yemen conflict escalating into regional war
articles.body:
Yemen conflict escalating into regional war
Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces have launched a major offensive against the Iranian-backed Houthis, with both sides claiming territorial gains as battles rage around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait connecting the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
The escalation comes after the Houthis took over the key territory around Bab el-Mandeb in September, one of the world’s most important shipping chokepoints, which has gained particular significance amid disruptions at the Strait of Hormuz caused by the US-Iran war.
On Monday, the Yemeni army claimed to have pushed north along the Red Sea coast toward Mocha, while announcing “a strategic offensive operation on Sanaa,” which serves as the de facto capital of the Houthi movement.
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, agreed with Türkiye and Pakistan to rapidly deploy military forces under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, also known as the “Muslim NATO.” The coalition already announced that 100 warplanes are supporting the Yemeni offensive.
The Houthis have denied the government gains, claiming to have made headway around Taiz, some 80km from the Red Sea coast. The group has also retaliated with ballistic missiles and drones against Saudi targets, claiming strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, military bases, and Aramco oil facilities, including the Rabigh refinery. Saudi Arabia has confirmed damage from Houthi attacks on airports at Jizan and Najran.
The Houthis have consistently accused Riyadh of waging an “aggression” and blockade against Yemen, arguing that Saudi military operations serve US and Israeli interests. Their Yemeni opponents, meanwhile, view Houthis – who identify themselves as part of the “Axis of Resistance” – as “terrorists” and insurgents who overthrew the internationally recognized government in 2014.
The conflict in Yemen in its current form began when the Houthis seized the capital of Sanaa more than a decade ago, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention. However, fighting largely subsided after a 2022 truce.
Amid the fighting in Yemen and continued US-Iran standoff, US President Donald Trump argued that record gas prices are being driven not by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz but by Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries.

articles.title: Fresh Intelligence Signals Massive Russian Strike Ahead, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
Ukraine has received fresh intelligence indicating that Russia is preparing a massive strike, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday, Oct. 6.
“We received updated intelligence today regarding Russian preparations for a massive strike. We are preparing countermeasures,” Zelensky said after a coordination meeting with government officials, military leaders, and key emergency services.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The warning came as Ukrainian officials worked on additional logistical arrangements in response to what Zelensky described as a Russian operation targeting the country’s logistics. Government officials and regional authorities had prepared those measures together, he said.
Deadlines have been set for a substantial share of the tasks discussed at the meeting, with the most urgent measures already being implemented, according to Zelensky.
Air defense preparations were a central focus of the discussion. The defense minister and Air Force commander briefed Zelensky on the distribution of air defense assets and the organization of defensive coverage around designated key facilities.
Zelensky said Ukraine was securing the necessary ammunition for its F-16 fighter jets, interception capabilities, and interceptor missiles. However, he singled out defenses against ballistic missiles as the most difficult supply challenge.
“The most difficult issue is defending against ballistic missiles, and the availability of these supplies depends entirely on our partners,” he said. “We are working with them daily.”
Russia Continues to Develop Cheap Cruise Missile Substitutes
Zelensky also said Russian forces had attacked several Ukrainian hospitals in Kramatorsk and Kryvyi Rih over the preceding 24 hours.
“The emergency services responded effectively, and it is important that the State Emergency Service of Ukraine responds promptly to every such situation in all of our regions. Thank you for your professional work!”

articles.title: Russia Behind Drone Strikes on Ships Off Bulgaria, Zelensky Says, as Radev Rules Out Invoking NATO Articles
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky denied Ukraine’s responsibility for the strikes on two Bulgarian civilian vessels in the Black Sea, instead pinning the blame on Russia.
In his evening address on Tuesday, Oct. 6, Zelensky said that the Ukrainian Navy had been in contact with its Bulgarian counterparts. According to him, they established that the ships were hit in a combined Russian strike using maritime and aerial drones. However, Ukrainian intelligence and special services were still gathering additional details.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The Ukrainian Defense Forces conducted no operations in this part of the sea,” Zelensky said. “This latest tragedy involving civilian vessels is part of Russia’s ongoing attempt to make the western Black Sea completely unsuitable for navigation.”
The President has ordered the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU), the Defense Ministry, intelligence services and other relevant agencies to cooperate as closely as possible with partners, so that both Ukraine and its allies are better able to defend themselves against such attacks.
Radev: Drones ‘either Russian or Ukrainian’
Zelensky’s statement came hours after Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said Sofia had not yet determined who launched the drones.
Speaking to reporters on Tuesday afternoon, Radev said the vessels were struck by both a maritime and an aerial drone, Bulgarian National Television (BNT) reported.
“We have yet to try to establish where the attack came from, but it is clear: they are either Russian or Ukrainian,” he said, adding that the situation is “extremely worrying.”
Lithuania Moves Closer Toward Scrapping Nuclear Weapons Ban
According to him, the ship that was moving north was the one that sank, and for which Bulgarian authorities did not have further information on what it had onboard at the time of the report.
The other ship that was damaged was traveling south, carrying wheat, he said.
Although it struck Bulgarian vessels, the attack could not be grounds for triggering NATO’s Article 4, which allows allies to request consultations; or 5, which invokes the alliance’s collective defense.
“We have much more serious attacks inside territorial waters. Keep in mind that this is 130 km [roughly 81 miles] from our coast; it falls within our exclusive economic zone, but these are considered neutral waters,” Radev said.
Still, the prime minister warned of a broader pattern, noting that ships are constantly being sunk in the Black Sea. “This is hardly the most serious incident,” he said. “But it is serious as a trend because, as I said, when a war is not stopped in time, it expands its geographic reach.”
Crew still missing
Earlier on Tuesday, the vessels were identified as the Able and the Alfa Watan.
Vessel-tracking data from VesselFinder showed the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan heading toward Romania’s port of Sulina. Its last known position was about 70 nautical miles off the Bulgarian coast, shortly after 2 a.m. local time.
The Able caught fire, and all 18 people aboard abandoned it, according to Rumen Nikolov, who leads rescue operations in Varna, as cited by Bulgarian public radio BNR.
The Bulgarian ferry Dioscuria picked up the crew, some of whom were reportedly hurt.
Euronews described the strike as the first such attack inside the economic zone of a NATO member state.
The incident is the latest in a widening campaign against commercial shipping. Moscow has increasingly targeted merchant vessels in retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil facilities and tankers.
On Monday, Oct. 5, a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying grain caught fire and sank after a drone struck it in the Black Sea.
On Tuesday, Odesa Regional Military Administration head Oleh Kiper said a Russian drone hit a Marshall Islands-flagged ship loaded with rapeseed oil. One person was killed and seven were injured.
Radev, a former president seen as pro-Russian, won in the April 2026 parliamentary election, which ended a stretch of seven national votes in four years.
His government has since said it would halt all weapons deliveries to Ukraine, after Bulgaria had been a key supplier of Soviet-standard artillery shells to the country.
The strikes follow increasing drone incursions, sabotage campaigns and cyberattacks conducted by Russia, which Ukraine’s Western allies say may be intended to test NATO’s collective resolve.

articles.title: Ukraine is fielding Turkey’s Korkut air defense guns, a Turkish cousin of the Gepard. One kind of Russian drone may be too fast for them
articles.body:
- Ukraine has acquired new Korkut air defense guns from Türkiye
- The Korkut is a pair of fast-firing guns on a tracked or wheeled chassis
- Ground-based guns are effective defenses against drones
- But the Russians are launching faster drones, and more of them are getting through
Ukraine has reportedly purchased Korkut self-propelled anti-aircraft guns (SPAAGs) from Türkiye. Effectively a Turkish take on the classic German-made Gepard SPAAG, a mainstay of Ukraine's defense against Russian one-way attack (OWA) drones, the Korkuts could help stiffen Ukrainian air defenses as winter looms and Russia intensifies its terror attacks on Ukrainian cities and power plants.
The problem for Ukrainian air defenders is that the latest jet-propelled Russian drones, the Geran-4 and Geran-5, are getting through. They fly at around 500 km/h, nearly three times as fast as an older, propeller-driven Geran-2, and in September Ukraine shot down just 55% of them, by Zelenskyy's count, against at least 90% of the slow ones, one analyst calculated. The Korkuts arrive in that gap. Ground-based guns are arguably Ukraine's most cost-effective anti-drone weapons, but they may not work so well against the fastest drones.
That means more Russian munitions are getting through. More Ukrainian homes are burning. More power plants are going dark. It's a crisis now. It'll be an even greater crisis when winter arrives and the temperature drops.
All that is to say, the handful of Korkut systems Ukraine has received from Turkish firm Aselsan are welcome, but they're not silver bullets against Russian drones.
A Korkut battery includes a command vehicle plus three tracked or wheeled vehicles armed with pairs of fast-firing, radar-cued 35-mm autocannons. The exact variant Ukraine received hasn't been disclosed; Middle East Eye's mention of 25-mm ammunition suggests it may be the smaller Korkut 100/25, built mainly to stop frontline drones. The Ukrainian Korkuts join a sizeable fleet of SPAAGs in Ukrainian service, most notably including potentially 90 or more 1960s-vintage Gepards with twin radar-cued 35-mm guns.
Ukraine is running short of its best missiles for hunting Russia’s jet drones. Now MiG-29s are firing 1970s weapons
The tracked Gepards are old but effective. They, like all SPAAGs, can only engage incoming drones and other targets at fairly short range: just a few kilometers. But they're cheap. A SPAAG might fire a few hundred dollars' worth of shells to bring down a $50,000 Geran. A surface-to-air missile can hit a Geran from much farther away, but even the cheapest missiles cost tens of thousands of dollars apiece—and the supply is limited.
Gepards and other gun-based air defenses, along with wide-area strategic radio jamming, were the twin keys to Ukraine's temporary victory over Russian Gerans as recently as late last year. That's when the Russians were still mostly launching propeller-driven Gerans, and the Ukrainians were shooting down most of them.
Slipping interception rates
Vanquishing the slow Gerans didn't solve a separate air defense problem—how to shoot down supersonic ballistic missiles—but it did minimize Ukrainian casualties and mitigate the overall damage to Ukrainian infrastructure. Only the best, priciest, and rarest Ukrainian air defenses such as the Patriot and SAMP/T can hit incoming ballistic missiles. As missiles have run out for those batteries, more Russian ballistic missiles have gotten through.
But now more Gerans are getting through, too. On 26 September, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had launched more than 2,730 jet-powered Gerans at Ukraine that month and that Ukrainian air defenses were shooting down 55% of them. Analyst and mapper Clément Molin set that against Air Force totals: of 5,437 drones launched between 1 and 26 September, the remaining 2,707 were slow Geran-2s and Gerbera decoys, and at least 90% of those were downed. The overall interception rate, he calculated, has fallen to close to 70%, from 86% to 90% earlier this year.
Ukrainian forces are scrambling to acquire more inexpensive surface-to-air missiles as well as faster interceptor drones. But they're racing against time and the growing preponderance of jet-propelled OWA drones. The Ukrainians' air defense problem may get worse before it gets better.
"Ballistic missile defense is a serious problem, but the increasing production of Geran-4, Geran-5, Banderol, and Filin jet-powered OWA drones/cheap cruise missiles will also be a growing challenge this fall and winter," Rob Lee, an analyst with the Foreign Policy Research Institute in Philadelphia, warned in August.
Winter weather reduces the effectiveness of interceptor drones and helicopters, Lee noted, and Ukraine will need more high-speed interceptors to counter the jet drones. "The interception rate for OWA drones will likely decrease."
But that doesn't mean the Korkut isn't helping forestall an even worse dip in the overall interception rate for incoming Russian drones. Ukrainian officials are reportedly pleased with the Turkish gun. "Korkut has been pretty much successful in countering the Russian attacks," a Ukrainian official told Middle East Eye. "There were of course some problems but nothing that couldn't be overcome through some small adjustments."
According to Middle East Eye, the Ukrainians are considering acquiring more Korkuts.
Read Also
- Ukraine cuts more than 4,000 vacant government posts and trims deputy ministers by about 20% in the first stage of civil service reform
- Ukraine’s war leadership sets new electronic warfare tasks as Russia’s jet-powered drones slip past nearly half of its air defenses
- Ukraine is third in world for cyberattacks after US and Israel, and first in Europe. Machine-speed assaults run continuously and without fatigue

articles.title: Yemen war puts Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defence pact to first test
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen war puts Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defence pact to first test
Saudi Arabia's defence alliance with Turkey and Pakistan has moved from words to action for the first time, as escalating fighting in Yemen puts the two-month-old pact's collective defence commitments to the test.
The three members of the Mecca Alliance agreed at an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Sunday to begin the "practical implementation" of their collective defence commitments following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
They also agreed to make previously agreed military forces and capabilities available for rapid deployment to the kingdom.
But the move does not necessarily mean Turkish and Pakistani forces will join Saudi Arabia in directly fighting the Houthis.
Instead, experts told The New Arab that Pakistan could concentrate on territorial defence and military support inside Saudi Arabia, while Turkey provides capabilities including surveillance, air defence and drones.
For Andreas Krieg, associate professor at King's College London's School of Security Studies, the decision marks a significant evolution of the alliance.
"This is the first point at which I would describe the Mecca Pact as operational rather than primarily declaratory," Krieg told The New Arab.
"The critical development is not simply that the three governments have invoked collective defence. It is that Turkey and Pakistan are altering their military posture in response to attacks on Saudi Arabia and have committed to deploy previously agreed capabilities," Krieg said.
"That is the threshold the pact had to cross if it was going to have any deterrent credibility."
What will Pakistan and Turkey actually do?
The Mecca Alliance was established in August amid growing regional instability. Its collective defence principle means an attack against one member is treated as a threat to all three.
The arrangement has drawn comparisons with NATO's Article 5, but Krieg cautioned against taking the comparison too far.
"I would describe the pact as Article 5 language without Article 5 infrastructure," he said.
NATO has spent decades developing integrated military commands, common doctrine and joint planning. The Mecca Alliance has existed for only two months.
"This is meaningful activation, but it is the operationalisation of a flexible alliance rather than the creation of a unified war-fighting structure," Krieg said. "Yemen is now providing its first real operational laboratory."
The three countries have not publicly disclosed exactly which forces or military capabilities Turkey and Pakistan will deploy.
Krieg expects their roles to be substantially different.
Pakistan could provide territorial and air defence, training, advisers and manpower to protect strategic infrastructure, but is likely to be cautious about offensive operations against the Houthis partly because of its relationship with Iran.
Turkey could provide intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, radar and air defence, unmanned systems, electronic warfare and naval surveillance.
Saudi Arabia would remain the principal combatant.
"That allows all three states to say collective defence is functioning without requiring all three to fight the same war in the same way," Krieg said.
What does it change inside Yemen?
For Saudi Arabia, the most important effect may not be additional forces fighting inside Yemen but greater protection from attacks at home.
Maysaa Shuja al-Deen, a senior researcher at the Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies, said the Houthis were likely among the threats Saudi Arabia had in mind when the agreement was designed.
Saudi Arabia is "the more vulnerable member state in this alliance, security-wise", she told The New Arab.
The Houthis have developed increasingly sophisticated missile and drone capabilities with Iranian support, allowing the group to strike targets well beyond territory it controls in Yemen.
Shuja al-Deen said Saudi Arabia's size and extensive economic infrastructure make defending against such attacks particularly demanding.
"No, it will not change the military situation inside Yemen," she said of the immediate effect of Turkish and Pakistani support.
Rather, "it will make the Saudis less vulnerable" to Houthi attacks.
That could nevertheless affect the war.
Saudi Arabia remains the principal external supporter of the Yemeni government and other anti-Houthi forces. If Riyadh reduced that support, Shuja al-Deen said, those forces would be placed in "huge trouble".
Stronger Saudi defences against missiles and drones - and the possibility of renewed Houthi ground operations towards the Saudi border - could therefore allow Riyadh to sustain its support for anti-Houthi forces for longer.
"When they become stronger in that sense, they can continue to support these anti-Houthi camp forces," she said.
Shuja al-Deen also warned that the threat to Saudi Arabia may not remain confined to missiles and drones.
She believes Houthi preparations and rhetoric indicate the group could eventually attempt another ground incursion across the Saudi border, although she stressed that it was unclear when such an operation might take place.
"I think the Houthis... are going to invade or to expand through the Saudi territories at some point in this war," she said. "I'm not sure when, but it seems from their preparation and from their discourse and media that they are going to do something like that."
The assessment comes amid heightened military activity in the Houthi stronghold of Saada along the Saudi border, where weapons and equipment have been moved towards frontier areas in recent weeks.
That possibility further increases the importance of the territorial defence Pakistan can provide, while Turkish and Pakistani support against missiles and drones could make Saudi Arabia better able to withstand Houthi pressure.
Turkish drones and Pakistani military expertise could provide additional support, Shuja al-Deen added, but she did not expect large numbers of Turkish or Pakistani troops to enter Yemen.
"Yemenis have plenty of fighters on both sides," she said.
Are Turkey and Pakistan now part of the Yemen war?
Direct Turkish or Pakistani intervention against the Houthis could risk widening a conflict already entangled with the regional confrontation involving Iran.
Shuja al-Deen said she did not currently expect the Houthis to retaliate directly against either country. Turkey is geographically removed from Yemen, while Pakistan occupies a sensitive position in Iran's regional calculations and maintains an important relationship with Tehran.
"I don't think they are going to widen the conflict at this moment to that extent," she said.
Krieg similarly expects Pakistan to remain wary of offensive action against the Houthis because Islamabad has strong incentives to avoid confrontation with Iran.
Turkey, meanwhile, is attempting to strengthen Saudi Arabia's position without closing the door to diplomacy.
Krieg said Ankara's preferred outcome was not the military destruction of the Houthis but a stronger Saudi negotiating position that could eventually produce a settlement.
Is the alliance aimed at Iran?
When Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan established the pact, they sought to reassure Iran that it was not intended as an anti-Iranian military bloc.
Its first activation has now come amid a war involving the Houthis, an armed movement closely aligned with Tehran.
Shuja al-Deen said the members had been explicit from the beginning that Iran was not the target.
But "it seems now, very obviously, that the Yemen war is the first test for this agreement", she said.
Krieg also cautioned against viewing the alliance simply as an emerging Sunni bloc designed to confront Iran.
"Iran and the Houthis are the immediate catalyst, but they are not the fundamental explanation," he said.
Instead, he sees the alliance as part of a broader Saudi effort to reduce the risks of relying overwhelmingly on the United States for its security.
Riyadh continues to depend on Washington for advanced aircraft, intelligence, missile defence, logistics and other high-end military capabilities, and is not attempting to replace its US security relationship.
"In that sense, I think Mecca is best understood as a supplement to the US architecture rather than an alternative to it," Krieg said.
Saudi Arabia brings financial resources and political weight to the arrangement, while Turkey contributes technology and its growing defence industry and Pakistan offers manpower, established military institutions and strategic depth.
"The Houthis triggered its first activation, but the alliance is really about how Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan intend to operate in a regional order where American power remains important but American reliability can no longer be taken for granted," Krieg said.

articles.title: Ballistic Missiles Hit Kyiv Hours After Zelensky Warns Russia Is Preparing ‘Massive Strike’
articles.body:
Multiple explosions rocked Kyiv early Wednesday after Ukraine’s military warned that Russian ballistic missiles were heading toward the capital, with damage reported across several districts.
A Kyiv Post journalist in the capital reported several strong explosions after the Ukrainian Air Force warned that a ballistic missile was heading toward the city.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The attack came only hours after President Volodymyr Zelensky warned in his nightly address that Ukrainian intelligence had received updated information indicating Russia was preparing a “massive strike.” He urged residents to take missile alerts seriously and said Ukrainian forces were ready to respond “as much as our defenses allow.”
Ukraine’s Air Force also warned of ballistic missiles heading toward Zaporizhzhia and other cities, while military monitoring channels anticipated a broader combined attack involving ballistic and cruise missiles as well as fast-moving jet-powered drones.
Damage reported across Kyiv
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko and the Kyiv City Military Administration reported damage in several districts as the attack unfolded.
In the Obolonskyi district, a strike was recorded in an area of non-residential development.
In Podilskyi, warehouse facilities were hit and damaged.
In Darnytskyi, burning debris fell on an open area.
In the Shevchenkivskyi district, another strike hit a non-residential area.
Air defenses were operating over the capital as officials repeatedly urged residents to remain in shelters.
Zelensky Warns of Massive Russian Strike as 3 Tu-160 Bombers Take Off
Kyiv under mounting pressure
The latest attack comes as Kyiv faces an intensifying Russian air campaign approaching winter.
Russia has increasingly targeted Ukraine’s energy and transport infrastructure, including railways, roads and bridges over the Dnipro.
The capital has also endured repeated daytime and nighttime drone attacks in recent days, while air raid sirens have sounded for prolonged periods and forced residents into shelters, basements and metro stations.
Scheduled power cuts had already plunged parts of Kyiv into darkness Tuesday evening in an effort to reduce strain on the damaged electricity grid.
Warning came hours before attack
Zelensky said Tuesday evening that Ukrainian intelligence had fresh information about Russian preparations for a large-scale attack.
“There is updated intelligence regarding Russia’s preparations for a massive strike,” he said, urging Ukrainians to respond to missile alerts.
He also stressed that Ukraine’s ability to repel incoming missiles remained dependent on continued weapons deliveries from allies.
The warning was followed later Tuesday by reports that three Russian Tu-160 strategic bombers had taken off from the Belaya air base.
Ukraine’s Air Force subsequently issued ballistic missile warnings for Kyiv, Dnipro and Zaporizhzhia.
The latest overnight attack adds to growing pressure on Kyiv’s energy and transport networks as winter approaches, with Ukrainian authorities warning that Moscow is increasingly combining missiles and drones in an effort to overwhelm air defenses.

articles.title: Russia is out to break Ukraine’s economy this winter, Jetten says—and the Netherlands will help keep Ukraine’s drone-hunting F-16s in the air
articles.body:
The Netherlands will help Ukraine with maintenance, spare parts, and ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten promised in a statement on 5 October. He made this and other statements following a phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Russia attacks Ukrainian cities with drones every day, increasingly with jet-powered ones. F-16 fighter jets are one of the effective options for shooting down these UAVs, but Ukraine has far too few of them. The F-16s are used very frequently and therefore require maintenance. About half of the aircraft spend extended periods abroad undergoing repairs and maintenance, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Financial Times this month. The process of returning the aircraft has taken too long, and Ukraine has lost time when the jets were most needed to protect Ukrainian airspace, he said.
“A further strengthening of Ukraine’s air defense is literally vital,” the prime minister said.
Russia’s aggression continues to escalate, and F-16 fighter jets can help stop it
Russia is deliberately attacking civilian facilities and energy infrastructure and wants to make Ukrainian cities uninhabitable, Jetten said, adding that “we must not allow this to happen.”
One effective solution is the use of F-16 fighter jets, while Ukraine faces shortages of both these aircraft and the missiles for them.
Ukrainian F-16 pilots lack air-to-air missiles and take off with only the aircraft’s cannon during some daytime missions, the War Zone reported on 2 September. The M61A1 Vulcan 20mm rotary cannon can pose a danger to civilians on the ground, the outlet noted.
Poland promised to provide Ukraine with F-16 missiles back in September, and several partners, including Poland, have already begun the process of transferring ammunition this month. Other partners include Spain and Belgium, which Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha mentioned during a meeting with journalists, Hromadske reported on 1 October.
Ukraine critically needs this ammunition, especially as Russia prepares new strikes, Sybiha said.
“Against the backdrop of the fact that we have not yet built up the capability to repel jet-powered drones, against the backdrop of preparations for new strikes, it was critically important to help our military shoot down these drones. The most effective right now—apart from air defense systems, which are very expensive to use constantly against drones—are F-16 fighter jets,” the minister said.
Zelenskyy held talks with the president of France and the prime ministers of Poland and the Netherlands about means of protecting against Russian strikes, he said in his address on 5 October. In particular, he thanked the Dutch prime minister for his prompt response.
Whether Belgian maintenance delays are the reason for the low number of operational F-16s in Ukraine remains disputed
Fewer than 50% of the F-16s delivered to Ukraine may be operational, Defense Express reports, citing a Wall Street Journal (WSJ) editorial published on 29 September.
The Belgian company that services F-16s for Ukraine takes as long as 40 weeks to complete the work, retired US Navy Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery told the WSJ.

“Bridges remain the main supply arteries of the Russian army. Damaging them blocks the delivery of fuel, ammunition, and personnel,” ATESH said.

articles.title: Satellite images reveal renewed activity at nuclear site Israel struck in Iran
articles.body:
High-resolution satellite images from VANTOR Technologies taken in September and October 2026 showed significant renewed activity at Min-Zadayi, a nuclear weapons development complex in northeast Tehran that was exposed and attacked by Israel during Operation Roaring Lion. Several buildings, and apparently underground structures as well, were destroyed in the strike, according to a report published by the Institute for Science and International Security.
The latest satellite images indicated the return of regular vehicle traffic around the site following an extensive cleanup operation that included removing rubble and debris and repairing damage to the hillside. In one area struck in March 2026, ongoing earthworks can be seen. The work is taking place on a surface designed to resemble a courtyard, where numerous craters were visible after the attacks on the site.
A significant presence of vehicles was observed throughout the site between early September and early October 2026. Cars were parked outside the security fence in a lot, while numerous private vehicles and trucks were seen inside the compound. Given what is known about the site, this activity may indicate an Iranian effort to restore a nuclear weapons development capability and recover what was lost in the attack on the complex.
According to the institute’s report, based on public reporting and statements issued by the IDF, the nuclear weapons work carried out there likely included research and development of nuclear warheads. The IDF originally said that “a group of nuclear scientists operated covertly to develop a key component of the nuclear weapons program,” adding that “the complex was intended to enable the restoration of the required technology and the advancement of capabilities for developing nuclear weapons.”
The X account @IntelliTimes published additional information about the complex. In a post dated Sept. 24, 2026, it claimed that infrastructure related to nuclear weapons had been established in 2022 and “absorbed some of the means from the nuclear warehouse” — a common reference to the Turquzabad site, which was exposed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in September 2018.
Netanyahu disclosed the site after Iran removed more than a dozen shipping containers from it, which were believed to contain nuclear material and equipment relevant to Iran’s nuclear weapons capabilities.
When the International Atomic Energy Agency visited Turquzabad in March 2019, it found evidence that nuclear material or contaminated equipment had been present at the site. Since then, the IAEA Board of Governors has pressed Iran to answer the agency’s questions about the current location of that material or equipment.
According to @IntelliTimes, Iran did not simply transfer the material or equipment to a new long-term storage site. Instead, it used the Min-Zadayi site in northeast Tehran to establish “an industrial nuclear command center for restoring the research, development and adaptation infrastructure for nuclear warheads,” including the means “to produce cores of enriched uranium and the explosive material required to cast the initiation chain into them.”
During rounds of fighting with Iran, extensive strikes were carried out against nuclear targets in the country. In late June 2025, the United States led a massive strike using B-2 bombers and Tomahawk missiles that hit Iran’s three main nuclear sites — Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan.
Following the attack, Iran formally acknowledged heavy damage to its facilities in July 2025, while the IDF released satellite images and assessed that the operations had succeeded in setting the nuclear program back by years. At the same time, the Israeli Air Force destroyed significant components at the Isfahan facility, though Western intelligence officials cautioned that the bombers’ impact had been limited mainly to external structures and tunnel entrances.
Despite months of prolonged fighting, former senior officials and intelligence agencies warned that the strikes had damaged the program but had not eliminated it entirely. Professional assessments published in August 2026 showed that most of Iran’s stockpile of uranium enriched to 60% remained intact, and that the Iranian regime had moved thousands of advanced centrifuges to protected underground sites deep inside the mountains.
That reality led, as reported in September 2026, to an acceleration in U.S. preparations for additional targeted strikes aimed at preventing Iran from breaking out to a nuclear weapon.

articles.title: Lithuanian parliament backs removing constitutional ban on nuclear weapons
articles.body:
Lithuania’s parliament voted Tuesday to advance a constitutional amendment that would remove a ban on weapons of mass destruction from the country’s constitution, potentially opening the way for allied nuclear weapons to be stationed in Lithuania.
The amendment passed its first reading with 106 lawmakers voting in favour, 18 against and six abstaining.
A final vote cannot be held until at least three months after Tuesday’s vote. The amendment will require the support of at least 94 of the 141 members of the Seimas to pass. Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas has said the final vote is scheduled for January 12.
Olekas said before the vote that removing the ban would strengthen Lithuania’s resilience and deterrence capabilities.
He said eliminating the restriction would also remove a legal distinction between Lithuania and other European Union and NATO countries.
“We will ensure stronger support that could be available to us,” Olekas said. “By addressing the legal exceptions that Lithuania had compared with other EU and NATO countries, they will be gone and we will be equal.”
Opposition conservative leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas urged lawmakers to support the amendment, saying neighbouring countries do not have similar restrictions. He argued that the existing constitutional provision prevents NATO allies from fully including Lithuania in the alliance’s nuclear deterrence planning.
“With the current restriction, we cannot fully participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence plans,” Kasčiūnas said. “Since nuclear deterrence is the queen of deterrence as a whole, this decision is strategically important.”
Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas also stressed the importance of deterrence, saying politicians should provide the country with every available tool to ensure its security.
Kaunas said Lithuania is surrounded by countries with strategic weapons, pointing to Russia’s Kaliningrad region and Belarus. He described the proposed constitutional change as a response to Moscow’s actions.
“We are responding to Russia’s aggression,” Kaunas said. “If Russia had not started the war in Ukraine, we probably would not be having the discussions we are having today.”
Article 137 of Lithuania’s Constitution currently states that weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases may not be stationed on Lithuanian territory. The proposed amendment would remove that provision.
Opponents call for referendum
The amendment faced its strongest opposition from lawmakers in the opposition Nemunas Dawn party. Fourteen party members voted against it and two abstained.
Aidas Gedvilas of Nemunas Dawn said he was surprised that parliament considered itself empowered to make such a fundamental change and called for a referendum.
“There are certainly alternatives to this constitutional provision. We could resolve this through a referendum,” Gedvilas said.
Three members of the mixed parliamentary group and one lawmaker from the Farmers and Greens Union and Christian Families Alliance also voted against the amendment.
The debate comes amid broader discussions in Europe about strengthening nuclear deterrence. French President Emmanuel Macron presented an idea in March for a new European nuclear deterrence framework under which partner countries could temporarily host France’s nuclear-capable strategic air forces.
The Financial Times reported in June that the United States was considering deploying nuclear weapons in several additional NATO countries in Europe.
Lithuanian military analysts have said Russian media has taken an interest in Lithuania’s plans to remove the constitutional ban.
In early September, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov warned that Lithuania could become a target for Russia if it allowed allies to deploy nuclear weapons on its territory.
Reactions from Moscow
The Kremlin warned Tuesday that the deployment of nuclear weapons or a permanent US military base in Lithuania would constitute an escalation and force Russia to take measures to protect its security.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted by Russian state media.
“A military base is part of military infrastructure. If someone’s military infrastructure – in fact, that of a major NATO member – is approaching our borders, of course, this can only be viewed as a step toward escalation,” Peskov said at a news conference.
“The same applies to the deployment of nuclear weapons on the territory of a neighbouring country,” he added.
Peskov was asked how Moscow would respond if Lithuania moved to lift its constitutional ban on deploying nuclear weapons while the United States considered establishing a permanent base there.
“All this will not help ensure stability and predictability on the European continent,” Peskov said. “On the contrary, to our regret, it would be another very significant escalation.”
“As for Russia, of course, Russia will have to take all necessary measures to guarantee its security,” he said.
Lithuanian officials have stressed that there are currently no plans to deploy nuclear weapons in the country. They say removing the constitutional restriction is intended to ensure that Lithuania does not face legal obstacles to participating in NATO’s nuclear deterrence arrangements.

articles.title: Ukraine’s battlefield gains may be pushing Putin to shift focus to early winter strikes, ISW says

Ukraine's battlefield successes appear to be forcing Russian President Vladimir Putin to reevaluate his theory of victory and shift focus toward long-range strikes to compel Ukraine to surrender, rather than advances on the battlefield, the Institute for the Study of War said on 4 October.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia used more than 800 jet-powered drones during the week of 27 September to 4 October. Ukraine currently intercepts only 50–60% of jet-powered drones, leaving it vulnerable to the large number of new drones Russia is deploying.
The late-September start and the campaign's aim
ISW said Russian forces began their winter 2026–27 strike campaign against Ukraine's energy infrastructure in late September and that the campaign is aimed at making civilian life unbearable enough to force Ukraine to capitulate.
Russian forces would step up attacks on military facilities, defense industry sites, and related infrastructure in Kyiv and elsewhere in Ukraine, the Russian Defense Ministry said on 4 October, according to Reuters. The announcement followed Zelenskyy's vow to increase attacks on Russian oil refineries.
The ministry also claimed its recent strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions were a response to alleged Ukrainian attacks on civilian targets inside Russia. Among the grievances it named were Ukraine's strikes on Leningrad Oblast during the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum in June and alleged strikes on electoral infrastructure in Moscow during the 18–20 September State Duma elections, according to ISW.
ISW called the Russian Defense Ministry's framing of the recent strikes as retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian civilian targets unfounded, saying many of its specific claims are "blatantly false." Russia has provided no evidence that Ukraine targeted electoral infrastructure, and Ukraine's 19–20 September strikes on Moscow targeted oil refineries and warehouses, the think tank said. The Russian strikes "are not an actual response to specific events," it concluded.
The 135 drones, the bridges struck seven times
Overnight on 3–4 October, Russia launched 135 Shahed-type and Gerbera-type drones, while also using decoy drones and Banderol or Dan-T loitering munitions. Ukrainian forces downed 123 drones and two loitering munitions, and strikes hit five locations, according to ISW, which cited the Ukrainian Air Force. Russian forces struck Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges seven times between 1 and 4 October in an effort to disrupt Ukraine's economy and daily civilian life, ISW said.
Ukraine builds new layers of defense against jet drones
More than 12 .50-caliber machine-gun turrets are already working in Kyiv against jet-powered drones, and eight more will be installed in Kyiv Oblast, Zelenskyy said, Suspilne reported. He added that F-16s help a lot against the drones, according to Ukrinform. Ukraine is set to receive 2,000 Bars interceptor drones through joint production with Germany, RBC-Ukraine reported.
Ballistic missiles may be Russia's next wave
Zelenskyy said Ukraine estimates Russia has up to 700 ballistic missiles in reserve and produces 130–140 a month. He made the remarks at a joint media briefing with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv, Ukrinform reported. Russia is likely stockpiling ballistic and quasi-ballistic missiles for intense strikes after its jet-powered drones lose their current advantage, ISW assessed.
