articles.title: Iran’s next move could leave the Middle East looking for the bomb
articles.body:
Iran’s next move could leave the Middle East looking for the bomb
In Tehran, discussions about Iran’s potential withdrawal from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) are growing increasingly urgent. Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmail Baghaei has recently acknowledged that the issue is being seriously considered by Iranian officials. His statements lend significant political weight to the discourse around Iran’s potential withdrawal from the NPT: One can no longer downplay it as something proposed by hardliners or fringe groups. While Baghaei also reaffirmed Iran’s commitment to its membership in the NPT and the associated obligations, he made it clear that the possibility of exiting the treaty is being considered.
This situation has been triggered by Tehran’s mounting frustration. Iran finds it increasingly difficult to justify why participation in the NPT demands constant concessions from it, while the country’s rights remain negotiable. Despite Iran’s regular affirmation of the peaceful nature of its nuclear program, disputes persist and external pressure continues to mount. This gives Iran reason to question the practical value of the agreement. The Iranian leadership is signaling that its willingness to remain a member of the NPT cannot be viewed as unconditional.
The NPT was designed to maintain balance: Non-nuclear states refrain from developing nuclear weapons and receive international guarantees, while their right to the peaceful use of nuclear energy is recognized by the treaty; nuclear powers, meanwhile, pursue negotiations toward nuclear disarmament. For Tehran, the critical issue lies in the balance of rights and responsibilities. Iran’s right to peaceful nuclear technology does not exclude the international monitoring of its nuclear program. But there is a difference between inspections and demands to relinquish nuclear technologies, and Iran believes that this line is increasingly being blurred.
A pivotal aspect of the NPT is the so-called ‘nuclear deal’ signed in 2015. Iran agreed to impose significant limitations on its nuclear program and accepted extensive international oversight in exchange for relief from sanctions. In 2016, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) confirmed that Iran had implemented the necessary measures to put the agreement into effect. However, in 2018, the US withdrew from the deal and reinstated sanctions. This unfortunate experience casts a shadow on how Tehran views any potential future compromises. Iran accepted the restrictions, but the change in Washington’s policy undermined many of the anticipated benefits of the deal.
Strikes against Iran and its nuclear facilities have further compounded the crisis of trust, raising concerns over physical security. The IAEA reported attacks on several Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025; this shows that even with international guarantees, the facilities remain vulnerable. It’s true that the NPT does not offer military protection or immunity from attacks. However, the main problem for Iranian political circles is that the international oversight of Iran’s nuclear program has failed to ensure a diplomatic settlement of disagreements.
This raises a poignant question for Tehran. If cooperation with international institutions does not prevent sanctions and strikes against Iran, then what argument can the supporters of the treaty bring up in favor of remaining a party to the NPT? The treaty’s supporters outline its theoretical benefits, but the country assesses its results. As the costs of external pressure rise, it becomes increasingly hard to convince anyone that further concessions will enhance security. Instead, there’s a growing perception that new compromises simply lead to new demands. This sense of injustice largely explains Iran’s current irritation.
Another factor is the unequal standing of the countries in the region. Israel is not a party to the NPT and does not face the same comprehensive oversight that Iran does. While Tehran is constantly questioned about its nuclear program, no one raises concerns about Israel. This situation strikes Tehran as fundamentally unfair; its participation in the treaty imposes restrictions that Israel does not have to deal with. From Iran’s perspective, Israel, which is not bound by the treaty, enjoys greater freedom, while Iran’s membership comes with constraints and threats. Consequently, the treaty’s opponents have a strong argument in favor of withdrawing.
One cannot dismiss the fact that the IAEA has grounds to question Iran’s compliance. The IAEA faces multiple restrictions in Iran when it comes to inspections, nuclear material tracking, access to facilities, and so on. The Iranian Foreign Ministry emphasizes that it remains committed to the NPT and expects respect for its rights under the treaty, noting that disagreements with the IAEA should be resolved through dialogue and inspections, not through threats or attacks on Iranian facilities.
The heightened public attention to Iran’s potential exit from the NPT is also tied to ongoing negotiations. The prospect of Iran’s withdrawal raises the stakes for the US and increases the cost of failing to reach an agreement. As long as Iran remains a party to the NPT, there are legal grounds for international oversight and the possibility of engaging in meaningful discussions about its nuclear program. Exiting the treaty would complicate this process and increase uncertainty. Tehran is signaling that maintaining the current negotiations framework requires political effort. If this framework is systematically undermined, there are no guarantees that it will exist indefinitely.
At the same time, Iran is raising the stakes. As long as Iran’s opponents believe that it will remain in the NPT despite pressure, the threat of withdrawal can be dismissed as mere rhetoric. Baghaei’s statements make it clear that the option of leaving the NPT is being seriously considered by Iranian officials. However, Tehran is in no rush to actually exit the treaty. The Foreign Ministry has reaffirmed Iran’s existing obligations while leaving the final decision to the country’s leadership and Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.
By openly discussing the possibility of withdrawing from the NPT, Tehran can analyze the reaction of Russia, China, the EU, its neighbors in the region, and also its own populace. This will help assess the potential support for such a move and see whether other parties are willing to offer conditions that might persuade Iran to remain a party to the agreement. The Foreign Ministry’s statement is most likely driven by several factors, including a strategic calculation in negotiations, internal disagreements within the leadership, and a growing dissatisfaction with external pressure.
Moreover, Tehran understands that withdrawing from the NPT could further escalate tensions in the region. Türkiye and Saudi Arabia may believe that Iran is about to develop nuclear weapons, prompting them to consider their own nuclear capabilities. Their argument would be straightforward: If Iran no longer feels bound by the prohibition against acquiring nuclear weapons, why should its neighbors refrain from doing the same? Although withdrawing from the treaty doesn’t confer a legal right to nuclear arms, this detail could easily be overlooked in political debates. Tehran faces a serious risk: In its quest to enhance national security, it may inadvertently push its neighbors toward a nuclear arms race, and ultimately have to confront new threats. Therefore, we can neither be confident of Iran’s inevitable exit from the treaty nor reduce the situation to mere bluffing.
Iran’s reaction to Russia’s proposal regarding the export of its enriched uranium should be considered in this light. Baghaei confirmed that Tehran is considering Moscow’s offer and will act in accordance with its national interests. This keeps the door open for negotiations. Before taking such a step, Tehran seeks clarity on what it will gain in return and how this will affect its nuclear program moving forward. While Russia’s proposal could facilitate an agreement, Iran wants to be sure that the potential transfer of enriched uranium is accompanied by a genuine reduction in external pressure. Trust in Moscow plays an important part in this, but Iran needs assurances that all the other parties will uphold their end of the deal.
The main takeaway from the statement by the Iranian Foreign Ministry is that Iran no longer wishes to view its participation in the NPT as grounds for America’s endless, unfounded demands. Tehran insists on discussing its rights, the predictability of its partners’ commitments, and the potential for peaceful development. For now, this demand is articulated through diplomatic language, allowing room for negotiation. However, it is rooted in a profound crisis of trust. If the NPT continues to be perceived in Iran as a source of restrictions without practical benefits (an outlook that appears increasingly likely), then the arguments in favor of remaining a party to the treaty will become weaker. At some point, it may cease to be an issue that raises the stakes in negotiations and may become a matter requiring practical resolution.

articles.title: Russia’s Jet Drones Could Reach 900 Km/h, Air Force Warns
articles.body:
Russia could eventually increase the speed of its jet-powered attack drones to 800-900 kilometers per hour (500-560 mph), posing a growing challenge to Ukraine’s air defenses, a senior Air Force official has warned.
Deputy Air Force Commander Col. Yurii Cherevashenko made the assessment during a meeting of the Ukrainian parliament’s Temporary Investigative Commission on Tuesday, Oct. 6, according to Suspilne.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Current Russian jet-powered drones are said too fly at around 600 kilometers per hour (370 mph).
“We have not seen such [speeds] yet, but we forecast them,” Cherevashenko said, referring to the projected 800-900-kilometer-per-hour range.
Jet drones could make up 80% of attacks
Cherevashenko said Russia had rapidly increased its use of jet-powered attack drones since July.
They currently account for around 40% of the drones used against Ukraine, while on some operational axes their share has reached 60%, he said.
“We forecast that around 80% of the drones used in strikes will be jet-powered,” Cherevashenko added.
Ukraine previously recorded an eightfold increase in Russian jet-drone launches between June and August. The faster aircraft are more difficult for mobile fire groups and conventional propeller-driven interceptor drones to pursue.
Jet-powered drones can also reach their targets more quickly, reducing the time available for Ukrainian air defenses and civilians to respond to warnings.
Ukrainian companies race to build faster interceptors
The Air Force is currently working with around 20 Ukrainian companies developing high-speed interceptor drones.
Rubio Calls on Russia to Clarify Suspected Plague Case
According to Cherevashenko, 14 companies have begun test flights, six have achieved results in destroying jet-powered drones, and three have produced systems the Air Force considers particularly promising.
Two models have already passed military codification, including an interceptor called Predator, or “Khyzhak” in Ukrainian.
Existing interceptor models reach around 460-500 kilometers per hour (285-310 mph), while some manufacturers claim speeds of up to 700 kilometers per hour (435 mph).
Ukraine is also testing five high-speed interceptor models, with one expected to reach production of approximately 400 units by the end of October.
Cherevashenko said interceptor drones in the quantities required by the Air Force were not expected before the end of November.
F-16s remain among the most effective defenses
Ukraine is also using F-16 fighter jets to engage Russia’s high-speed drones.
“F-16s are among the most effective means of countering jet-powered UAVs [unmanned aerial vehicles],” Cherevashenko said. “Any aircraft has a limited service life, and we are using that resource at an exceptionally high rate.”
Maintaining the aircraft in constant readiness is therefore difficult and requires continued assistance from Ukraine’s partners, he added.
Kyiv is seeking large quantities of 20-millimeter ammunition for the F-16’s onboard cannon, which offers a cheaper alternative to using scarce AIM-9 and AIM-120 air-to-air missiles against drones.
Cherevashenko said another key method was destroying the drones before launch by striking their bases, known as droneports.
Several such facilities have already been hit, he said, although many are heavily fortified with concrete and remain difficult to destroy.

articles.title: Karaganov: Russia can win a nuclear war in Europe
articles.body:
Karaganov: Russia must be prepared to use nuclear weapons
The debate on the use of nuclear weapons has moved into the practical realm, so while NATO is discussing the Russian Foreign Ministry’s warning of a full-spectrum response in the event of an attempt to blockade Kaliningrad Region, Russian experts are discussing nuclear deterrence and President Vladimir Putin’s speech at the Valdai Forum last week.
Russia must be prepared to use nuclear weapons in cases of extreme necessity.
Responding to questions about nuclear weapons, Putin recalled the saying that if a gun is hanging on the wall, it will eventually go off, but the Russian leader called for such a scenario to be avoided.
“At the heart of this escalation lie arrogance and overconfidence. This is a path to the brink of the abyss. All the more so today, when the arsenals of the world’s leading powers contain weapons capable of destroying all life or, at the very least, reducing the Earth to a catastrophic state. We are all familiar with the well-known saying: if a gun is hanging on a wall somewhere on stage at the beginning of a play, it is bound to go off eventually. We must bear this in mind,” said the president.
As Putin emphasized, Russia understands that in the event of a direct attack by NATO countries, “the enemy will be twice as numerous and have far greater economic potential” and Russia’s competitive advantage lies in the fact that no one else in the world possesses such weapons of destruction, he noted.
“How can we stand up to an aggressor? We are not a threat to anyone. We are simply saying that we do not have all that many means of defending ourselves. We will have to use our competitive advantages in this struggle,” concluded Putin.
Why do we need nuclear weapons?
Tensions and conflicts between countries are on the rise worldwide and the West, particularly the EU, having suffered a strategic defeat, is desperate for revenge. Nuclear weapons are necessary to prevent major wars, but this only works if the threat is taken seriously, and at present far too many people have forgotten what a nuclear war entails, so they treat the matter lightly.
Many, particularly Western European politicians, want war; they are actively whipping up military hysteria in their own countries. For the time being, they are acting through the Ukrainians, but they have also begun actively stirring up their own populations.
The Western European elites must be punished for their aggressive policies, meaning Ukraine must be crushed and demilitarized, while the purely Russian regions must be reunited with Russia and an EU that has lost its mind must begin to truly fear.
Without the active use of nuclear deterrence, this can’t be achieved. Now, I hope it will never come to that, but Russia must be prepared, in the event of absolute necessity, to use nuclear weapons effectively and victoriously.
How effective is nuclear deterrence?
Nuclear deterrence has weakened considerably. First, decades have passed not only since the US first used nuclear weapons in combat against Japan, but also since the last known tests. Secondly, the Americans have for a long time deliberately downplayed the role of nuclear weapons in order to emphasize their advantages in other areas of armaments.
Furthermore, people’s mindsets and public sentiment have changed, given that we, the older generation, particularly in Russia, are more acutely aware of the threat of nuclear war, and of war in general, and have therefore been seriously committed to the cause of peace. In the past, it was almost considered improper even to speak of the possible use of nuclear weapons.
Now circumstances have changed significantly and that’s precisely why we need to step up nuclear deterrence and intimidation to the point of being genuinely prepared, God forbid, to use nuclear weapons to prevent a larger-scale war.
Seeking peace through non-nuclear means alone could prove far too costly for Russia and it would be a shame to sacrifice the health and lives of our men simply to quell the aggression of those same Western Europeans.
What would be the consequences of using nuclear weapons?
The reaction of the international community would have to be disregarded because it makes absolutely no difference what the rest of the world thinks or says.
Nevertheless, it would pose a huge moral problem, as the use of nuclear weapons is a grave sin, but, unfortunately, there is very little hope that these Europeans will come to their senses without coming face to face with the threat of nuclear annihilation.
If we refuse to use nuclear weapons, as many are calling for, including here in our own country, we will deprive ourselves and the world of the most effective tool for preventing war and give aggressors free rein, but they can only be restrained by the threat of their use.
If nuclear weapons were used, there would be other negative consequences as even a limited and effective nuclear war would remove the taboo on other countries using nuclear weapons in their own regional conflicts, so I therefore continue to regard such use as a last resort.
Why is the European Union preparing for war with Russia?
There are two reasons for the aggressive anti-Russian sentiment in the EU. First, Western European elites have deteriorated significantly during the period of relative peace in the second half of the 20th century, although we hope that not all of them are complete madmen.
And secondly, they are trying to stir up military hysteria in order to distract their peoples from widespread failures and thereby retain power.
Under these circumstances, it would be sensible and rational for us to strengthen our reliance on nuclear weapons and modernize our arsenal, particularly the part of it aimed at other European countries. At the same time, it is important to continue dialogue with the US in order to avoid a global nuclear conflict.
Nuclear weapons have safeguarded us for 80 years since the end of the Second World War. Nuclear deterrence is the main reason why, throughout these decades, the states of Europe, and subsequently the European Union, have remained relatively peaceful. Throughout their history, they have repeatedly attacked not only Russia but also a vast number of countries across the globe, and they are the primary cause of many of humanity’s misfortunes, such as racism and colonialism.
Western Europe is now returning to its usual state, which is a belligerent one and this means the time has come to remind these Europeans once again who they are and what their belligerence leads to. If the current Ukrainian or German regime, or any other non-nuclear country in Europe, were to acquire nuclear weapons, we would be obliged to launch a preemptive strike because we’d have to stop them. It would be a short war, as a result of which these countries would cease to exist.
Is it possible to win a nuclear war?
It’s possible to win a nuclear war in Europe because the US will never risk its own territory for the sake of the Europeans. If France or the UK continue to stick their necks out, a preemptive, devastating strike could be launched against them. But, I repeat, God forbid.
I hope Western Europe comes to its senses and that this can be avoided. In the meantime, much of Europe should be placed behind a security cordon and a security system should be built within the framework of Greater Eurasia, excluding the Western subcontinent. That said, it will be possible and necessary to cooperate with individual European countries if they shake off the rule of the current madmen in Brussels and Berlin.
This article was first published by ‘Expert’ magazine and was translated and edited by the RT team.

articles.title: UK Tory leader defends 'Israel-inspired' missile system proposal
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Conservative leader Badenoch defends 'Britannia Shield' missile system plan
The leader of the UK's Conservative Party has denied that her party’s proposed £10 billion 'Britannia Shield' air and missile defence system would replicate Israel’s Iron Dome, while arguing that Britain needs greater protection against aerial threats.
The Conservatives announced the proposal on Monday, with The Sun describing it as an "Iron Dome" for Britain. The party said Britannia Shield would be a new integrated air and missile defence system designed to protect the UK from aerial threats.
But speaking to Times Radio and BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Tuesday, Kemi Badenoch denied that the Conservatives were proposing to build a British version of Israel’s system, despite the party’s own press release describing Britannia Shield as "in essence a British Iron Dome".
Badenoch said the proposed system would instead be tailored to the threats facing Britain.
"We are designing something specific for the kind of threat that we face here," she said, adding that the Conservatives had used the name Britannia Shield to make clear that the proposal was a British system rather than a replication of Israel’s.
But the proposal has raised questions over what kind of threats such a system would need to address, how effective it could be and whether £10 billion would be enough to deliver it.
Israel operates a multi-layered air defence network consisting of systems including Iron Dome, David’s Sling, the Arrow family and the newer Iron Beam laser system. Each is designed to address different types and ranges of airborne threats. Iron Dome is designed primarily to intercept short-range rockets, while Iron Beam is intended to supplement Israel’s existing air-defence capabilities.
Badenoch said Britain would need a system designed around the changing nature of warfare, particularly the increasing use of drones.
"There’s a new type of warfare; drone warfare requires different kind of air and missile defence," she told BBC Radio 4.
She gave the example of drones or missiles being launched from vessels close to the English Channel and targeting critical national infrastructure.
What would Britannia Shield defend against?
Sam Cranny-Evans, a defence analyst and consultant and an Associate Fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told The New Arab the threats Britain could face included Russian cruise missiles, one-way attack drones and ballistic missiles.
However, he said many Russian weapons would have to travel over European territory to reach the UK, meaning cruise missiles and drones launched from the high north or from submarines in the Atlantic could represent a more credible threat.
The UK already has several elements of an air and missile defence network, Cranny-Evans said, including the Sky Sabre medium-range ground-based air defence system, Typhoon fighter aircraft equipped with air-to-air missiles and Type 45 destroyers.
The Type 45s provide the UK’s only ballistic missile defence capability, although Cranny-Evans said this was currently underpowered and future missile integration would improve it.
"The main gaps really are scale - not enough launchers or missiles for a big attack," he said.
The proposal comes amid heightened tensions between London and Moscow, with Russia repeatedly warning of "consequences" over Britain’s military support for Ukraine.
While there is no indication of an imminent Russian attack on the UK, the repeated threats form part of a broader security environment in which Britain is increasingly being confronted by hostile rhetoric and activity from Moscow.
How realistic is a £10 billion system?
Badenoch said the Conservatives would spend £10 billion on the system - £1 billion a year over 10 years - with the money coming from savings identified by the party.
But the proposal has already prompted questions over whether such funding would be sufficient for a nationwide air and missile defence network.
Cranny-Evans said comparing Britannia Shield directly with Israel’s Iron Dome was unhelpful because Iron Dome is only one part of Israel’s wider integrated air defence network and is primarily designed to intercept rockets and drones.
He said developing a wider layered air defence network for the UK was possible, but the opportunity cost would be significant.
"It is possible but the opportunity costs would be huge for very marginal benefit," he said.
"£10 billion would be much better spent on properly arming the RAF and Royal Navy, and ensuring the Army is ready to fight".
Cranny-Evans also warned that the cost of an air defence system was not simply a question of buying launchers and radar.
"The issue with air defence is always the interceptors," he said.
"If you spend billions on launchers and radars but don't buy enough missiles to fire from them, then there's no point having the launchers".
He pointed to the PAC-3 MSE interceptor as an example, saying each missile can cost around $4-6 million, while a credible air defence system would require substantial stocks of interceptors.
The more capable the missiles you want to defend against, the more you have to spend on the interceptors," he said.
Could Israel play a role?
Israel’s extensive experience with integrated air and missile defence has also raised questions over whether Israeli technology or expertise could feature in a future British system.
But Cranny-Evans said Israeli involvement in Britannia Shield was unlikely.
"MBDA has all of the capabilities that the Israeli companies could provide and good chunks of what they produce are made in the UK," he said.
"Lockheed Martin would probably be the next most obvious choice."
The comments suggest that while Israel’s experience could provide a reference point for Britain, the UK would have domestic and international defence companies capable of providing much of the technology required.
Relations between both countries also took a hit last month after the UK-led Western sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, prompting Israel to close the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem.
Badenoch has said Britannia Shield would be designed to protect critical national infrastructure, military facilities and overseas territories, including Cyprus and the Falkland Islands.
The UK maintains two sovereign base areas in Cyprus, including RAF Akrotiri, which was hit by an Iranian-made drone in March days after the US and Israel launched their war on Iran.
Asked how the system would be funded, Badenoch said the party had already identified savings, including welfare cuts. These include reinstating the two-child benefit cap and restricting allowances for local housing.
She said tax cuts would not be introduced until there was enough money to fund the defence programme.
"We know that difficult choices have to be made," she said.
Badenoch is expected to address the final day of the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham on Wednesday.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russia strikes civilian vessels in Black Sea off Bulgaria's coast
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Russia strikes civilian vessels in Black Sea off Bulgaria's coast
Key developments on Oct. 6:
- Drones strike merchant vessels in Black Sea off Bulgaria and Ukraine, killing at least one
- Russian losses to Ukrainian drones surge in early October, Madyar says
- Despite intensified Russian attacks, 62% of Ukrainians ready to endure war as long as needed, poll finds
- Shadow fleet tanker reportedly ablaze near Russian port city Sochi
- Klitschko's promise of 50 mobile shelters for Kyiv set to fall far short
- Poland to deploy Patriots near Ukrainian border, announces $26 billion civil defense plan
Drones struck several merchant vessels in the Black Sea on Oct. 6, including two ships in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. A Russian strike on a separate civilian vessel killed at least one crew member and injured several others.
One crew member, a steward, was killed, and seven others were injured when a Russian drone struck a merchant vessel flying the Marshall Islands flag in the Black Sea, according to Odesa Oblast Governor Oleh Kiper. The vessel was carrying rapeseed oil and was damaged in the strike, with a fire breaking out in the superstructure.
"By deliberately targeting civilian shipping and port infrastructure, Russia is grossly violating the norms of international law, thereby posing a threat to global food security," Kiper said.
Separately, two merchant ships, the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan and the Palau-flagged Able, were hit by drones of unknown origin about 112 kilometers (70 miles) off Bulgaria's coast on Oct. 6, according to Bulgarian broadcaster Nova. The incident is believed to be the first reported drone attack on commercial shipping inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said in the evening that Ukrainian forces did not conduct operations in this area of the Black Sea. He said that Ukraine verified the details with Bulgaria and concluded it was a Russian attack, calling it a combined attack with sea and air drones.
The Togo-flagged vessel suffered severe structural damage and sank. The fate of its crew remains unknown, with the search for survivors continuing. NOVA reported that life jackets had been spotted near the vessel, but no people had been found.
The second vessel caught fire following the attack. All 18 crew members were rescued by a Bulgarian ferry. Two sailors were seriously injured, one with severe burns, the other with a head injury. The crew members are Indian and Turkish nationals, according to Nova.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev convened an emergency meeting with representatives of state institutions following the attacks. He described the attacks as a "gross violation of international law" and warned that such attacks pose growing risks to Black Sea shipping, increase insurance costs, and further complicate maritime transport.
read also
Russian losses to Ukrainian drones surge in early October, Madyar says
Russian casualties attributed to Ukrainian drone strikes rose sharply during the first five days of October compared with the same period in August and September, Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, known by his callsign "Madyar," said on Oct. 6.
Between Oct. 1 and Oct. 5, Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces recorded 2,699 Russian troops killed or wounded, compared with 1,931 during the same period in September, Brovdi said in a Telegram post. The figure represents a 39.7% increase, according to Brovdi.
Compared with the first five days of August, the reported number of Russian casualties was 76.5% higher, rising from 1,529 to 2,699.
The largest increase was recorded in the area of responsibility of the Ukrainian National Guard's 1st "Azov" Corps, covering the Dobropillia-Pokrovsk sector in Donetsk Oblast, according to Brovdi.
krainian drone operators recorded 1,268 Russian troops killed or wounded in that area during the first five days of October, compared with 884 in the same period in September — a 43% increase. The figure was almost twice as high as the 664 casualties recorded during the first five days of August, representing a 91% increase, Brovdi said.
The figures cited by Brovdi cover only casualties attributed to Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces and do not include casualties from other Ukrainian military units.
Ukraine's General Staff said on Oct. 1 that Russian forces suffered an estimated 46,230 personnel losses in September, the highest monthly figure recorded by Ukraine so far in 2026.
Ukraine has increasingly relied on drones to inflict casualties and disrupt Russian operations along the front line.
read also
Despite intensified Russian attacks, 62% of Ukrainians ready to endure war as long as needed, poll finds
Some 62% of Ukrainians are ready to endure Russia's war for as long as necessary, according to a Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) poll published Oct. 6.
The share has remained largely unchanged since late July and early August, despite the beginning of intensified Russian attacks using jet-powered drones and strikes on civilian infrastructure during the survey period. KIIS said the results show that the attacks had not led to a decline in Ukrainians' willingness to endure the war as of Sept. 21.
Another 4% of respondents said they were ready to endure the war for about a year, while 23% said they could continue for only several months or up to six months.
The remaining 11% were undecided.
"Despite the intensification of Russian terror against the civilian population — and the fact that our Western partners' response has not always been sufficiently decisive or backed by concrete actions — Ukrainians are prepared to continue bearing the burden of war until an acceptable peace is achieved," KIIS Executive Director Anton Grushetskyi said.
The survey was conducted from Sept. 12-21, when Russia had begun a new campaign of attacks involving jet-powered drones and strikes on civilian infrastructure. KIIS noted that the survey was completed before subsequent attacks on bridges across the Dnipro River.
The findings also show that 79% of Ukrainians believe Ukraine will ultimately win the war, including 47% who are certain of victory and 32% who said they rather believe Ukraine will prevail. Only 7% believe Russia will win, while 14% were undecided.
However, confidence in an eventual Ukrainian victory has declined since late July. At that time, 85% said they believed Ukraine would win, including 60% who were certain of it.
The poll was conducted through computer-assisted telephone interviews with 1,002 adults across all regions of Ukraine controlled by the government.
read also
Shadow fleet tanker reportedly ablaze near Russian port city Sochi
A ship is burning on the Black Sea near the Russian port city of Sochi, Russian independent media Novaya Gazeta Europe reported on Oct. 6, citing Russian Telegram channels.
The ship might have been attacked by naval drones, Novaya Gazeta Europe said, while Russian authorities have not commented on the incident. Meanwhile, fire and thick black smoke can be seen above the city in videos published on social media.
Russian Telegram channels said that the vessel in question might be the Liberia-flagged tanker Aframax Rea. The online marine traffic data provider MarineTraffic last located the ship 23 hours ago on the Black Sea near the border between Russia and Georgia, close to Nizhneimeretinskaya Bay.
The vessel is a large crude oil tanker and was included on Ukraine's sanctions list as part of Russia's shadow fleet on Feb. 12, 2026.
Sochi has increasingly come under Ukrainian drone attacks over the past year, with strikes on its port and an oil depot reported in September alone. The city is around 650-700 kilometers (400-435 miles) from the Ukrainian border in Russia's Krasnodar Krai region.
read also
Klitschko's promise of 50 mobile shelters for Kyiv set to fall far short
Kyiv City Mayor Vitali Klitschko's September promise that the capital will receive "40 to 50" mobile shelters "within a month" is set to fall short after it was revealed on Oct. 6 that only 14 will arrive by the end of the year.
"We have already purchased shelters and within a month, the first batch, roughly, as far as I remember, 40 or 50 units, will be set up at transport stops where there are no stationary shelters nearby. And we are continuing this program," Klitschko said on Sept. 12.
But the Kyiv City State Administration (KMDA) told media portal Slidstvo.info on Oct. 6 that far fewer will arrive on a far longer timescale, despite Klitschko saying some had already been purchased.
Currently, only four mobile shelters operate in the city, installed by private organizations, according to Slidstvo.info. Meanwhile, KMDA's press service told the media portal that the city required at least 620 mobile shelters and 7,894 conventional ones.
The municipal transport company Kyivpastrans is supposed to buy the 14 mobile shelters after its new financial plan is approved, Slidstvo.info reports. The new shelters will be placed at Kyivpastrans branches and at the final stops of public transport lines.
The estimated costs are around Hr 54.2 million (about $1.2 million) in total, including VAT, while a single shelter for 50 people costs about Hr 4.8 million (about $107,000), Slidstvo.info said. The city's budget for public safety and civil protection for 2027 to 2029 sits at Hr 300 million.
According to the city administration, the capital's several district administrations did not request funding for mobile shelters when the city budget was drafted, and the city itself did not buy any shelters, Slidstvo.info said.
read also
Poland to deploy Patriots near Ukrainian border, announces $26 billion civil defense plan
Poland will station Patriot air defense batteries in its Lublin region, bordering Ukraine, Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz announced on Oct. 5, according to Polish Radio. The same day, Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced his government will adopt a civil defense program worth 102.4 billion zlotys ($26.4 billion).
Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Patriot batteries are meant to reassure the residents of the Lublin region and protect Lublin airport and its air traffic, Polish Radio reported. Amid rising tensions between Russia and Poland, Russia has repeatedly violated Polish airspace.
The defense minister also announced that new military formations, including unmanned systems forces, will be created in the region, Polish Radio said.
Tusk announced his government will adopt a draft resolution for the Population Protection and Civil Defence Programme for 2027-2031, Polish state news agency Pap wrote.
"Five years of full funding for the program, we are talking about very large sums guaranteed for the protection of civilians and civil defense. It will be mainly investments," Tusk said.
While previous programs only paid for emergency purchases such as generators, local governments had pushed for a longer, better-funded program, Tusk said.
The money will be spent on shelters, equipment, rescue bases, stockpiles, and securing water and energy supplies during natural disasters and wartime, the prime minister said. Additionally, funding will go toward warning systems and ICT security, Tusk said. Of this money, 30 billion zlotys (about $7.7 billion) will be allocated to the regional authorities, according to him.

articles.title: Turkey and Pakistan Preparing to Deploy Troops in Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan have agreed to move toward the practical implementation of their collective defense commitments and to prepare for the deployment of coordinated military forces and capabilities on Saudi Arabian territory.
This is stated in a joint statement following an emergency meeting of the Strategic Political and Defense Committee of the Mecca Defense Alliance.
The meeting was convened amid a deteriorating security situation around Saudi Arabia and a series of Houthi attacks on the kingdom’s territory.
Following the meeting, the parties decided to “immediately proceed with the practical implementation of collective defense commitments,” ensure the allocation of agreed-upon military forces and assets, and create the conditions for their rapid deployment in Saudi Arabia.
At this time, the specific number of troops, the composition of the units, their weaponry, or the timeline for their deployment have not been disclosed. It is noted only that the deployment will take place in accordance with agreed-upon mechanisms and the national legislation of the three states.
The parties separately reaffirmed the principle that the security of each of the three states is inseparable from the collective security of the entire alliance.
Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan signed the Mecca Agreement on Collective Defense on August 7, 2026. It stipulates that an armed attack on one of the participating states will be considered an attack on all of them.
Since signing the pact, the allies have not yet demonstrated an operational response to the first Houthi attacks — in particular, following the strike on the Saudi Aramco oil refinery in Jazan.
At a meeting on October 5, the allies also took another step toward establishing a permanent organizational structure. Retired Pakistani Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood was appointed as the first secretary-general of the Mecca Defense Alliance; he will serve in this position for three years.
The establishment of the secretariat had already been planned following the results of the first meeting of the Strategic Political and Defense Committee, which took place on August 31 in Istanbul. At that time, the parties agreed to locate the permanent secretariat in Saudi Arabia and determined that the first secretary-general would be a representative of Pakistan.
They also announced their intention to develop joint military capabilities, defense industry cooperation, joint technology development, and weapons production.
On September 25, the foreign ministers of the three countries, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, had already discussed the establishment of the alliance’s secretariat, committees, and working groups. At that time, they also agreed to hold urgent consultations among the chiefs of staff regarding possible assistance to Saudi Arabia.
In a joint statement on October 5, Turkey, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia condemned attempts to attack Mecca and Medina, as well as strikes on the kingdom’s cities, civilian targets, and economic infrastructure.
Amid an escalation of Houthi missile and drone strikes in September, Turkey announced its readiness to provide Saudi Arabia with military support in specific technical areas. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan emphasized at the time that the three countries already have allied obligations under the Mecca Agreement.
At the same time, Riyadh is receiving military aid from outside the trilateral alliance — the United Kingdom sent an RAF Voyager refueling aircraft to Saudi Arabia to refuel Saudi fighter jets during operations to repel Houthi attacks.
France has also announced the deployment of military personnel and air defense systems to Saudi Arabia to protect the area around the port of Yanbu.
In August, Saudi Arabia led a naval coalition of 14 countries formed to counter the Houthi blockade and protect shipping in the Red Sea and adjacent straits. The coalition included, among others, Turkey and Pakistan.

France Prepares First Submarine-Launched Nuclear-Capable Missile Test in Three Years
France is preparing its first submarine-launched ballistic missile test in three years, with the nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine Le Vigilant expected to fire the new M51.3 during a long-range trial over the Atlantic, according to French outlet Ouest-France on October 5.
Strategic weapons analyst Étienne Marcuz said the missile is expected to travel roughly 4,700 kilometers, or about 2,920 miles, although that distance is well below the weapon’s estimated maximum range.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The M51.3 will be launched without a nuclear warhead from waters off France’s Finistère coast, where maritime restrictions have already been imposed through October 21.
The test comes after Le Vigilant completed an extensive maintenance period that began in fall 2023 at France’s Île Longue strategic submarine base.
The overhaul included work on the vessel’s nuclear reactor, weapons systems, and other critical equipment. French ballistic missile submarines typically undergo sea trials after such major maintenance, with an M51 launch serving as one of the most important checks that the submarine’s strategic weapons complex is fully operational.
A similar test was carried out by Le Terrible in April 2023 following its own major refit. This time, however, France will be testing the newest operational version of its sea-based deterrent missile.
The M51.3 officially entered operational service in October 2025. Compared with earlier versions, the new variant is reported to offer improved range, greater accuracy, and better ability to penetrate missile defenses. It is also designed to carry France’s new TNO-2 nuclear warhead.
France conducted the first qualification launch of the M51.3 in November 2023 from a land-based test facility at Biscarrosse. That missile was also unarmed and flew toward the Atlantic Ocean.
The M51.3 is a three-stage, solid-fueled submarine-launched ballistic missile developed as the latest evolution of France’s M51 family. Paris does not disclose its exact performance, but earlier M51 versions have been estimated to reach approximately 8,000 to 10,000 kilometers, or roughly 5,000 to 6,200 miles, at speeds of up to Mach 25.
Previous M51.1 and M51.2 missiles could carry multiple thermonuclear warheads with individual yields estimated at roughly 110 to 300 kilotons. The M51.3 is believed to retain broadly similar dimensions to its predecessors, measuring around 12 meters long, 2.3 meters in diameter, and weighing roughly 52 metric tons.
The missile is also expected to become the primary strategic weapon of France’s future SNLE 3G ballistic missile submarines, which are scheduled to begin replacing the current Le Triomphant-class fleet after 2035. ArianeGroup develops and manufactures the M51 family.
Earlier, France’s Air and Space Force has rehearsed one of the country’s most consequential military missions: breaking through hostile defenses and delivering a nuclear-armed missile to a precise launch point using Rafale fighters.

articles.title: Ukraine’s war leadership sets new electronic warfare tasks as Russia’s jet-powered drones slip past nearly half of its air defenses
articles.body:
Russia keeps upgrading its jet-powered drones, and Ukraine's electronic warfare is racing to keep up. Kyiv has set extra tasks for its military and manufacturers to scale up the most effective electronic warfare approaches, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after a meeting of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief's Staff on electronic warfare and infrastructure protection.
Russia keeps modifying its jet-powered Shaheds to beat each new Ukrainian defense, and Ukraine's answers have to keep pace. The race is tight: from 1 to 26 September, air defenses downed only 55 percent of the 2,730 new jet-powered drones, against 90% of the slower ones.
Hidden relays blunt Kyiv's jammers
Jamming has to improve because Russia keeps finding new ways around it. On 3 October, presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said someone had installed Russian MESH radio repeaters in Kyiv, a short control channel that guides Shahed drones onto their targets. As long as they are there, he said, closing the city with electronic warfare will not be effective.
"As long as online control of drones exists, not only the bridges but the air defense assets will be under threat," Flash stressed.
Sanctions aim at the supply chain
Beyond the jamming task, the Staff turned to where Russia gets the parts for those drones. Defense Intelligence reported on Russia's technological priorities for this year and next, and on supplies of critical components and equipment for its weapons production, Zelenskyy said.
New sanctions packages will follow, with Defense Intelligence due to send proposals to the Ukrainian government and the National Security and Defense Council, and Ukraine is working to align its sanctions with partners' jurisdictions.
The Staff also set the main tasks for supplying Ukrainian forces with long-range drones next year.
"The main criterion is that we must be able to respond in kind to Russian strikes," Zelenskyy emphasized.
Those parts, and the drones built from them, keep changing
In August, Intelligence Deputy Chief Vadym Skibitskyi said Russia remained fully dependent on Chinese turbojets for the Geran-4 and Geran-5, each costing about $35,000 to $40,000.
However, two months later, Ukraine reported the Geran-4 had received a locally built engine and a new optical navigation system. Kyiv has to stay attuned to changes to keep pace with the technology race, and so far, it is still trying to catch up rather than get ahead.

Sweden will deploy its JAS 39 Gripen fighter jets to Poland to reinforce NATO’s eastern flank.
The fighter jets will primarily be based at and operate from airfields in Sweden, while a small forward detachment will be stationed in Poland to provide technical and operational support for the flights.

articles.title: Russia’s neighbor backs push to lift ban on nuclear weapons, prompting outcry from Moscow
articles.body:
The Kremlin on Tuesday warned a preliminary decision by Lithuanian lawmakers to lift a constitutional ban on hosting nuclear weapons and the potential deployment of a NATO military base in the country will mark "another significant escalation" of regional tensions.
The comments come shortly after Lithuania's parliament voted in favor of advancing a constitutional change on deploying nuclear weapons on its territory. It is the first of two ballots required for the change, with the latter scheduled for Jan. 12 next year.
The country, which is a member of both the European Union and NATO and shares a border with Russia's Kaliningrad exclave on the Baltic Sea, has been looking to remove the constitutional ban to strengthen its resilience amid growing security concerns.
Lithuania has been one of Ukraine's staunchest allies during Russian President Vladimir Putin's more than 4½-year conflict with Kyiv, providing extensive military equipment and financial support.
President Donald Trump, meanwhile, said he would consider Lithuania's request for a permanent U.S. military base in the country. "They are friends of mine. They are great people, so we will certainly look at it," Trump said Monday.
Asked about the developments, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that they "cannot be perceived as anything other than a step toward escalating tensions, just as the deployment of nuclear weapons in a neighboring country cannot," according to Russian state news agency Tass.
"Neither of these developments will contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent. On the contrary, they will, to our regret, mark yet another significant escalation of tensions. As for Russia, of course, Moscow will be forced to take all necessary measures to guarantee its own security," Peskov said.
Article 137 of Lithuania's constitution explicitly prohibits the deployment of weapons of mass destruction and the establishment of foreign military bases on Lithuanian territory. The proposed amendment, which will require the support of at least 94 of the 141 members of parliament to pass, would remove that provision.
Lithuanian Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said scrapping the restriction would bolster the country's resilience and remove a legal distinction between Lithuania and other EU and NATO countries.
"We will ensure stronger support that could be available to us," Olekas said, according to state broadcaster LRT.
"By addressing the legal exceptions that Lithuania had compared with other EU and NATO countries, they will be gone and we will be equal," he added.

articles.title: Ukraine Claims Record Barrage on Russia With 1,750 Drones, 17 Flamingo Missiles
articles.body:
Ukraine launched a record-breaking number of drones and missiles at targets across Russia over the past 24 hours on Tuesday, according to Russia’s defense ministry.
Russian air defenses claimed to have intercepted and destroyed 1,750 fixed-wing drones and 17 Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missiles, as well as two guided aerial bombs and a US-made HIMARS rocket.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The reported drone total exceeds the previous record of 1,671 Ukrainian drones claimed by Russia on Aug. 18, when attacks were reported across 15 Russian regions, occupied Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas.
The number of Flamingo missiles reported over the 24-hour period is also unprecedented. Russia had previously claimed to intercept no more than three to six Flamingos in a single day.
The figures have not been independently verified.
Moscow among the main targets
The record-breaking barrage included repeated attacks on Moscow and the surrounding region.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 650 drones were heading toward the capital early on Oct. 6, with 105 destroyed as they approached the city. He later reported another 68 drones intercepted by air defenses.
Moscow Region Governor Andrei Vorobyov said 185 drones were destroyed across 16 municipalities.
According to Vorobyov, two people were killed and nine injured. Forty-seven private homes were damaged in several towns, while an apartment building in Lobanovo, near Domodedovo, was also hit.
Major oil facility targeted
Among the reported targets was the Volodarskaya Linear Production and Dispatch Station, a major Transneft facility and one of the Moscow region’s key fuel-storage and distribution hubs.
Power Cuts Return After Russian Strikes Damage Grid
The facility handles up to 3 million metric tons of petroleum products annually, including gasoline, jet fuel and diesel supplied from the Moscow and Ryazan refineries. Some of the fuel is delivered to airports serving the Moscow aviation hub.
The extent of any damage to the facility was not immediately clear.
The scale of the attack also disrupted air travel across Moscow. More than 200 flights were reportedly delayed or canceled at the capital’s airports from midnight.
The Sheremetyevo airport saw the largest disruption, with around 47 departures and 106 arrivals affected. The Vnukovo airport reported disruptions to 28 departing and 23 arriving flights, while four flights were affected at the Domodedovo airport.

articles.title: Ursa Major lands $91M to power a mini missile for F-35s
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy awarded Ursa Major $137 million for solid rocket motors for the Compact Air-to-Air Missile and the Naval Modular Missile.
- The $91 million CAAM contract covers a 7-inch motor, and the $46 million NMM contract covers a 10-inch quad-pack motor.
The U.S. Navy has awarded Ursa Major two contracts worth a combined $137 million to develop and qualify solid rocket motors for two new missiles: a small air-to-air missile for fighter jets and a ship-launched interceptor meant to eventually replace the Standard Missile family.
The Colorado company announced the awards on Oct. 5. The larger contract, worth $91 million, covers the motor for the Compact Air-to-Air Missile, or CAAM. The second, worth $46 million, covers the motor for the medium-range version of the Naval Modular Missile, or NMM. Funding comes through the Office of the Under Secretary of War.
CAAM is a short-range missile the U.S. Navy is developing for close-in air combat, sized to be carried inside the weapons bays of stealth fighters and future carrier-based drones. The Navy first showed the concept publicly in August, and service officials described it as an “inner boundary” weapon meant to increase how many missiles an aircraft can carry internally.
For CAAM, Ursa Major is designing a 7-inch (178 mm) motor. That is the same diameter as the AIM-120 AMRAAM and wider than the 5-inch AIM-9X Sidewinder, the Navy’s current short-range air-to-air missile. The company says the motor uses Highly Loaded Grain, a propellant design that packs more fuel into the motor case, giving a small missile more energy in the same volume. Ursa Major said it is building the development motor with the same methods it plans to use in full production, so it can move to high-rate manufacturing once the design is qualified.
The second contract covers a 10-inch (254 mm) motor for the medium-range NMM. The company described it as a quad-pack motor, meaning four missiles are sized to fit in a single shipboard launch cell, as the U.S. Navy already does with the Evolved Sea Sparrow Missile. Ursa Major said the motor is designed for high annual production volumes and compatibility with existing Navy shipboard launch systems. The U.S. Navy wants NMM to reach full capability by fiscal 2032 as a replacement for the Standard Missile family.
“By investing in CAAM and NMM, the Navy and OUSW are building solid rocket motor capacity now and getting new tactical air and naval capabilities into development sooner,” said Jason Meredith, president of Solid Missile Systems at Ursa Major. “Our Lynx manufacturing approach and growing energetics capacity enable us to design, build, test, qualify and field these motors faster to support the warfighter. Production is the bottleneck in missile programs right now, and that’s the part we’ve been building for.”
Lynx is Ursa Major’s name for its manufacturing process, which uses additive manufacturing, or industrial 3D printing, to produce most motor parts. Solid rocket motor production in the United States has for years been concentrated in two suppliers, Northrop Grumman and L3Harris, which owns Aerojet Rocketdyne. The Pentagon has been funding new entrants to expand capacity as demand for interceptors and long-range missiles has grown.
The new awards follow earlier work with the U.S. Navy. In July, the Navy gave Ursa Major $10 million to take its version of the MK 104 motor through critical design review and static fire testing. The MK 104 is the dual-thrust motor that powers Standard Missile-2 and Standard Missile-6 interceptors on Aegis destroyers and cruisers. In February, the company completed a $25 million cost-share program with the Navy and the Office of Strategic Capital, in which it designed, built and static-fired a 10-inch Highly Loaded Grain motor and developed a proprietary propellant for it. That work was carried out with the Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division at China Lake, California, and the Naval Surface Warfare Center Indian Head Division in Maryland.
Ursa Major is headquartered in Berthoud, Colorado, and runs additive manufacturing operations in Youngstown, Ohio. The company said its next steps on both programs are design, testing and qualification of the motors.

In an editorial, Kayhan discussed the reopening of channels for bypassing financial sanctions through Russia's banking system. Iran's Central Bank has so far transferred more than $1.5 billion of its funds through the Russian banking network, thereby utilizing the Russian route to circumvent US financial sanctions.

Shargh: Diplomacy backed by strength and readiness for defense
In its analysis of Araghchi's meeting with foreign ambassadors, heads of diplomatic missions, and representatives of international organizations in Tehran, Shargh argued that Iran's foreign minister sought to present a clear picture of Tehran's evolving foreign policy. The central message was that the door to diplomacy remains open, but it is now supported by a stronger readiness for defense. The core message of Araghchi's remarks is neither negotiation alone nor resistance alone, but rather the simultaneous pursuit of both. Viewed from this perspective, Araghchi's recent statements can be seen as an effort to define Iran's foreign policy at a stage when war, negotiations, the Strait of Hormuz, and regional relations have become more interconnected than ever.
Jam-e-Jam: It was the enemies, not Iran, that chose war
In a commentary, Jam-e-Jam highlighted Iran's ethical outlook and its approach to international engagement. While Western governments accused the Islamic Republic of warmongering and alleged that Iran sought to eliminate certain regional countries and resolve disputes through military force, Iran consistently stated that it preferred understanding and negotiation in dealing with contentious foreign-policy issues, including the nuclear question. The newspaper pointed to numerous rounds of negotiations and serious dialogue with global powers and neighboring countries as evidence that Iran favors engagement over confrontation. In particular, over the past year and several months, Iran repeatedly demonstrated its willingness to negotiate on nuclear matters by accepting proposals for talks. Nevertheless, Iran's adversaries chose the path of conflict and imposed two, or arguably three, wars on the country during the past 18 months. Iran's ethical and humanitarian view of power was once again distinguished from what it characterized as the aggressive and inhumane approach of its opponents.
Khorasan: Iran is fully prepared
In an article examining current Iranian and American policies, Khorasan argued that Iran's foes have entered a phase of "operational patience," seeking to select the most effective and least costly option from among various scenarios. However, this patience stems not from caution but from weakness, and Trump knows that losing one or both chambers of Congress would significantly complicate his position. Military limitations continue to constrain any potential action by the US military. While Iran's opponents may view the situation as static, realities on the ground remain dynamic and subject to change. Under these circumstances, it predicted that war could eventually begin. However, it emphasized that Iran remains committed to serious negotiations, though not in a manner that would imply surrender or deception. The article concluded that Iran is preparing for the worst-case scenarios, harbors no optimism regarding future developments, possesses a broad range of response options, and regards maintaining public calm as the most crucial element of national security.
Ettelaat: Escalating crisis in the region
Ettelaat discussed that indirect communication between Tehran and Washington is continuing, but even more significant are the military and political signs suggesting a growing possibility of a new conflict. According to the paper, Iran says it has received the US response to Tehran's seven-day trust-building proposal concerning the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and is currently reviewing it. At the same time, Washington is reinforcing its forces in the region and Donald Trump has spoken of a decision regarding Iran that could proceed through either an "easy path" or a "hard path." Meanwhile, Iranian military and political officials have spoken of greater readiness for any future conflict and of improving missile capabilities. The newspaper noted that the principal disagreement between the two sides remains clear: Iran views the reopening of Hormuz, an end to pressure on shipping, and sanctions relief as the main pillars of negotiations, whereas the United States continues to place the nuclear issue at the center of its proposals.  According to the article, this disagreement, combined with the growing US military posture in the region, has created a situation in which diplomacy has not entirely collapsed, yet discussions about the possibility of political pressures evolving into a new confrontation are becoming increasingly frequent.

articles.title: When the UN agreed with the UK Green Party on Zionism
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
When the UN agreed with the UK Green Party on Zionism
The Green Party’s decision to adopt a motion classifying Zionism as a form of racism has caused uproar in the UK. The motion calls Zionism an ideology which supports an “ethnonationalist Jewish state” and calls for a “single democratic state in all of historic Palestine”.
The Green Party’s leader, Zack Polanski, did not vote on the motion, but found himself banned from Israel as a result.
Rabbi Charley Baginsky of the Movement for Progressive Judaism described the motion as “incredibly sinister” and told LBC she was “really distressed” at the vote, saying that Zionism was a key part of many Jewish people’s identity.
The Board of Deputies of British Jews said that the move would stoke “anti-Jewish hatred”, citing attacks on Jews in the UK in the past year.
The resolution was even opposed by leading members of the Green Party itself.
Caroline Lucas, the party’s former leader and its first-ever MP, said, “I view the Israeli government as racist, I believe its actions in Gaza amount to genocide, and I support the BDS campaign. And yet I remain firmly opposed to this resolution.”
She justified this by claiming that Zionism was historically a response to the racist persecution of Jews in Europe.
Media coverage in the UK has been extremely critical, with The Economist calling the motion “shameful” and the Daily Mail suggesting that the Greens were now the UK’s “first openly anti-Semitic party”.
It is often forgotten, however, that the UN itself once classified Zionism as racism.
UN condemnation of Zionism
While the UN was instrumental in the creation of Israel, with the majority of its members voting in favour of the 1947 Partition of Palestine, by 1975, African and Asian states had gained independence from European colonial rule and formed a large proportion of the world body’s membership. Most of these voted for UN General Assembly Resolution 3379, which determined that Zionism was “a form of racism and racial discrimination”, alongside the Arab League countries which sponsored and proposed it.
The Soviet Union, which was one of the first countries in the world to recognise Israel, had by that time become an ally of Arab countries and, along with its East European allies, also voted in favour. The resolution passed with 72 votes for and 35 against, with the US and its Western European allies voting against.
The vote took place at a time when Israel’s 1967 occupation of the West Bank and Gaza was relatively new. Israel subjected the Palestinian population of those territories to military rule while denying them citizenship. It also began establishing settlements in the territories in violation of international law.
Memories of the 1948 Nakba, in which Zionist forces expelled the vast majority of the Palestinian population, were also much fresher than they are today.
South Africa and Israel
Israel at the time was also a close ally of apartheid South Africa, with the two countries cooperating in defence, intelligence, and the development of nuclear weapons, with both viewing themselves as outposts of “civilisation” in a hostile environment.
As a South African government publication put it at the time, “Israel and South Africa have one thing above all else in common: they are both situated in a predominantly hostile world inhabited by dark peoples."
It was very easy to draw parallels between the two countries and the statements of Israeli leaders themselves appeared to confirm them. As Yitzhak Navon, Israel’s president between 1978 and 1983, said, “The very point of [the Israeli] Labor [party’s] Zionist programme is to have as much land as possible and as few Arabs as possible!”
These parallels helped explain the overwhelming African and Asian support for the UNGA resolution.
Israel, however, bitterly rejected the resolution, with its ambassador, Chaim Herzog (father of Israel’s current president), claiming that some of Israel’s Palestinian citizens – within the 1948 boundaries – had gained high-ranking positions within its government and military.
US ambassador to the UN Daniel Patrick Moynihan told the UN that it was “about to make anti-Semitism international law."
Repealing the resolution for ‘peace’
By 1991, the global environment had changed. The collapse of the Soviet Union had deprived Arab countries of a key strategic ally and supplier of weapons and changed the balance of power across the world. The Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and the subsequent Gulf War had left the US in a much stronger position in the Middle East.
Israel demanded that the UN repeal Resolution 3379 as a precondition for its participation in the 1991 Madrid peace conference, which eventually led to the 1993 Oslo Accords between the PLO and Israel.
The UN General Assembly duly repealed the resolution under US pressure, with even some Arab countries – such as Egypt, Morocco, and Oman – staying away rather than voting against.
However, all of the original factors behind the 1975 resolution remained. The Oslo Peace Process ended up entrenching Israel’s military occupation of the West Bank, its settlement policies, and its encirclement and siege of Palestinian communities – notably Gaza.
The number of Israeli settlers in the West Bank has gone up from just a few thousand in 1975 to around 700,000 today.
Human rights groups such as Amnesty International have concluded that Israel is committing “the crime of apartheid” both within its 1948 boundaries and in the West Bank and Gaza, long after apartheid as a ruling system ended in South Africa.
Israeli leaders are engaging in much more bloodthirsty rhetoric than Navon’s “as few Arabs as possible” remarks, with far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir recently calling for “30-40” Palestinians to be killed every day.
What may have changed, however, is the increasing censorship regarding discourse on Israel and the growing and deliberate conflation of criticism of Israel with anti-Semitism.
Singers who chant “Free Palestine” at music concerts are attacked on the grounds that they make Jews feel unsafe, while artwork by Palestinian children displayed at a UK hospital is removed for the same reason.
By passing a motion equating Zionism with racism, the Green Party only stated a position once held by a significant section of global opinion. However, it did so at a time when Israel is far more aggressive in pushing its narrative than it was 50 years ago.

articles.title: Yemeni Government Forces Claim to Have Regained Control of Mocha
articles.body:
Yemeni government forces, backed by the Saudi-led coalition, have announced that they have regained control of the strategic port city of Mocha and positions near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera reported this.
However, the Houthis deny losing control of Mocha and claim their units remain in the city’s streets.
The large-scale operation was carried out as part of a counteroffensive that the army of Yemen’s internationally recognized government is launching toward the country’s capital, Sanaa, which has been held by the group since 2014.
The Saudi-led coalition deployed around 100 fighter jets to provide air cover and strike militant targets.
The government forces’ advance began following a September offensive by the Houthis, during which they captured Mocha and the nearby islands.
At the time, the port seizure was possible due to the extensive use of drones and support from Iranian specialists who provided the group with intelligence.
Mocha is crucial for logistics and control of the region, as regaining control of the city allowed government forces to block key Houthi supply routes in the area of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The loss of the port posed a threat to civilian and military vessels in the Red Sea, as the situation around this major shipping route puts direct pressure on global oil prices.
Earlier, the Yemeni Houthis have also established the production of missiles and drones using equipment and components of Chinese origin that enter the country as dual-use goods.
During a detailed inspection in July, authorities found phenolic resin in one of the containers — a heat-resistant material that can be used in missile production — as well as tail fins and other components resembling those used in ballistic missiles.
Later, authorities inspected three more containers linked to the same supply network at the port of Aden. They contained suspected missile airframe components, guidance systems, launch equipment, computer numerical control (CNC) machines, and two-cylinder engines suitable for use in drones.

articles.title: Expert says moving Estonia's units near border has limited strategic impact
articles.body:
Expert says moving Estonia's units near border has limited strategic impact
As Estonia strengthens its defenses, the country is shifting military units closer to the Russian border and expanding long‑range strike capability. Security expert Rainer Saks says moving units by less than 100 kilometers offers little strategic benefit, arguing that Estonia's real vulnerabilities lie in air defense and attack‑drone capacity.
Recently, the EDF's 1st Infantry Brigade moved its Jõhvi staff company and brigade headquarters from Tapa, and next year a company will relocate from Jõhvi to Narva. The shift toward the eastern border is part of preparations for active defense.
"I wouldn't call this a strategic advantage. It's more routine work. A decision was made years ago that we begin defending the country at the state border. It makes sense to move certain functions and units closer to the border," said Tarmo Kundla, commander of the 1st Infantry Brigade.
"So that in a crisis we don't have to start moving there — we're already there. If someone thinks this makes us a target, they're right. If we're sitting in our bases as targets when war breaks out, then we've done something very wrong," said Defense Minister Martin Herem.
According to Saks, relocating units may be justified in terms of military planning, but strategically the change is minor.
"No matter where we place our forces, they are vulnerable if we lack air defense. If the air‑defense issue is solved, that becomes a major achievement in defense planning. Until air defense is sufficient, placing units at specific points is less important," Saks said.
Herem says air defense is improving month by month. Additional ammunition for existing systems will arrive this year, and long‑range strike capability is being developed.
"We have HIMARS. We previously received loitering munitions — essentially winged drones similar to Russia's Lancet. We already have them in Estonia, and the unit is trained," Herem said.
Some HIMARS munitions have already arrived, though not the 300‑kilometer‑range missiles.
"Russia could previously plan operations against Estonia knowing it could mass forces right near the border, use aircraft from close range, and fire missiles from close range. If Estonia could bring that 300‑kilometer zone under fire control, it would be a major change," Saks said.
The Financial Times reported on Monday about changes in Estonia's defense planning. Saks says it is important to show foreign media that Estonia is preparing countermeasures — sending a message to both Russia and allies that Estonia's defense forces are capable.
--
Editor: Johanna Alvin, Argo Ideon

articles.title: Ukraine Will Receive Belgian F-16s Once the Transfer of French Onboard Electronic Warfare Systems Is Approved
articles.body:
Belgium’s transfer of three F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine will take place immediately after it signs an agreement with France to transfer the technology to a third party.
Belgian Defense Minister Theo Franken announced this in an interview with Ukrinform.
The need for additional approval arose because Belgium upgraded its F-16s with French radar warning systems. According to the defense minister, the approval process should not take long.
“We can do this fairly quickly. Our F-16s were modernized using French electronic warfare technology, so when we send them to Ukraine, we must have an agreement signed by France regarding transfer to a third party,” Theo Franken noted.
Immediately after receiving official permission from France, the Belgians will begin organizing logistics to ship the aircraft.
Belgian F-16 fighter jets are equipped with the French Carapace radar warning and threat detection system, developed by Dassault Electronique (now part of the Thales Group). The system is integrated into the aircraft’s fuselage and detects radiation from enemy radars, warns of missile launches, and automatically controls countermeasures, including the deployment of chaff and flares.
Belgium plans to transfer the first three F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of the year.
On September 29, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced the delivery timeline.
In June, Theo Franken said the country expects to deliver seven aircraft by the end of the year: four as a source of spare parts and three for combat missions.
The overall plan calls for transferring 53 Belgian F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of 2029.
According to the schedule, five aircraft are planned for delivery in 2027, 14 in 2028, and another 27 are expected to arrive in 2029.

articles.title: Former German spy chief arrested on espionage charges. He made at least seven trips to Russia after leaving office.
articles.body:
Former German spy chief arrested on espionage charges. He made at least seven trips to Russia after leaving office.
Germany’s Federal Prosecutor’s Office said it detained August Hanning, the former head of the country’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND), on suspicion of espionage and attempted treason. His former bureau chief, Manfred D., was detained along with him.
Hanning led the BND from December 1998 to November 2005. Investigators said that in 2010, he arranged for Manfred D. to pass him classified intelligence agency information in exchange for money. By 2022, Hanning had obtained roughly 2,000 internal BND documents, including materials on Iran’s nuclear program and the Russian armed forces.
In one instance, he used the documents to prepare an analytical report for an officer of a foreign intelligence service, though it is not clear which country was involved. Süddeutsche Zeitung, NDR, and WDR reported that this episode was not connected to Russia.
Hanning also communicated for many years with another foreign intelligence officer, whose country is also unclear, and passed him political information, including material he obtained from Manfred D.
The Insider, an independent Russian investigative outlet, found that Hanning flew to Russia at least seven times between 2015 and 2019. The trips were short, with some lasting less than a day.
Süddeutsche Zeitung reported that rumors about Hanning’s ties to Russia have circulated since his diplomatic work in East Berlin during the era of East Germany, though no evidence ever supported them.
In 2013, Hanning testified in a London court case as a security expert, backing businessman Oleg Deripaska in a dispute over the sale of a stake in Rusal.
Hanning also worked as a consultant in the Russian division of the London consulting firm G3 and served on the supervisory board of the Latvian PNB Banka. While working at PNB, he acted as a mediator in a dispute between two businessmen of Russian origin. Security firms linked to Hanning also include people with ties to Russia.
