articles.title: French submarine fires new nuclear weapon
articles.body:
France has fired its latest submarine-launched ballistic missile for the first time from the boat Le Vigilant, with President Emmanuel Macron watching from the deck of a frigate, the president stated in a post published after the launch.
Writing in French from aboard the multi-mission frigate Auvergne, Mr Macron said: “Aboard the multi-mission frigate Auvergne, I witnessed the first firing of the new M51.3 ballistic missile from the nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine Le Vigilant. Very few nations possess such expertise.”
He thanked the defence procurement agency DGA, the Atomic Energy Commission, ArianeGroup, Naval Group and the French Navy, and said: “This technical success is a new demonstration of the credibility of our deterrence, whose sustainability is assured. To be free, one must be feared. And to be feared, one must be powerful.”
The missile was launched off Finistère in western Brittany without a nuclear warhead fitted, and flew to a designated impact area in the North Atlantic several hundred kilometres from any coastline. France has described the trial as validating the operational capability of Le Vigilant’s strategic weapon system after a long refit, and the boat has recently emerged from the major overhaul the French call an IPER before returning to the deterrent patrol cycle.
The M51.3 is the third operational version of the missile, which was declared in service last October with improved range, accuracy and penetration performance over the preceding M51.2, and carrying the newer TNO warhead. ArianeGroup builds the family, which entered service in 2010, and the missiles arm the four boats of the Triomphant class. A further version, the M51.4, was contracted to the same company in August last year and is expected during the next decade, alongside the third-generation submarines that will replace the current fleet.
Published range figures for the M51 run to somewhere between 8,000 and 10,000 kilometres, though France does not confirm them and the real figure is classified.
Mr Macron set the firing against his own record on defence spending, saying he had launched the renewal of French capabilities in 2017 and that the armed forces budget will have doubled over ten years. He added that the programme for hypersonic and manoeuvring strategic missiles that will arm the airborne component of the deterrent was launched this year, a reference to the weapon intended to succeed the ASMP-A carried by Rafale squadrons.
France designs, builds and owns every element of its deterrent, from the warhead through the missile to the boat, whereas the Royal Navy draws its Trident II D5 missiles from a common pool held at King’s Bay in Georgia.
The two countries are also closer on nuclear matters than they have been at any point since the war. Under the Northwood Declaration signed last year, Britain and France agreed to coordinate their deterrents and stated that there is no extreme threat to Europe that would not prompt a response by both, which was the first time either had said so in those terms.
Mr Macron closed by saying that French nuclear deterrence “protects us and will continue to protect us”.

articles.title: Poland and Lithuania prepare to evacuate one million Baltic residents to Poland in event of war
articles.body:

Poland and Lithuania are jointly preparing plans for the evacuation of one million or more residents of the Baltic states into Poland in the event of a war or other major crisis, amid growing concern in the region over potential Russian aggression.
On Monday, the two countries’ interior ministers met to discuss the issue following a recent large-scale Lithuanian mobilisation exercise that also involved Polish officials. The pair also addressed their joint response to the migration crisis on the borders orchestrated by Russia’s ally Belarus.
“In crisis situations, it is best to cooperate. It is best to prepare such plans through mutual understanding, thus attempting to address potential situations,” said Lithuanian interior minister Martynas Katelynas, speaking alongside his Polish counterpart, Marcin Kierwiński, at the Budzisko-Kalvarija border crossing.
“As for this crossing here, this place that connects us with Poland, this plan foresees approximately one million, and perhaps even more, refugees who will be able to be evacuated from our countries in the event of war,” he added.
The three Baltic states – Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia – are seen as a primary potential target for Russian aggression. NATO states, including Poland, have in recent months warned of the growing possibility of Moscow conducting some form of “provocation” against the alliance’s eastern members.
Lithuania last week finished a major exercise testing its national mobilisation system in the event of war or other crises. For the first time, it included elements relating to cross-border evacuation of civilians from the Baltic states to Poland.
Alongside thousands of Lithuanian officials, a 20-person Polish team, led by representatives of the interior ministry, took part in the exercise.
This has allowed Poland to develop “an agenda and action plan for what must be adjusted very quickly: cross-border evacuation plans, infrastructure and alternative border crossings in an emergency, as well as reception points”, said Kierwiński, adding that “we will begin intensive work” on implementation.
Poland already has extensive recent experience in receiving civilians fleeing conflict. In 2022, it became the primary destination for the millions of refugees fleeing Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Poland’s government and civil society quickly implemented measures to support the refugees, almost one million of whom remain in the country.
Almost 80% of Poles say they would want Poland to come to the aid of the Baltic states if they were attacked by Russia
The poll follows controversy over comments by a senior opposition figure casting doubt as to whether Poland should come to their defence https://t.co/l3dj02ETZ5
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 10, 2026
The two ministers also used their meeting to discuss their joint response to illegal migration. Both countries have been the target of a crisis engineered by Russia’s ally Belarus, which has encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to try to cross into Poland, Lithuania and Latvia.
In response, Poland last year introduced checks on its borders with Lithuania and Germany. Those measures have been repeatedly extended, including last week, when Poland announced that they would remain in force until at least March 2027.
“Border controls with Germany and Lithuania allow us to catch people illegally crossing the border from the Baltic states,” said Kierwiński on Monday. “As soon as there are grounds to end these controls, we will discontinue them. But for now, we have decided that they will remain in place for at least another six months.”
Poland is reintroducing controls on its borders with Germany and Lithuania to prevent the “uncontrolled flow of migrants”, in particular those returned by Germany after entering illegally
"Poland’s patience is running out," says Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/Pttd3FvpHA
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 1, 2025
Katelynas emphasised that “Lithuania and Poland share a common goal: to ensure the protection of our borders and effectively prevent irregular migrants from moving through our countries and across the Schengen area”.
He also noted that an agreement between the two countries on cooperation between police, border guard and customs services is currently being finalised.
“Poland and Lithuania are like brothers and sisters who support each other and will continue to do so,” said Katelynas.
Kierwiński likewise expressed his satisfaction that the two countries “speak with one voice…because this part of Europe, the eastern flank of NATO and the EU, must speak with one voice to address and counter the threats posed by Russian imperialism and the difficult situation beyond our eastern border”.
EU chief @vonderleyen has thanked Poland for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” during a visit with PM @donaldtusk to the border with Belarus.
She emphasised the “urgency” of protecting the EU’s frontier from the “predator” Vladimir Putin https://t.co/O9bhmLha44
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2025
Last month, Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental.
Poland has already recently suffered airspace violations by Russian drones, a missile and a helicopter. It has also been the primary target for Russian sabotage operations in Europe.
In response, the Polish government has moved to expand the network of warning sirens along the Ukrainian border, launched a campaign informing the public how to respond to aerial threats, and started more clearly marking bomb shelters.
The Polish-Lithuanian border area, which sits between Belarus and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and is known as the Suwałki Gap, is seen as a potential target for Russia in the event of war. Poland and Lithuania held joint military exercises there in 2024 to test their defensive capabilities.

articles.title: Zelensky warns Russia preparing mass strike
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned on Oct. 6 that Russia is preparing a large-scale attack on Ukraine and urged citizens to take air raid alerts seriously, citing recent intelligence.
"Please, please, take care of yourself. Please respond to signals of missile danger," Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
The president said Ukraine's emergency services and air force were ready to respond to the Russian attack "to the extent that our means of protection allow."
Zelensky called on Ukraine's allies, particularly in Europe and the U.S., to transfer any means of protection to the country if they can.
"The world is bigger than Russian evil, and protecting life must be a common cause. I thank everyone who is really helping," he said.
He did not specify when the attacks were expected to take place.
At least 13 people were killed and 104 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day as a Russian air strike damaged a hospital in Kryvyi Rih, local authorities said on Oct. 6.
In recent weeks, Russia has increasingly launched jet-powered attack drones toward the capital around the clock, bringing air raid alerts, air defense fire, and explosions into the middle of workdays, commutes, and afternoons in the city.
At least 16 people were killed and more than 100 others injured in Kyiv and the surrounding region between Sept. 25 and Oct. 2, according to a Kyiv Independent count based on official reports. The highest number of injuries came on Sept. 25, when at least 59 people were wounded as drones caught residents in the middle of the working day.
Some 62% of Ukrainians are ready to endure Russia's war for as long as necessary, according to a Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) poll published Oct. 6.
The share has remained largely unchanged since late July and early August, despite the beginning of intensified Russian attacks using jet-powered drones and strikes on civilian infrastructure during the survey period. KIIS said the results show that the attacks had not led to a decline in Ukrainians' willingness to endure the war as of Sept. 21.

articles.title: Ukrainian Strikes Destroyed a Span of the Chonhar Bridge, Which Russia Uses to Supply Its Troops
articles.body:
On the Chonhar Road Bridge, which connects the occupied part of the Kherson region with Crimea, one of the spans collapsed following new strikes by the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
This is evidenced by satellite images released by the OSINT project Dnipro OSINT.
In images taken as of September 26, at least three large holes in the road surface were visible on the bridge and the nearby crossing. The damage hampered traffic and caused traffic congestion, particularly for freight vehicles.
A satellite image from September 30 already shows the collapse of one of the road bridge’s spans.
At the same time, traffic through the Chonhar transportation hub has not completely ceased: the Russians are using the nearby old road bridge as well as a makeshift crossing.
The current destruction followed a series of attacks in June. On the night of June 7, the Defense Forces damaged the road bridge with Behemoth and FP-2 strike drones, after which traffic across it was restricted. On June 9, the invading administration reported a second strike and a complete closure of traffic.
Afterward, the Russian military deployed a pontoon bridge nearby to partially offset the loss of traffic capacity on the permanent bridge.
As early as June 12, satellite images showed significant traffic on the pontoon bridge: dozens of Russian trucks were observed in front of it. The Ukrainian Defense Forces later struck this alternative route.
Due to the damage to the Chonhar crossing, the Russians also had to organize alternative routes through Armiansk and Perekop. At the same time, the Chonhar route remained one of the supply routes for the Russian forces in the occupied south of Ukraine.
The Chonhar route, however, remained one of the supply routes for the Russian forces in the occupied south of Ukraine.
The Chonhar bridges had been targeted by Ukrainian strikes before. In June 2023, the crossings over Syvash were struck, in particular with Storm Shadow cruise missiles, and in August of that same year, the Defense Forces attacked the Chonhar and Henichesk bridges again.
The Chonhar transportation hub is crucial for Russian logistics between occupied Crimea and the mainland in southern Ukraine. This route connects to Highway R-280, which Russia uses as part of a land corridor through the occupied territories in the south.

articles.title: Ukraine Set Record for Destroying Russian Air Defense Systems and Radar Stations In September
articles.body:
In September 2026, the Ukrainian Defense Forces intensified their strikes on targets deep within Russian rear areas and set a record for the number of air defense systems and radar stations destroyed since the inception of the e-Points (e-Baly) program.
This was reported by the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
By the end of September, 33,087 invaders had been confirmed killed — a figure surpassed only in March and April 2026.
A notable achievement in September was the highest number of Russian air defense systems, particularly radar stations, destroyed since the program’s inception. The destruction of one Russian air defense system at a distance of 552 km was also recorded.
In September, the number of confirmed target strikes at distances exceeding 20 km from the front line exceeded 11,000 for the first time.
The number of strikes at a depth of over 50 km also set a record. A significant portion of these attacks targeted the Mariupol-Crimea logistics route, which Russian troops use to supply their forces in southern Ukraine.
The program’s results indicate a gradual shift in combat operations from the immediate front lines to the enemy’s rear areas.
Every result within the program is recorded on video in the DELTA combat system and verified by the Brave1 defense innovation cluster.
The e-Points system works as follows: confirmed strikes are uploaded to DELTA, after that units receive points that they can spend on equipment on the Brave1 Market. Since March, military personnel have also been allowed to exchange e-Points for equipment components.
The overall trend toward an increase in Ukrainian strikes behind enemy lines is clearly evident in individual operations as well. In September, the Unmanned Systems Forces, in particular, struck dozens of energy facilities in the occupied territories.
To systematize such operations, Militarnyi launched the Deep Strike map in September, which tracks strikes on military, industrial, energy, and other targets in Russia and the occupied territories.
Another notable development in September was the increased effectiveness of Ukrainian air defense against attack drones.
Despite Russia’s increased use of jet-powered UAVs, Ukrainian units shot down 28% more Shahed-type drones in September than in the previous month.
At the same time, specialized interceptor drones are playing an increasingly important role in combating such targets. In May, the share of Shaheds shot down by these drones reached 40%. Since the beginning of September, the Defense Forces have neutralized about 55% of Russian Geran jet-powered drones.

articles.title: Ukraine is third in world for cyberattacks after US and Israel, and first in Europe. Machine-speed assaults run continuously and without fatigue
articles.body:
Only the US and Israel were hit by more cyberattacks than Ukraine this year. Ukraine ranked third in the world and first in Europe among the countries whose organizations and users were most often targeted by cyberattacks in the first half of 2026, accounting for 4.8% of all victims worldwide, up from fifth in the world and third in Europe a year earlier, Microsoft said in its Digital Defense Report 2026.
Microsoft processes more than 165 trillion security signals a day, which lets it show how often attackers go after customers in each country. Russian state hackers aimed 14% of their recorded activity at Ukraine, more than at any country except the US.
The era of machine-speed cyberattacks is here
Government agencies and services were the most targeted sector worldwide at 27%, up from 17% in 2025. Phishing drove 23% of intrusions Microsoft investigated, up from 7% a year earlier, and the median time from finding a vulnerability to weaponizing it has fallen well below 24 hours.
The use of artificial intelligence is pushing cyberspace into an era of “machine-speed” attacks that operate continuously and without fatigue, according to Dev.
“Many AI agents act on behalf of users and with their access rights, so a compromised agent combines user-level access with machine-scale actions,” Natalia Burlakova, Security Sales and Engineering Lead at Microsoft, says.
Deception beats code in attacks on Ukraine
Ukraine's own agency data show a similar pattern. Malware accounted for 33% of cyber incidents in the first half of 2026, and social engineering 31%, the State Service of Special Communications and Information Protection reported on 30 September. System infections made up 15%, and system compromises 4.5%.
Attackers rely less on technical complexity than on trust, according to the report by Ukraine's computer emergency response team, CERT-UA. Hacker groups create fake pages that mimic CERT-UA, Ukraine's Parliament's document management system, and the Brave1 defense technology platform.
Microsoft urges five government steps
Microsoft asks governments to prepare for faster-moving threats by assigning roles and coordinating agencies in advance of a crisis, and to treat AI security as part of national resilience. It also asks them to plan for incidents that spread, noting that 52.2% of intrusions involving valid accounts led to additional credential theft.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: High Command sets tasks on electronic warfare, sanctions, supply of long-range drones to AFU
articles.body:
Following a meeting of the High Command, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the assignment of additional tasks for the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) and manufacturers in the field of electronic warfare, the preparation of new sanctions packages against Russia, and key objectives for supplying Ukrainian forces with long-range drones for the coming year.
According to him, detailed reports were presented during the meeting on the capabilities of electronic warfare systems and their use in protecting infrastructure. Zelenskyy said this component of defense accounts for a significant portion of the neutralization of Russian "suicide drones."
"Defense Intelligence of Ukraine also reported on Russia's technological priorities for this year and next, and on the supplies of critical components and equipment that Russia receives for weapons production to meet them," according to a post shared by the president on Facebook.
According to him, based on the findings of the Main Intelligence Agency's report, new sanctions packages will be prepared, and the intelligence agency will submit relevant proposals to the Cabinet of Ministers and the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (NSDC).
"We are also working to synchronize our sanctions accross partners' jurisdictions," Zelenskyy said.
In addition, during the meeting, the High Command identified the main tasks for supplying Ukrainian forces with long-range drones for the coming year. The president emphasized that the main criterion in this regard must be Ukraine's ability to respond in kind to Russian strikes.
"The key criterion is that we must be able to respond to Russian strikes in kind," Zelenskyy said.

articles.title: Lithuania takes further step towards lifting nuclear weapons ban
articles.body:
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that Lithuania’s move, alongside broader plans to expand US and NATO military infrastructure in the region, risked further escalating tensions.
Lithuania has taken a step towards removing a constitutional ban on nuclear weapons from its territory, bringing the Baltic state closer to the legal position of its neighbours as European allies debate how to strengthen NATO’s deterrence in the face of Russia.
The Lithuanian parliament, the Seimas, voted 106-18, with six abstentions, on Tuesday to advance a constitutional amendment removing a provision that bars weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases from Lithuanian territory.
The change still requires a second vote after a constitutionally mandated three-month waiting period. At least 94 of the Seimas’ 141 members must back it on both occasions. The final vote is expected on January 12.
“This constitutional amendment would enable Lithuania’s armed forces to participate fully in the planning and exercises of all of NATO’s deterrence measures,” said Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen, leader of the Liberal Movement parliamentary group.
Currently, Article 137 of the Lithuanian Constitution stipulates that weapons of mass destruction and military bases of foreign states may not be located in Lithuania, which borders Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave. This means that under current laws, allied aircraft or ships carrying nuclear weapons could not enter Lithuanian territory for deterrence purposes.
Added urgency in Lithuania's case
Supporters of the amendment argue that the constitutional provision has become a legal obstacle to Lithuania’s full participation in NATO’s nuclear deterrence arrangements and leaves the country at a disadvantage compared with other NATO allies.
“Our neighbouring countries, such as Latvia, Estonia and Poland, have no such restrictions either,” Remigijus Motuzas, chairman of the Seimas Foreign Affairs Committee, said during a parliamentary session in September. “We cannot be less protected than other NATO countries. We must send a signal that Lithuania is a full part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence.”
NATO describes nuclear deterrence as part of its collective defence, alongside conventional and missile-defence capabilities. The Alliance also says its nuclear policy remains consistent with its commitments to arms control, disarmament and non-proliferation.
For Lithuania, the issue has taken on added urgency. “NATO deterrence, including nuclear deterrence, is part of collective defence,” Motuzas said, adding that Russia has rapidly modernised its nuclear arsenal in recent years and deployed nuclear weapons close to Lithuania — in Kaliningrad and Belarus.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that Lithuania’s move, alongside broader plans to expand US and NATO military infrastructure in the region, risked further escalating tensions, Reuters reported.
The warnings come as Russia has stepped up its nuclear rhetoric towards NATO. Moscow recently threatened nuclear retaliation in the event of what it described as attempts to isolate its Kaliningrad exclave, which borders Lithuania and Poland.
Finland has already made the move
Lithuania is not acting in isolation.
Finland, which joined NATO in 2023 after decades of military non-alignment, removed its own statutory prohibition on nuclear weapons earlier this year, citing the need to ensure that Finnish law did not restrict the country’s ability to fulfil its obligations as a NATO ally.
In June, the Finnish parliament approved amendments to the Nuclear Energy Act repealing the country’s ban on nuclear explosives. The legislation entered into force on July 1.
“This historic reform strengthens the security of Finland and of NATO as a whole,” Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said on X.
Helsinki has stressed, however, that the change does not mean Finland intends to acquire or host nuclear weapons, and that NATO has no plans to station them there.
Finland has since joined a French-led initiative aimed at strengthening European security through closer cooperation on nuclear deterrence. French President Emmanuel Macron has proposed what Paris calls “forward deterrence” — closer cooperation with European allies around France’s independent nuclear capabilities.
The United Kingdom, Germany, Poland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Greece, Denmark, and Norway have already signed up to France's initiative.

articles.title: Report: Iranian drone plot to kill US pilots forced B-1 bombers out of UK base
articles.body:
The United States urgently withdrew all 12 of its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Britain after intelligence warned of a potentially complex Iranian drone attack targeting the aircraft and U.S. personnel at the base, according to American media reports. 
The Wall Street Journal reported that U.S. and European officials believed Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps was behind plans to damage the bombers and kill personnel, including American pilots.
U.S. officials said the suspected plan may have resembled Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb, in which drones were smuggled deep into Russia and launched near military airfields, damaging several strategic aircraft. The possibility raised concerns that small drones launched close to a base could threaten even heavily protected military installations.
President Donald Trump acknowledged Monday that intelligence about a threat had influenced the decision to move the bombers. "We had an idea that there might be a threat, and why would I leave them there?" he said. Asked whether those behind the threat were linked to Iran, Trump said: "They would be linked to Iran."
Vice President JD Vance said Washington believed Iran was continuing a decades-long pattern of terrorism against the United States and others. "So we are being extremely cautious," he said. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was more cautious, saying he could not confirm a direct connection between the suspected plot and the redeployment.
British officials said RAF Fairford remained safe and declined to comment on U.S. military decisions. The U.S. Air Force said the bombers had returned to their home stations in the United States.
Trump later addressed the war with Iran during a campaign rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, where he played down rising fuel prices. "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe," he said, adding: "They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay."
Trump also said the war would end "very soon" and was "essentially almost over with." Referring to Iran, he added: "They always say they have a big threshold for pain. They need it."

articles.title: The Seimas of Lithuania supported lifting the constitutional ban on nuclear weapons
articles.body:
The Seimas of Lithuania supported lifting the constitutional ban on nuclear weapons
Kyiv • UNN
In the first reading, the Seimas of Lithuania approved lifting the ban on weapons of mass destruction. The final vote is scheduled for January 12.
The Seimas of Lithuania supported in the first reading the repeal of the ban on nuclear weapons. This is reported by LRT, according to UNN.
Details
In the first reading, the Seimas supported an amendment to the Constitution stipulating that the country’s basic law will no longer prohibit weapons of mass destruction from being stationed on the country’s territory.
The initiative was supported by 106 lawmakers, while 18 voted against and six abstained.
At the same time, the second and final vote may take place no earlier than three months later, after which the amendment, as in this vote, must be supported by at least 94 of the 141 lawmakers.
Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said that final adoption was scheduled for January 12 next year. He told journalists that repealing the ban increases the country’s resilience and has a deterrent effect.
The importance of deterrence was also emphasized by Defense Minister Robert Kaunas. According to him, the task of politicians is to provide every possible tool to ensure the country’s security.
In response, Russian dictator Vladimir Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that "the deployment of a NATO base and nuclear weapons in Lithuania will become another stage in escalating tensions." He added that the Kremlin "will be forced to take measures."

articles.title: A 28-year-old plague researcher died in Russia. Authorities have imposed a quarantine but deny any threat of plague, and locals are struggling to make sense of it.
articles.body:
A 28-year-old plague researcher died in Russia. Authorities have imposed a quarantine but deny any threat of plague, and locals are struggling to make sense of it.
Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee of a plague research institute, died overnight on October 1–2 in Shelekhov, a city just outside Irkutsk. Authorities then isolated about 200 people who had been in contact with her and imposed quarantine restrictions at the hospital where she had been admitted a couple of days before her death. Around the same time, media outlets and social media users began circulating reports that she had died of pneumonic plague after contracting it at her institute. Almost immediately, however, pro-government outlets deleted these reports from their websites, and authorities began denying that plague was involved, saying Shipilova had died of pneumonia.
The news outlet People of Baikal traveled to Irkutsk and Shelekhov to investigate whether negligence could have caused Shipilova’s death and whether local residents believed there was a threat of plague. Meduza is translating its report in full.
“The smell was unbearable, really acrid,” a resident of the building, a woman around 40, tells People of Baikal. She thinks it was a strong disinfectant. Residents opened the doors to the stairwell because “you could barely breathe.”
The people who arrived told residents that “Rospotrebnadzor sent us,” referring to Russia’s consumer protection and public health agency. “We asked what happened. They told us some young woman had died from a deadly virus,” the woman told People of Baikal. “They didn’t know anything else. They said, ‘We came to work, they told us to go disinfect the place, so we came and disinfected it.’”
Residents did not yet know that their neighbor, 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, had died at Shelekhov District Hospital overnight on October 1–2. She worked at the Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. Immediately after her death, reports spread across the Irkutsk region that she had died of pneumonic plague.
Since then, the building where Darya lived has been disinfected twice more. None of the workers mentioned a “deadly virus” again. They still wore gas masks while disinfecting the building, but this time they were in white protective suits.
“The second time, a woman from their team knocked on our door and asked for water to mix the solution,” Shipilova’s neighbor recalled. “I said, ‘What are you spraying for?’ By then I knew everything [about the plague rumors]. She goes, ‘It’s for cockroaches.’ But we don’t have any cockroaches in our building. Then I see her packing her little [protective] suit into a bag. I’m like, ‘Well, that explains it.’”
‘A woman who may have died of plague’
An employee of the plague institute, speaking anonymously, told People of Baikal that Darya Shipilova developed cold symptoms at work. “She didn’t have a fever, but then she got worse and developed swelling.”
Shipilova was hospitalized on September 29 and died at Shelekhov Hospital overnight on October 1–2. Officials have not explained why she was taken there. Most likely, it was because the inpatient facility had previously been used as a COVID hospital.
Immediately after Shipilova’s death, Shelekhov Hospital was placed under quarantine. Governor Igor Kobzev said the reason was “a particularly dangerous infection.” Official statements did not mention the word “plague.”
That same day, October 2, Anna Popova, the head of Rospotrebnadzor and Russia’s chief public health officer, flew to Irkutsk. She attended an emergency meeting of the regional commission responsible for public health and epidemic prevention. Officials, doctors, and law enforcement and security personnel approved an “emergency action plan” at the meeting.
People who had been in contact with Darya were isolated and placed under medical observation. Authorities did not disclose the exact number. The television channel REN TV reported that there were about 200, but deleted its posts that same day. The people who had been in contact with Shipilova were housed in at least two hospitals in Irkutsk and Shelekhov.
People of Baikal’s sources in law enforcement and security agencies said her contacts were taken away in ambulances escorted by the Federal Security Service, or FSB.
An Irkutsk resident told People of Baikal that her friend, a nurse at Shelekhov Hospital, had been quarantined. “Everyone there was worried. The bosses were freaking out, and that means things are bad,” she said, quoting her friend.
Employees of the plague institute were isolated inside the institute itself. One employee told People of Baikal: “They quarantined 200 of us. Kept us there for three days, took swabs twice a day. But they did feed us. We slept on chairs, and those who didn’t have a spot slept on their jackets. I slept on my jacket. We didn’t sign any documents. They let us go on Sunday.”
There was no official information about what had happened to Darya. On the afternoon of October 2, Irkutsk journalist Pavel Stepanov wrote that, according to his information, Shipilova had “broken a test tube with a pneumonic plague sample in it” and “concealed what happened.” This account spread widely but has yet to be confirmed. Rumors that Darya had visited Buryatia shortly before her death also circulated online.
On Friday evening, October 2, Buryatia’s leader, Alexey Tsydenov, denied that she had visited the region. More significantly, he became the first official to mention plague, saying that the “woman who died of plague in the Irkutsk region” had not visited Buryatia. That same day, however, Tsydenov edited his post to read “a woman who may have died of plague.”
‘She was very afraid of infecting anyone’
Darya Shipilova was born and raised in Irkutsk. In high school, she decided to become a doctor. A former classmate tells People of Baikal she was “smart, honest, and responsible.” Others who spoke to the outlet, including her colleagues, also call Darya “responsible.”
“Dasha was really anxious about infecting anyone if something went wrong. You could tell from how often she disinfected her hands, even outside work,” says a colleague at the plague institute.
In the summer of 2022, Darya graduated from Irkutsk State Medical University with a degree in medical biochemistry. That same year, she joined the Irkutsk Plague Institute, where she had previously interned. She initially worked as a laboratory assistant and became a researcher a year and a half later.
Darya continued her studies, entering a residency program in clinical laboratory diagnostics. The plague institute paid for her training. Shipilova completed her residency with honors in 2024. She worked in the plague microbiology department until at least January 2025.
In the spring, Shipilova and her colleagues from the institute spoke at the annual All-Russian Congress on Infectious Diseases in Moscow. She gave a presentation titled “Studying the Antibiotic Susceptibility of Yersinia pestis from Natural Plague Foci in Siberia.”
Darya’s interests extended beyond science. At 17, she graduated from music school. In 2025, she and other institute employees took part in the “Songs of Victory” competition for employees of the regional Rospotrebnadzor office. They performed the song “Maisky vals” (“May Waltz”). A year later, Shipilova and her colleagues won the “Musical Entertainment ABC” quiz. In August 2026, Shipilova took part in drills for public health emergency rapid response teams.
“Dasha was really smart,” says an Irkutsk resident who studied in the same department as Shipilova. “Not many people from our department get jobs at the plague institute. I did an internship there. It’s a serious facility. They take everything seriously, and it’s safe.”
Darya lived in a two-story brick building in an outlying neighborhood of Irkutsk. The neighborhood is considered rough. The building is surrounded by old wooden barracks-style housing, and many of the buildings are 60 to 70 years old.
Neighbors call Shipilova “calm” and her parents, who visited their daughter often, “quiet people who don’t drink.” Darya had a dachshund in her apartment, and her father often walked it.
Darya was very close to her mother. Like her daughter, Svetlana Shipilova works in health care. Rumors have spread among Darya’s neighbors that Svetlana “couldn’t bear her daughter’s death and died of a heart attack.” That is not true: Her mother, like other family members, is still quarantined at a hospital in the city.
How pro-government outlets published and deleted reports
On October 2, the pro-government newspaper Izvestia reported that following Darya Shipilova’s death, authorities in Irkutsk had opened a criminal investigation under Part 2 of Article 236 of the Criminal Code — “Violation of public health and epidemic prevention rules resulting in a person’s death through negligence.” Izvestia soon deleted the report, along with other articles about a possible outbreak of pneumonic plague in Irkutsk.
The Kazan branch of Argumenty i Fakty deleted a report on the death of the Irkutsk laboratory assistant that it had published on October 2. The article remained in the Yandex search engine’s cache. The Kuzbass edition of Moskovsky Komsomolets deleted a report that Rospotrebnadzor had denied Irkutsk hospitals were being placed under quarantine. That article also remained in Yandex’s cache.
Government agencies also deleted information. On the morning of October 3, the Baikalsk administration recommended that residents temporarily avoid traveling to Shelekhov, citing “unofficial information” that plague had been detected there. Two hours later, city authorities deleted the post.
That same day, management at the Irkutsk Aluminum Smelter, Shelekhov’s main employer, introduced a mask requirement on its premises. “Contradictory information about the plague situation is circulating in Shelekhov,” director Artyom Fominykh said. A day later, Fominykh said in another post that “the mask requirement at IrkAZ is unrelated to the quarantine at Shelekhov Hospital” and was prompted by respiratory illnesses.
“All our employees know this isn’t the first time. We bring back mask requirements from time to time during cold and flu season,” the plant’s director wrote, urging people “not to spread rumors.”
Throughout Saturday, October 3, authorities issued no official statements. Governor Kobzev posted on his Telegram channel about a forum for young workers and a meeting with the head of Russia’s health care regulator, Roszdravnadzor. There was not a word about the suspected plague that the whole city was discussing.
Meanwhile, several municipal hospitals in Irkutsk introduced quarantines. These included City Clinical Hospitals No. 1, 3, and 10, as well as the city’s Ivano-Matreninskaya Children’s Clinical Hospital.
Irkutsk Regional Clinical Hospital stopped admitting visitors on October 3, according to a patient. “The sister of a seriously ill patient in my room used to visit her. Since Saturday, staff have been bringing everyone’s care packages up, and they brought mine right to the room. Today I went downstairs for a food delivery. They wouldn’t let the delivery driver past the security desk.”
Over the weekend, residents bought up antibiotics at pharmacies in Irkutsk and Shelekhov. “There were fights at some pharmacies on Saturday,” an employee of the plague institute tells People of Baikal. “They cleaned the pharmacies out of antibiotics! Even the really, really old ones. People were panicking because everywhere you heard the words ‘plague’ and ‘pneumonic.’”
‘Listen, the situation is completely under control’
Rospotrebnadzor did not comment officially until Sunday afternoon, October 4. The agency told TASS that the plague institute employee had suffered from “pneumonia of unknown cause.” It also said no accidents involving pathogenic microorganisms had occurred at the institute. Rospotrebnadzor did not publish any statements on its own platforms.
According to Rospotrebnadzor, institute employees had not sought medical care for infectious diseases. Among those who had been in contact with Darya, two cases of COVID-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection were detected.
“Pneumonia of unknown cause” means that a patient had inflammation of the lungs, but doctors could not identify the specific microorganism that caused it: a bacterium, virus, or fungus. Rospotrebnadzor did not explain this in its statement or address why hundreds of people had been quarantined over pneumonia.
On the evening of October 4, Governor Kobzev repeated Rospotrebnadzor’s statement on his Telegram channel. The next day, he said that “the public health situation in Irkutsk and Shelekhov District is currently stable.”
On Monday, October 5, Kobzev said in a video statement: “Listen, the situation is completely under control. It’s unpleasant, of course, but the doctors and Rospotrebnadzor have done everything possible to make sure all of them [people who had contact with Shipilova] are under observation. Life goes on in the city, and life goes on in Shelekhov.”
That same day, Vladimir Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged people to listen only to Rospotrebnadzor’s official statements, rather than trust rumors and speculation about plague online.
“Rospotrebnadzor is staffed by highly qualified professionals in this field. Let’s listen to their official statements,” the Kremlin spokesman said.
Residents of the Irkutsk region bought up antibiotics and protective masks over the weekend
On October 5, U.S. President Donald Trump said the United States was ready to help Russia following reports of suspected pneumonic plague. Trump said that in Russia, “they call it pneumonia.”
On October 6, the Shelekhov district administration responded to Trump’s offer. Deputy Mayor Yelena Sofyina said: “Let me answer directly. We can handle this ourselves. The situation is completely under control.”
‘They went into quarantine just in case’
Authorities insist there is no plague in the region and that hospitals are operating as usual, but quarantine measures remain in place. On October 5, People of Baikal learned of restrictions at a psychiatric clinic in Irkutsk. A source told the outlet it was “something like a quarantine”: “They say they introduced it just in case.” The clinic had made no official announcement of the restrictions or posted any notices. A patient learned of them from a security guard when he tried to go to a store.
The Irkutsk Perinatal Center also introduced access restrictions. Blogger Ulyana Gavryunina reported them on social media and confirmed them to People of Baikal. On October 5, she arrived for a checkup. Her mother, who accompanied her, was not allowed into the maternity hospital. Since Friday, the center has admitted only pregnant patients.
“[At the hospital] they explained that there’s still unconfirmed information about a virus that might even be worse than coronavirus, and they don’t yet know what kind of virus it is or how to handle it, with the babies being so little. That’s why they introduced the quarantine. And no one knows how long it’ll last,” Ulyana told People of Baikal.
At the entrance, staff took Ulyana’s temperature and asked her to show her tongue. They gave her two health checklists to fill out. One was titled “Checklist for a suspected particularly dangerous infection: ‘Plague.’”
The checklist asked how the pregnant patient felt, whether she had been in contact with anyone who had arrived from abroad or was ill, and whether she had a fever or a stuffy nose.
The center barred partners from attending births during the quarantine. Ulyana had chosen to pay to give birth there so she could have someone with her. Now she is considering canceling her contract and wants to give birth in Angarsk, where she lives, because in Irkutsk “things feel unsettled, it’s really inconvenient and stressful, and there’s no point anymore.” In Angarsk, “everything is calm,” both in the city and at the maternity hospital.
An employee of the Irkutsk Plague Institute believes the city’s hospitals went into quarantine “just in case.” “Our scientists are working around the clock now. Samples just keep coming in. That’s because everyone admitted to a hospital with any signs of a cold is swabbed [for plague] and tested. That goes for absolutely every hospital.”
‘There are still no final findings on her death’
The Irkutsk Plague Institute is not commenting officially. An employee does not believe Darya broke a test tube in the laboratory: “That doesn’t happen here. But even if she had broken one, you’re working in a sealed containment cabinet, in sealed protective gear. Nothing would happen at all.”
A former university classmate of Shipilova’s who interned at the plague institute agrees: “Besides the strict safety measures, everyone there gets vaccinated against plague — even students who come for internships.” The medical professional says: “I can’t even imagine what could have happened there, even in theory.”
The plague institute’s employees have now been released from quarantine. “They took swabs from everyone for three days in a row, but everyone is completely healthy. Today is a normal workday for us,” one of Shipilova’s colleagues told People of Baikal on Monday, October 5. “Things are calm.”
Speaking anonymously, she said several times that “there are still no final findings [on the causes of Darya’s death].” “Tests are still being done, and there are no results at all yet. They’re still trying to determine the cause of death. Everything will settle down in a week, when the results are ready.”
Hi, I’m Vladislav Gorin.
I’m the host of Meduza’s daily Russian-language news podcast. This summer, the Russian authorities opened a criminal case against me — not for committing a crime, but for telling the truth about Russia and its war against Ukraine.
Because the Kremlin has branded me a criminal, I can’t go home. I also can’t safely travel to countries like Turkey — even though it’s a NATO member — because I could be arrested and extradited to Russia. I can’t even renew my passport at the consulate anymore.
None of this is going to stop me. I know there are hundreds of thousands of people in Russia who don’t want this war and who still believe in freedom and democracy, and they deserve access to independent journalism. Please support Meduza so I can keep reaching them.
‘The theory that there was no outbreak is unconvincing’
A Russian physician, who asked to remain anonymous, tells People of Baikal that he sees two possible explanations for what happened. Either Darya Shipilova was indeed found to have plague (or another particularly dangerous infection), but officials “contained it and decided not to talk about it publicly.” Or authorities and doctors still do not know exactly what happened, are “conducting an epidemiological and laboratory investigation,” and fear “panic and being held responsible.”
The physician finds the theory that there was no outbreak unconvincing. “A young employee of a plague institute suddenly develops a severe infection and quickly dies. Afterward, the hospital is closed, and the institute’s employees and her relatives are isolated. And an epidemiological investigation is conducted. That doesn’t prove it was plague, but it gives journalists sufficient grounds to investigate that possibility.”
The doctor suspects that “some potentially significant epidemiological event” did occur at the plague institute. He says the internal investigation and the isolation of a large number of employees point to this. Darya may not have realized that she had been at risk of exposure. Or she may have known about an incident but underestimated its seriousness.
The physician is skeptical of Rospotrebnadzor’s statement that Shipilova’s illness was “unrelated to her work.” Definitive laboratory confirmation takes up to 10 days. That time is needed to test blood, sputum, tissue, and other samples from Shipilova’s body.
“You can’t definitively identify the pathogen in a single day after the autopsy,” the physician said.
A former university classmate of Darya Shipilova’s who interned at the plague institute and now works at an Irkutsk hospital told People of Baikal the same thing. She called Rospotrebnadzor’s official reference to “extensive laboratory testing” in Shipilova’s case “rather vague wording.”
“It all depends on the testing method. And nowhere have they said exactly which test they performed.”
‘I’ve saved patients like that, but they let my daughter die’
Darya’s mother, 64-year-old Svetlana Shipilova, was still quarantined at an Irkutsk hospital on October 5. She told the outlet Glubina that samples and swabs were being taken from her every day. “They’re testing for something, looking for something. Maybe they’re worried about some other infection, so we don’t catch COVID or something in here.”
Shipilova said that as of October 5, she still had not received an official report on her daughter’s death. “I’m waiting for something official,” she said. “Not just something in the media, but from Rospotrebnadzor. It has to be an official document.”
Svetlana says she is “having a very hard time” and does not want to “read nasty things about my child”: “I know the truth. I’m fending off stupid people I know who believed all this. The smart ones didn’t believe it, of course. Even some medical professionals don’t understand that it’s impossible to break that test tube. Even if you fling it against a wall. Only someone who doesn’t know what they’re talking about could say that. Even hypothetically, you simply can’t spill what’s inside or break the tube. They’re that well protected.”
People who knew Darya also do not believe she could have broken a test tube. “They dragged her name through the mud without even finding out what happened,” a former schoolmate says. A friend tells People of Baikal: “I can’t square this whole story with the Dasha I knew. It’s like they’re talking about someone else. Knowing how hardworking and responsible she was, it just doesn’t add up for me.”
Svetlana Shipilova calls her daughter “a hard worker”: “Such a pure, pure soul. Her boss is taking it hard because she knew Dasha and knew why she hired her. It’s really hard to get a job at the plague institute. She saw how Dasha worked when she was interning there. She realized what a pure soul she was, such a workaholic,” she says. “I’ve saved more than one patient like that, but they didn’t save my daughter. They just let my daughter die.”
Darya has not been buried, and it’s not clear when the funeral will be. “Who’s going to bury her when we’re locked up in here?” her mother says.
Darya’s neighbors are worried that “no swabs at all” have been taken from them. “The clinic has called me every day since Friday to ask how I’m feeling. They say if I develop symptoms, I have to see a doctor. But no one tells us anything — what the illness was, what’s going on at all. It’s like we don’t exist. We’re shocked they haven’t quarantined us. We’ve all been in contact with her. We probably shouldn’t be going to work. We should be staying home.”
A notice at the building’s entrance asks residents who were not home during the disinfection to call the phone numbers listed “due to a sharp increase in illness in your building.” Among them is the number for the internal medicine department at Irkutsk City Hospital No. 10.
The residents who spoke to People of Baikal’s reporters say they feel well and have no symptoms.
‘There’s no panic in Shelekhov’
There is “no panic” in Shelekhov, where Darya Shipilova died, one resident tells People of Baikal. We arrived on a weekday, after the governor’s statements that the situation was stable. Mothers were walking with their children in the city park, and teenagers were riding bicycles. In stores, the shopping center, the local café, and the park, no one was wearing a mask. A few people wore them on buses — mainly older women and children.
The local café is busy at lunchtime. The word “plague” drifts over from just one table, where two women are eating and talking quietly. Everyone else is talking about other things.
The registration area at the Shelekhov outpatient clinic is packed with visitors. The clinic is operating as usual. Receptionists sit at desks, with visitors across from them and no protective glass screens between them. The electronic appointment system malfunctions: The terminals freeze, then print out stacks of tickets, slowing down registration. Only sample collection has been suspended since October 2. A notice still hangs on the procedure room door: “No blood samples will be taken due to quarantine,” followed by five exclamation points. The receptionists do not know when collection will resume.
The inpatient facility, a four-story brick building on the hospital campus, is closed for now and expected to remain so until the end of the week, the receptionists say.
A colorful banner on the inpatient building reads: “Doctors serving in the special military operation,” the Kremlin’s term for the war in Ukraine.
The plastic-framed windows are open, but no patients are visible near them. The door is wide open too. A trash can on the threshold and a mop handle across the doorway are meant to stop visitors from walking in. There are no quarantine notices, only a notice about access restrictions.
A female security guard in a black uniform came out to meet us. Her only protective gear was an ordinary face mask from a pharmacy.
“Is it really plague?” the journalist asks her.
“Who’s going to tell us? We only read about it online. A particularly dangerous infection — that’s all,” she replies.
There is a pharmacy at the hospital. The journalist asks for antibiotics and says plainly: “I want to keep some at home in case of a plague epidemic.” The pharmacist is not surprised. She initially offers a drug costing 680 rubles, but then sells the cheapest one, for 100 rubles. Antibiotics are available, and there is no rush to buy them.
At a pharmacy on the other side of town, another pack of inexpensive antibiotics is sold without anyone asking for a prescription. A mask requirement notice is posted on the door, but the pharmacist is not wearing a mask. The notice has been there since 2020, she says, laughing conspiratorially: “But I didn’t wear a mask back then either.”
At the entrance to the Irkutsk Aluminum Smelter (IrkAZ), however, even the groundskeepers sweeping up leaves are wearing masks. This is Shelekhov’s main employer. Its director introduced a mask requirement on October 3, and it remains in place.

articles.title: South Korea has become one of Russia’s biggest fuel suppliers. Some shipments are arriving on sanctioned tankers.
articles.body:
South Korea has become one of Russia’s biggest fuel suppliers. Some shipments are arriving on sanctioned tankers.
By the end of summer, South Korea had become Russia’s second-largest supplier of petroleum products, and sanctioned tankers were among those used to ship the fuel, The Guardian reported.
Tankers made 14 voyages from several South Korean ports to Russia’s Far East in July and August, carrying 176,000 tons of fuel, mostly diesel, according to The Guardian.
Seven tankers plied the routes, three of them under British and EU sanctions. One, the tanker Chongchon, did not even enter South Korean ports: its fuel was transferred from another vessel at sea, a method that conceals the cargo’s origin.
In at least two more cases, sanctioned tankers loading at South Korean ports officially listed Japan as their destination but instead headed for Vladivostok. Exactly who owned and sold the fuel remains unclear.
Russia imported 368,000 tons of petroleum products by sea in August, with 112,000 tons supplied by South Korea. Only India supplied more fuel to Russia that month.
South Korea’s Foreign Ministry declined to comment on the shipments or the use of sanctioned tankers. It said only that Seoul “supports, and is actively taking part in, international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery.”
South Korea has supplied Ukraine with humanitarian aid since the full-scale war with Russia began, along with non-lethal military equipment such as body armor and demining vehicles, The Guardian reported. But Seoul is trying to balance its support for Kyiv against its desire to maintain good relations with Moscow, and has only partially joined Western sanctions, mainly through export controls on industrial equipment and high-tech goods.
The fuel shipments, amid a crisis in Russia caused by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries, could expose Seoul as a “weak link” in Western efforts to pressure the Kremlin, The Guardian concluded.
The Guardian’s report on fuel shipments from South Korea to Russia came amid a diplomatic row between Seoul and Kyiv. At the U.N. General Assembly in late September, Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had transferred to South Korea two North Korean soldiers captured in early 2025.
Seoul accused Zelensky of violating an agreement to keep the transfer secret, noting that Ukraine itself had originally insisted on the secrecy. South Korea demanded that Kyiv issue an official apology.
Today, South Korea’s foreign minister, Cho Hyun, said he had received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, Andrii Sybiha, but that its level was different “from the level we expect.” He said Seoul now intends to “take firm measures.”

articles.title: Yemen hits Saudi airports, Aramco in 3 operations
articles.body:
Yemen's armed forces said they carried out three special operations with numerous ballistic and cruise missiles and drones against targets in Saudi Arabia, hitting Riyadh's King Khalid airport, the Aramco refinery in Rabigh, and Abha airport.

The second operation targeted the Aramco refinery in Rabigh, causing a fire at the site. The third operation targeted Abha airport, Khamis Mushait base, the Akfa camp in the Asir region, and other sensitive positions in Najran and Jizan.

Saree warned all global airlines using Saudi airspace about continuing their flights. articles.title: Gyurov Attacks Yotova: “Do We Have a Commander-in-Chief?” After Ship Attack
articles.body:
Presidential candidate Andrey Gyurov, along with We Continue the Change (PP) and Democratic Bulgaria (DB), accused President Iliana Yotova of failing to respond adequately after two commercial vessels were attacked by drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea and called for an immediate meeting of the Consultative Council for National Security (CCNS).
The criticism came hours after the drone strikes were reported, with one of the two ships sinking.
Prime Minister Rumen Radev called an emergency meeting at the Council of Ministers in response to the incident. He described the attack on the civilian vessels as "an absolutely unacceptable attack within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone," but did not identify the party to which he was directing the statement or say whose drones had struck the ships.
Attacks against civilian vessels in the Black Sea have become more frequent since Russia began its full-scale war against Ukraine. The incident is the first reported drone attack on ships inside Bulgaria's exclusive maritime economic zone.
PP Chairman Asen Vassilev said Bulgaria was inadequately protected despite the larger military budget. He blamed the country for not joining NATO's anti-drone initiative and said information-sharing with allies had been weakened after Chief of Defense Admiral Emil Eftimov resigned.
Vassilev said Yotova should have called the CCNS immediately after the attack, but argued that this "will not happen again."
"It would be normal to protect Bulgarian territorial waters, or at the very least to understand why they were not protected. Unfortunately, there is no real president or commander-in-chief," the PP leader said.
DB likewise demanded that the CCNS be convened. Ivaylo Mirchev, co-chair of Yes, Bulgaria, said the war could no longer be described as being "300 kilometers away from Bulgaria," pointing to the sinking of ships inside the country's exclusive economic zone. He accused Yotova of responding inadequately.
Mirchev said legislation requires the security council to convene every three months. He noted that its most recent meeting was held in February 2025 and addressed the spread of drugs and narcotics among young people.
He also attacked the government's handling of the ship incident and pointed out that Radev's statement did not identify where the attack had come from.
Mirchev contrasted that response with the authorities' handling of the drone incident near Kardam in August, which he said prompted a considerably stronger institutional reaction.
"When the drone is Ukrainian, Radev speaks out loudly. When there is evidence that the drones are Russian, he speaks of an 'incident' and says not a word about the attacking party," Mirchev said.
He further questioned the time taken to respond, saying around eight hours passed between the attack and the deployment of a Bulgarian aircraft.
Gyurov, a parliamentary candidate backed by the PP and DB coalitions, also sharply criticized Yotova. He said she neither made a public statement nor convened the CCNS in the hours after the ships were attacked.
"Supreme Commander-in-Chief is not a ceremonial title. Responsibility is proven during the most critical moments," Gyurov said.
He said the strikes showed that Bulgaria was confronting a real threat and questioned whether the country had a Commander-in-Chief capable of responding immediately. Gyurov accused Yotova of remaining silent for more than seven hours after the attack.
The two vessels targeted in Bulgarian waters were commercial general cargo ships: ALFA WATAN, which sails under the Togo flag, and ABLE, which sails under the Palau flag.
ALFA WATAN suffered critical structural damage before sinking east of the Bulgarian coast. Its crew remains missing as the search continues.
All 18 sailors aboard ABLE were rescued. One suffered severe burns, another sustained a head injury, and several others suffered minor injuries.
The reports of the attacks in Bulgarian waters came one day after another vessel was involved in an incident off the Romanian coast. Two sailors died in that case, while Ukraine accused Russia of using drones to attack the ship.
On Sunday, another vessel that had previously been attacked off Odesa was reported to have entered Bulgaria's maritime zone. Russian drones had struck the ship in August, after which its crew abandoned it. Its maneuvering systems are no longer operational, leaving the vessel drifting uncontrollably for two months.
Attacks on civilian vessels in the Black Sea have increased since Russia launched its full-scale war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Air Force: Intensive use is rapidly shortening F-16 service life
articles.body:
Air Force: Intensive use is rapidly shortening F-16 service life
According to Ukrinform, Colonel Yurii Cherevashchenko, deputy commander of the Ukrainian Air Force’s air defense division, made this statement during a meeting of the Verkhovna Rada’s Temporary Investigative Commission.
When asked whether Ukrainian aircraft, particularly the F-16s, are actively engaging Russian jet drones, Cherevashchenko said: “The F-16 is one of the most effective means of countering jet UAVs.”
At the same time, he was asked whether maintenance and the service life of the aircraft are the main challenges for the F-16s. He confirmed this and explained that aircraft have a limited service life, and Ukrainian planes are being used at an extremely high rate.
“Therefore, keeping the aircraft in a constant state of readiness is a very difficult task. And here, the assistance of our partners is critically important,” the deputy commander emphasized.
When asked whether Russian jet drones are being destroyed directly at their bases and launch sites, Cherevashchenko noted: “In general, the best option here is to destroy them at their bases and launch sites, the so-called drone ports. We’ve already carried out several such strikes. But these are heavily fortified facilities, reinforced with concrete, so it’s not easy to take them out. This is one of the key components of countering jet-powered UAVs.”
As reported by Ukrinform, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten stated after a phone call with President Volodymyr Zelensky that the Netherlands would assist Ukraine with maintenance, spare parts, and ammunition for F-16 fighter jets.

articles.title: Russia says potential deployment of NATO base, nuclear arms in Lithuania to raise tensions
articles.body:
Burc Eruygur
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
The Kremlin said on Tuesday that the potential deployment of a NATO military base or nuclear weapons in Lithuania would inevitably be seen by Russia as a step toward raising tensions.
Commenting on a vote by Lithuania’s parliament to advance a constitutional amendment that would remove a ban on deploying nuclear weapons on the country’s territory, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told a press briefing that the move cannot be viewed as “anything other than a step toward escalating tensions.”
“Neither of these moves will contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent. On the contrary – and to our regret – they will mark yet another significant escalation of tensions,” Peskov said.
He added that Russia will, consequently, be compelled to take “all necessary measures to guarantee its own security.”
The remarks come as the Lithuanian parliament, the Seimas, voted earlier Tuesday to advance a constitutional amendment that would remove a ban on the deployment of nuclear weapons on the country’s territory.
According to public broadcaster LRT, the amendment passed its first reading with 106 lawmakers voting in favor, while the final vote for the amendment is scheduled for Jan. 12.
The parliament conducted a vote late last month on amendment, receiving 99-13, with five abstentions, in favor of the proposal.
Peskov also commented on remarks by US President Donald Trump concerning reports of cases of pneumonic plague in Russia, saying it is always good when mutual assistance is offered.
He said Russia's public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor is providing "comprehensive information" on the situation in the country's Siberian region of Irkutsk.
Last week, Russian media outlets said Rospotrebnadzor defined the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region as stable amid reports of a person being diagnosed of a “pneumonia of unknown etiology.”
The reports said measures had been taken in connection with the case, which involved an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East. The employee has died.

articles.title: Ukraine’s drone pilots hit 76.5% more Russian infantry than two months ago: 2,699 in first five days of October
articles.body:
Ukraine's drone pilots are killing and wounding far more Russian infantry than they did a month ago. Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces confirmed that their pilots took out 2,699 Russian infantry from 1 to 5 October, 39.7% more than in the first five days of September, Commander Robert "Madiar" Brovdi wrote on Telegram on 6 October.
The Unmanned Systems Forces, the branch of Ukraine's military that fights with drones, count only losses verified by their own pilots in the military's Delta system, so the full picture of Russian losses is larger, Brovdi stressed. Compared with the first five days of August, the rise is 76.5%, from 1,529 losses, which he ties to denser and more frequent Russian assaults.
The sharpest growth occurred in the area of the 1st Azov Corps of Ukraine's National Guard on the Dobropillia-Pokrovsk axis in Donetsk Oblast, as fighting for fortress-belt cities continues. Drone pilots recorded 1,268 Russian losses there, 43% more than the 884 of early September and 91% more than the 664 of early August.
"Russia's hidden mobilization is in action. This is the beginning," Brovdi said ironically.
Russia doubles its monthly recruitment pace
Russian recruitment, mobilization, and contracts run at about 70,000 people a month, twice the 35,000 monthly average from January to August 2026, Brovdi noted on 16 September, when he forecast 12,500 losses for his pilots in September.
He expected the toll to keep climbing. Bigger records still lie ahead because of Russia's unannounced mobilization, Brovdi added on 24 September.
Drone pilots outpaced August by a quarter
September was completed above that forecast. The pilots logged 13,358 Russians killed or wounded, 25.35% more than the 11,010 of August, an average of 445 a day against 355, Brovdi reported. By his count, that equals the full assault infantry of one battalion every day, and his pilots hit a Russian target every 42 seconds.
Two sets of axes took the heaviest toll. In the first 24 days of September, the Dobropillia and Pokrovsk axes accounted for 4,018 losses, and the Oleksandrivka and Huliaipole axes for 3,021, according to Brovdi. The first of those groups covers the same Dobropillia-Pokrovsk axis where the Azov corps zone recorded the sharpest October rise.

He added: “The same applies to the deployment of nuclear weapons on the territory of a neighboring state. Lithuania, a member of the EU and NATO, borders Russia and close Moscow ally Belarus. The U.S. has kept an armored battalion of almost 1,000 troops there since 2019, in overlapping rotations, meaning the troops arrive and leave every few months.

articles.title: Air Force’s Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile Has First Flight Test
articles.body:
The U.S. Air Force has conducted the first flight test release of its developing hypersonic cruise missile, with that test taking place in Australia.
An Air Force spokesperson confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine on Oct. 6 that the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile flight test had occurred. The spokesperson did not specify a date.
The HACM flight test happened over a “designated Australian test range, gathering crucial data to advance the program’s objectives,” according to the spokesperson. The Woomera Test Range in the desert of southern Australia is commonly used to test missiles, aircraft, and projectiles.
The War Zone first reported on the test on Oct. 5.
“This effort is part of the Southern Cross Integrated Flight Research Experiment, a collaborative agreement built on more than 15 years of partnership between our two nations,” the spokesperson wrote in an email.
The spokesperson declined to provide further details regarding the method of test, platform used to conduct the test, flight times, durations, or speed.
RTX, the prime contractor on the missile, deferred any comments to the Air Force. Northrop Grumman, the missile’s engine-maker, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
HACM came out of a Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency program to develop a concept for a hypersonic air-breathing weapon and traces its origins to the Boeing X-51 Wave Rider project.
In April 2020, the Air Force issued an industry call for proposals on the potential weapon. It formally established the HACM program in 2022, picking RTX for the munition and Northrop for the scramjet engine.
HACM is one of two hypersonic weapons the Air Force is pursuing, along with the larger AGM-183 Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon, or ARRW.
The munition uses a conventional rocket booster to reach high speeds, then ditches it and engages the scramjet engine to reach and maintain speeds above Mach 5, or 3,300 miles per hour, at high altitudes.
HACM recently saw a yearlong delay because of design problems, and the Air Force cut its flight count for rapid-prototyping tests from seven to five. A 2024 GAO report said the program had a “zero margin” in its development timeline at the time, and it has since been declared behind schedule and over its original budget.
USAF is seeking about $1.2 billion to mature and field the missile in its fiscal 2027 budget proposal. It has also asked for a dedicated production line for the missile and requested $404 million for the first operational lot.
The Air Force plans to begin fielding HACM in fiscal 2027 and expects to move it to full-rate production by fiscal 2029.

articles.title: Ukraine cuts more than 4,000 vacant government posts and trims deputy ministers by about 20% in the first stage of civil service reform
articles.body:
Ukraine is thinning its state bureaucracy. Central government bodies will cut more than 4,000 vacant positions in the first stage of a civil service reform, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi says, with the number of deputy ministers to fall by about 20% and deputy heads of other central bodies by nearly 18%.
The reform aims to build a professional state apparatus that can carry out tasks quickly and effectively, Koretskyi said. It comes as Ukraine faces an economic crunch, and about $20 billion in EU aid is on hold, blocked by reforms Kyiv has not completed.
The cuts are only the visible first step, and the final headcount is not set yet. The number of deputies will be tied to the volume of tasks each office carries, Koretskyi states.
"The most important thing is that we are running a functional diagnostic of the state apparatus," he continues.
The Ukrainian government will assess which functions the bodies have and whether they align with the state's realities and priorities, and only then will it define the structure and final headcount.
Training is tied to the job
Another track reshapes how officials learn. Training will be linked to the tasks of each specific post, with outreach and internships for young people and a separate program for veterans, Koretskyi says.
The Public Administration Council, which brings together officials, members of parliament, and experts, has resumed work, presenting a detailed plan on the task and assigning responsibility for each area.
The squeeze that forces the cuts
The reform lands in a tight budget. The war is costing Ukraine about $155 billion a year, and with Western aid running late, Kyiv has frozen almost everything except the army, pensions, and public wages.
On 1 October, the state suspended a veterans' gym subsidy that had cost about $13 million and drawn more than 800,000 users, for lack of funds.
