articles.title: Europe is learning the wrong lesson from Russia's drone war
articles.body:
Europe is learning the wrong lesson from Russia's drone war
A sign reading "No drone zone" at Brussels Airport in Zaventem, Belgium, on Nov. 5, 2025. (Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images)
Megi Benia
Founder and Director of the Strategic Security Initiative
European governments are preparing for a form of confrontation that their current investments do not fully match.
While Russian-linked sabotage usually uses drones, logistics networks, criminal intermediaries, and deniable proxies against European cities, official policies and national strategies remain focused on detecting and intercepting each incident as it arises.
This approach treats only the instrument of attack, leaving the vulnerability it exploits mainly overlooked.
That vulnerability is clear: Europe's security architecture remains slow, fragmented, and expensive to mobilize across agencies and national boundaries.
In this environment, drone incursions become just separate incidents, while the problem of long, inefficient responses remains unaddressed. The incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4 with a quadcopter carrying plastic explosives that went unnoticed by security systems and landed near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft without detonating, belongs to a wider pattern of Russian sabotage activities against European cities, especially those targeting the major airports across the continent.
Each case, whether or not an attack was intended or completed, leaves the same residue of uncertainty, and that uncertainty is what makes cheap, deniable activity so effective against institutions that are otherwise highly capable.
A drone flying near or above an airport can disrupt the normal performance of critical civilian infrastructure by forcing the immediate closure of airports, overloading the work of police and intelligence services, and occupying resources even if no attack follows.
Democratic governments have legitimate reasons to take ambiguous threats seriously, but that very prudence can hand Moscow and its proxies an operational advantage, since an attacker capable of creating enough doubt to interrupt normal activity has no need to defeat an air-defense system at all.
Thus, the strategic value of such operations is their ability to force the defender to spend time, resources, and political capital determining whether an attack is actually taking place.
Under these conditions, Europe may win individual tactical engagements while losing the broader struggle over resources, resilience, and tempo.
More importantly, Europe's reading of Russia's drone campaign in Ukraine has focused attention on counter-drone technology, sensors, and interception systems, all of which are necessary for protecting infrastructure but cannot compensate for the institutional fragmentation that an adversary is actively exploiting.
In fact, Ukraine's experience demonstrates the importance of an organizational approach.
Against years-long Russian drone attacks, Ukraine has progressively connected battlefield reporting, air-surveillance data, acoustic and other sensor inputs, drone feeds, and intelligence into increasingly integrated situational-awareness and command systems, including the DELTA platform, allowing information from different sources to be brought together and distributed to those responsible for action.
It has also adapted its response architecture by combining centralized information with distributed defensive capabilities, enabling units and mobile teams to respond to threats without waiting for every decision to move through a complicated process of hierarchy.
As a result, Ukraine streamlined the process of detection, identification, decision, and action. This is a useful model that Europe should explore.
Attribution is another problem, because deniable sabotage is designed to take advantage of the interval between an incident and a verdict.
When investigators need weeks to establish responsibility, as it was during the Leipzig incident, where German authorities took around four weeks to publicly assign responsibility to Russia, attribution becomes a retrospective exercise and no longer functions as an indispensable aspect of deterrence and defense.
Indeed, public attribution requires credible evidence, and obtaining one might take a long time before authorities establish rock-solid data. .
However, when a citizen is suddenly stranded at an airport due to a drone-related disruption, the consequences of delayed decision-making are immediate and tangible.
To effectively address these challenges, Europe needs to organize counter-sabotage efforts that would incorporate connections, allowing aviation authorities, law enforcement, intelligence services, and armed forces to share information across institutional and national boundaries before an incident becomes a crisis.
In this process, applying lessons from the Ukrainian experience is essential because Ukraine has been forced to solve the problem Europe now faces, and it has learned to turn fragmented information into a usable operational picture and then convert that picture into action before an adversary can weaponize the gap.
Intercepting a drone can prevent an incident, but it cannot address the broader system behind it, leaving the entire process supporting a single drone operation largely intact.
Herewith, success should not be measured by the number of intercepted drones, as it reflects little about the capabilities of the entire system.
The decisive advantage is ensuring that Russia, not Europe, is forced to react, robbed of initiative, denied the ability to dictate the tempo, and made to confront operational costs and risks. Because only by reclaiming the initiative can Europe shift from a posture of reaction to one of control and force its adversaries onto the defensive.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

articles.title: US conducts first flight test of HACM hypersonic missile — web portal
articles.body:
NEW YORK, October 6. /TASS/. The United States has carried out the first flight test of the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile (HACM) at a test range in Australia, The War Zone (TWZ) portal reported.
The US Air Force’s hypersonic missile, developed by Raytheon in collaboration with Australian specialists, has finally entered, according to the website, "the flight test phase." At least one test has been conducted so far at the Woomera Test Range in Australia.
The HACM program has faced significant delays, the website reports, and the US Air Force took a risky step by scaling back the overall scope of testing in an effort to stay on schedule. The stated goal is "to initiate a rapid fielding effort and procure HACM in fiscal year 2027," according to TWZ.
According to a US Air Force spokesperson, the HACM tests were conducted as part of joint "continuous work to advance long-range strike capabilities." He did not specify when the testing occurred.
The technical specifications of the HACM missile are classified. According to media reports, the missile consists of two stages, a rocket booster and a scramjet cruiser, which separates from the booster and eventually dives toward its target. The missile is capable of reaching speeds of up to Mach 7. Its range is approximately 500 km.

articles.title: Taiwan Air Force plans US F-16V support talks next year

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Air Force plans to send personnel to the US next year to attend a meeting on procuring operational-support equipment, weapons, and ammunition for its F-16V Block 70 fleet.

The F-16V Block 70 program involves more than delivering the aircraft themselves. Establishing operational capabilities also requires integrating avionics, electronic warfare systems, logistical support, and various weapons, Liberty Times reported.
The new fighter variants are equipped with the L3Harris Viper Shield all-digital electronic warfare system, which can detect, identify, and counter electronic threats. The system is integrated with the AN/APG-83 Active Electronically Scanned Array radar.
Taiwan’s F-16Vs can carry AIM-120 beyond-visual-range air-to-air missiles, AIM-9-series short-range missiles, AGM-88 anti-radiation missiles, AGM-84 Harpoon anti-ship missiles, and Joint Direct Attack Munitions.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Defense Ministry says some suppliers cannot build weapons ordered, and drops contracts to free $346 million for front
articles.body:
Ukraine is canceling part of its planned military purchases and moving the money to other priorities. Ukraine's Defense Ministry has announced that it, together with the General Staff and the Logistics Forces Command, will free about $346 million by terminating some weapons contracts and dropping some planned purchases.
What the army planned to buy in 2024 and 2025 may no longer be suitable for the front, the ministry noted, because technology and tactics change quickly. The review comes four days after the Ukrainian government drew about $1.1 billion from the defense reserve to pay soldiers in October amid a looming economic crisis.
The ministry gives five reasons for the review: some weapons no longer match combat tasks, certain suppliers cannot build the planned volume, certain models have not been codified, partners already cover some needs, and cheaper means can perform specific jobs in larger numbers.
"For us, there is one criterion: does the item work for results in combat today. Every hryvnia released from irrelevant contracts must reach the troops as the weapons needed right now and in the right place," Col. Yurii Pohribnyi, commander of the Logistics Forces, says.
The procurement agency calls each producer
The General Staff set the final list of purchases for review, and the ministry forwarded the documents to the Defense Procurement Agency to implement the decision. For specific items, delivery volumes were adjusted rather than canceled, which the contracts allow when needs change.
Affected producers have been informed, and the agency is discussing each item with suppliers based on the status and payments of each contract. Artem Romaniuk, acting director of the agency, has explained that further steps on each contract will depend on the army's current needs and the contract terms. The list of weapons stays secret for security reasons.
Funds freed up by terminating contracts and canceling planned purchases will be redirected to the urgent needs of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.

articles.title: Oil tanker ablaze after sea-drone attack off Russian Black Sea coast
articles.body:
Oil tanker ablaze after sea-drone attack off Russian Black Sea coast
A Liberian-flagged oil tanker has caught fire off Russia’s Black Sea coast after being attacked by unmanned boats near Sochi, the Russian Transport Ministry has said. All 23 members of its crew, who are Indian nationals, were rescued and no injuries have been reported.
The Aframax Rio, which was carrying crude oil, was struck by sea drones on Tuesday, according to the ministry. The attack triggered an oil fire in the Black Sea, with emergency crews initially unable to approach the tanker because of the intensity of the blaze.
Russian Transport Minister Andrey Nikitin convened an emergency response headquarters, while the ministry said sufficient personnel and equipment had been deployed to deal with the consequences.
Authorities temporarily closed beaches in the nearby federal territory of Sirius as a precaution. Local officials said subsequent monitoring found pollutant concentrations below permitted limits and that there was no immediate danger to public health.
In a separate incident on Tuesday, two merchant vessels were struck by unidentified naval and aerial drones in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, some 128km off its coast. The Togo-flagged Alfa Watan suffered critical damage and sank, while the Palau-flagged Able caught fire. Eighteen crew members were rescued from the latter vessel, two of them with severe injuries.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev condemned the attacks as a “blatant violation of international law and maritime law” and warned that repeated strikes were disrupting Black Sea shipping and driving insurance costs higher.
Kiev has not publicly claimed responsibility for the strikes. Ukraine has, however, sharply expanded attacks on Russian oil infrastructure and commercial shipping in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov in recent months, using combinations of naval and aerial drones to strike vessels linked to Russian ports.
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky vowed over the weekend to intensify attacks on Russian oil refineries, prompting Moscow to announce that it would expand strikes on Ukrainian military-industrial facilities and related infrastructure. Moscow has already been targeting vessels it says are carrying military or dual-use cargo to Ukrainian Black Sea ports, while the Russian Defense Ministry said Zelensky would bear “full personal and political responsibility” for any further escalation.
The strikes have also become a factor in the global fuel market. US President Donald Trump said on Monday that rising American gasoline prices were now being driven less by disruption around the Strait of Hormuz and more by Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries.
“What’s driving up gasoline is no longer the Strait of Hormuz,” Trump wrote, arguing instead that Russian refineries “are being blown up by Ukraine.”
Trump had previously urged Zelensky to “stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” saying the campaign was “hurting the world.” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has similarly said Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy assets and refined products are contributing to a broader “energy shock.”

articles.title: Syria's new rulers and Hezbollah: An unlikely détente?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Syria's new rulers and Hezbollah: An unlikely détente?
Lebanon’s Hezbollah and Syria’s post-Assad government have a contentious relationship formed in the bloody crucible of the Syrian civil war, when Hezbollah intervened against the Syrian opposition in 2013 in defence of the ailing regime of Bashar Al-Assad.
However, a recent Reuters report suggests that the two sides have held secret meetings in Turkey designed to defuse tensions between them, which may suggest a relative détente.
This follows sporadic clashes on stretches of the non-demarcated Syrian-Lebanese border since the fall of the regime, and accusations by the Syrian government that Hezbollah is operating cells inside the country.
According to the report, both sides agreed they held no hostility towards one another, and that Syria assured Hezbollah that it would not invade Lebanon.
Syrian officials also reportedly asked Hezbollah to help stop cross-border smuggling, and to dismantle its sleeper cells.
The Syrian government’s English-language platform quickly denied the report, stating “these claims are false. No such meeting took place”.
The Turkish Presidency’s communications directorate also denied the report, claiming it was "entirely unfounded". Hezbollah has not publicly commented on the report.
However, if these meetings did indeed occur, it would reflect a developing relationship between them from battlefield foes to pragmatic, albeit suspicious, partners.
A bitter history
After the 2006 war with Israel, Hezbollah and its former leader, Hassan Nasrallah, were once looked upon favourably by large parts of the Syrian population.
That changed in 2013 when the armed group intervened in Syria to bolster the Assad regime. “Hezbollah formed the elite troops fighting on behalf of the regime,” explains Issam Al-Reis, a senior researcher at ETANA, a Syrian research organisation, to The New Arab.
“By 2013, as the regime’s military weakened, they became the main force fighting the opposition,” he added.
“They often faced off against HTS [which formed Syria’s new government in 2024], and so they have both lost people fighting each other.”
Early on in its intervention, Hezbollah was implicated in the 2013 siege of Al-Qusayr, in which they restricted access to food, water, and medical supplies into the town, in a strategy that may have resulted in the deaths of hundreds of people according to the UN’s Commission of Inquiry.
Similar tactics were subsequently employed by the Shia group during the sieges of Homs and Aleppo.
HTS, in the guise of its previous iteration, the Al-Qaeda-affiliated Jabhat Al-Nusra, had claimed a number of bombings in Lebanon that killed dozens, many of them centred upon the largely Shia Dahiyeh in southern Beirut.
It is within this context that the relationship between Hezbollah and the forces that would become Syria’s new government became “one of extreme hostility,” Nicholas Blanford, a Beirut-based analyst at the Atlantic Council, tells The New Arab.
As Syria’s civil war developed, Blanford also acknowledges that their relationship developed an important “sectarian element”.
“It became an enmity not just between battlefield opponents but Shiite and Sunni Islamists.”
This enmity didn’t disappear following the fall of the Assad regime in 2024.
A new Syria
HTS launched its offensive the day after the ceasefire between Hezbollah and Israel began following the 2024 war. Over 11 days, it rolled back years of territory hard-won by the regime and its Lebanese ally.
Whilst Hezbollah’s leader Naim Qassem pledged to “thwart” the offensive, crippled by its recent confrontation with Israel, the armed group was able to do little to save Assad.
In the closing hours of Assad’s regime, tens of thousands of Syrian Shias, Hezbollah associates, and regime officials flooded into neighbouring Lebanon - many remain housed in Hezbollah funded refugee camps in north Bekaa.
Following the fall, relations between the two floundered. The Syrian government has repeatedly accused Hezbollah of running a network of cells within the country designed to destabilise the country’s fledgling post-war recovery or potentially incite conflict with Israel.
Last week, Syria’s Ministry of Interior announced the arrest of three individuals who they claim were part of a Hezbollah-affiliated cell, as they had been attempting to set up rocket launchers in the southern Syrian province of Deraa.
According to Al-Reis, following the 2018 reconciliation between the regime and the armed groups in southern Syria, Hezbollah recruited approximately 5,000 fighters from the factions.
“It has retained contacts in southern Syria and has been attempting to reconnect and recruit from that network,” he explains to The New Arab.
Hezbollah has repeatedly denied the accusations. In September, however, the intelligence branch of Lebanon’s Internal Security Forces carried out a series of raids, arresting five individuals, some with links to Hezbollah, who were allegedly training Syrian nationals in Lebanon for operations inside Syria.
Equally, the new Syrian government’s relations with Lebanon have been overshadowed by reports of US pressure on President Ahmed al-Sharaa to intervene militarily against Hezbollah.
Whilst al-Sharaa has repeatedly denied any intention to invade Lebanon, stating “we are looking for economic channels, not military ones,” in a June interview with Al Mashhad, it has nevertheless inflamed historical memories in Beirut.
Syria occupied large parts of Lebanon between 1976 and 2005.
“Since independence, some in Syria have continued to see Lebanon as an extension of ‘historical’ Syria,” says Blanford. “There are concerns that the new government may have this mentality, but so far they appear to be prioritising state-to-state relations.”
Syria has adopted a ‘no enemies’ approach to its post-Assad foreign policy. One element of it has been a rapprochement with Russia, which, in 2016, intervened in the Syrian civil war on behalf of the regime.
In October 2025, al-Sharaa visited Russia and met Vladimir Putin, a meeting which paved the way for Syria and Russia to agree on a deal in August which will hand over Russia’s bases on the Syrian coast to the Syrian military whilst allowing a small Russian contingent to remain on site.
However, Syria has not pursued a similar rapprochement with Iran. The countries still has no formal diplomatic relationship, and last week, Mohammed Al-Jafal, advisor for Afro-Asian Affairs at Syria’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, stated that any new relationship between the two “must respect Syria’s sovereignty”.
“The intensity of hostility to Hezbollah and Iran is much deeper than towards Russia,” says Blanford. “Russia is seen as a global player that will ultimately need to be accommodated with.”
The difficult relationship has also complicated Damascus’ engagement with the Lebanese state due to the “suspicion that Lebanon is controlled by Hezbollah,” Sam Heller, a Beirut-based Researcher with Center for International Policy, tells The New Arab.
“Bilateral engagement has been slow and incremental due to this, although the Syrians are slowly developing a feel for the make-up of Lebanon’s politics and the extent of Hezbollah’s real influence.”
Why now?
Before this recent meeting, there have been some signs of a potential softening of Hezbollah and Syria’s relationship. In July, Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Al-Shaibani said Damascus was open to meeting with Hezbollah. In August, Qassem said that “there is no impediment to a public meeting”.
The southern regions of both Syria and Lebanon are facing a sustained Israeli occupation, which may have influenced Ankara’s decision to facilitate talks.
“Turkey is playing a leading role regionally in opposing Israeli actions in Lebanon and Syria,” says Al-Reis. “For them, playing this intermediary role may be more about trying to balance Israel than anything.”
Hezbollah, meanwhile, is interested in “establishing a predictable relationship without recurring fears of border clashes and potential military escalation on a new front,” says Heller.
However, for Blanford, it seems that Hezbollah is operating a “dual policy,” of beginning to engage diplomatically with Syria’s rulers whilst still working to destabilise them in parallel.
Syria’s government may be more concerned about the risk of destabilisation posed by Hezbollah. Cells affiliated with the group have on several occasions been caught setting up rocket launchers in southern Syria - just one successful rocket launch against Israeli positions could invite a fierce Israeli response.
Yet analysts say that it remains politically difficult for the Syrian government to acknowledge talks between them due to the intensity of animosity from large parts of the Syrian population.
“Ultimately talks may just be driven by a sense that each side could undermine the other,” says Blanford.
“That despite the history of bloodshed between them, it is better for their own [respective] interests to reach some understanding.”
Cian Ward is a journalist based in Damascus, covering conflict, migration, and humanitarian issues
Follow him on X: @CP__Ward

articles.title: Russians held at U.S. immigration detention center plan hunger strike over poor conditions
articles.body:
Russians held at U.S. immigration detention center plan hunger strike over poor conditions
Fourteen Russians held in an immigration detention center in the state of Georgia have signed a collective complaint about the conditions of their detention and announced that they plan to begin a hunger strike. Copies of the complaint were obtained by Vot Tak, Agentstvo, and The Insider. Four sources familiar with the conditions in detention confirmed the document’s authenticity to Agentstvo. Here’s what we know so far.
Russians held in an immigration jail in Georgia say they are not treated for illness, are fed poorly, and have limited contact with the outside world
One of the most serious allegations in the collective complaint is the lack of medical care. The Russians say that while detained, they receive almost no treatment. Emergency care is only provided in cases of loss of consciousness or severe bleeding. For fever, high blood pressure, or acute pain, detainees may have to wait “a week or more” for treatment.
Alexei Kovalko, one of the authors of the complaint, said he once lost consciousness while having blood drawn. After he was revived, he asked staff to let him lie down, still feeling weak and dizzy. He was taken to a room that contained only a toilet and left lying on the bare concrete floor for several hours.
Kovalko said an even more acute problem is dental care. “My personal experience: numerous complaints about tooth pain and requests to see a dentist have been ignored for almost two years. They aren’t even registered in the system,” the Russian wrote in the complaint.
He and the other authors of the complaint also cite poor-quality water and bad food (they are mostly given canned and frozen food); cold cells (they have to sleep in their clothes); and noise in common areas (televisions there aren’t turned off until 2 a.m., which interferes with sleep, especially since earplugs are banned).
The complaint separately lists problems with communication: paper mail is delivered selectively, email is unavailable, and phone calls are expensive. Many of the people held at the jail are going through court proceedings over their immigration status, and these rules severely limit their ability to communicate with lawyers and defend themselves.
“The goal of this facility is to deport the maximum number of people and create conditions in which it’s impossible to defend your case in immigration court,” the complaint states. Its authors believe this is confirmed by the behavior of the detention center’s warden. He has repeatedly told the people held there that they will not be living in the U.S., and once told the Russians: “Don’t worry, we’ll send you back to your cozy Gulag.”
The immigration jail in Georgia was converted from a regular prison. Conditions there have largely remained the same
The immigration detention center named in the collective complaint is the D. Ray James Correctional Facility in Folkston, Georgia, named after a former mayor of the city. It is owned by GEO Group, one of the two largest private prison operators in the U.S.
The facility previously operated as a federal prison. In 2025, it was converted into an immigrant detention center. The people held there are not necessarily criminals and are not serving criminal sentences; for them, detention means being deprived of their liberty over a possible deportation while their case is being considered in immigration court. In practice, however, conditions in detention centers can resemble those in prisons.
Dmitry Valuev, president of the organization Russian America for Democracy in Russia (RADR), told Vot Tak that conditions in American immigration detention centers are difficult, but not everywhere are they as harsh as at the D. Ray James facility in Folkston.
“There are select detention centers where vegetables and fresh fruit are given out regularly, even daily, but there are many others where fruits and vegetables aren’t part of the regular diet. The same goes for medical services — people with chronic illnesses suffer a great deal, because treatment in detention centers is mostly very basic, without advanced diagnostics,” Valuev said.
He stressed that immigration detention centers are normally meant for short-term detention — up to several weeks — and that food and medical care standards there are designed with that in mind. In practice, however, people can remain in detention for years, and in those cases, the conditions effectively become torturous.
Russians (and detainees from other countries) plan to start a hunger strike. They want to be transferred to another facility
The collective complaint bears the signatures of 14 people. According to materials obtained by outlets that received a copy of the complaint, all of them are Russian. Among them are the complaint’s authors, Alexei Kovalko and Alexander Borovkov, and 12 other men who have been held in Folkston for five to 30 months. Kovalko, for example, has been in the jail for more than two years — 28 months.
The Russians relayed through relatives that they plan to declare a hunger strike on October 6 to protest the conditions of their detention. According to them, about 50 detainees in total plan to take part in the hunger strike — not only Russians but also Latin Americans, Iranians, Afghans, Chinese nationals, and people from other countries.
“Everyone wants to be released or transferred to other detention centers where they could get a fair hearing on their cases, bail requests, and petitions. At the same time, they’re demanding improved detention conditions,” Polina Gerdyukova, the wife of Andrei Gerdyukov — one of the signatories of the complaint who has been held in detention since February 2026 — told the independent Russian investigative outlet Agentstvo.
The flow of Russians seeking asylum in the U.S. increased after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. People who end up in immigration jails are usually those who crossed the border from Mexico and requested asylum in the U.S., or who were detained later while already in the country. As of spring 2026, RADR estimated the number of Russians in U.S. detention centers at 700–800 people.
After Donald Trump returned to power, U.S. authorities began detaining and deporting foreigners more aggressively. RADR believes that around 300–400 Russians may have been deported over the past year alone. They are being sent back to Russia even though they may face criminal charges or military conscription there.
At least two cases are known in which Russians who had sought asylum in the U.S. were detained on criminal charges after being deported back to Russia. The first involves serviceman Artem Vovchenko: after arriving in Russia, he was sent to a pretrial detention center on charges of abandoning his military unit, but he managed to get transferred to a civilian hospital and escaped from there. The second case is the prosecution of businessman and activist Leonid Melekhin, who was ultimately sentenced to six years on charges of justifying terrorism.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: Commandos land from German submarine on Scottish coast
articles.body:
British commandos have come ashore at Cape Wrath from a German attack submarine and directed the guns of a Portuguese frigate onto targets inland, during the largest test of every part of the UK Commando Force in fifteen years, according to the Royal Navy.
The landing took place during Exercise Strike Warrior, which the service describes as the first occasion since the war in Afghanistan on which all the specialist elements of the formation have worked together. More than 2,000 personnel from six nations are taking part, drawn from the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Canada, Germany, Norway and the United States, and deployed across the Western Isles, the North-West Approaches, Galloway, the Borders and the North Sea.
Navy and Army commandos from 148 Battery Commando Forward Observation Battery, the unit trained to carry out reconnaissance and call down naval gunfire from behind enemy lines, left the submarine in inflatable raiding boats and established an observation post on the cliffs at the most north-westerly point of mainland Britain. From there they directed the guns of the Portuguese warship NRP Dom Francisco de Almeida onto positions ashore.
The battery’s operations officer, who cannot be named for operational reasons, said: “This level of complexity and coordination of live assets has not been achieved by 148 Battery for nearly 30 years.
“We wanted to demonstrate to our partners across the United Kingdom Commando Force, wider UK Defence and NATO Special Operations Force community the type of missions we are prepared to execute against future threats.
“Warfighting is our focus, and we are prepared to employ specialist assets to deliver Multi-Domain Fires and Targeting.”
Three navies were involved in the single sequence at Cape Wrath. The German submarine found the targets, the commandos put themselves ashore without being seen, and the Portuguese ship supplied the firepower. The Royal Navy has not identified the submarine.
Earlier in the exercise the same battery controlled the naval gunfire of ships from Standing NATO Maritime Group One, the alliance’s standing task group in northern European waters. The Dutch frigate HNLMS Van Amstel and the Royal Canadian Navy frigate HMCS St John’s both worked with commandos in observation posts to bring their guns onto targets.
Eight warships and 19 aircraft are taking part in Strike Warrior, which began on 28 September and finishes on Friday. Alongside the gunnery serials, the exercise has covered amphibious landings, boarding operations, intelligence and surveillance missions, logistics and sustainment, maritime security and anti-submarine warfare. Commandos have flown drone missions including strikes and resupply to troops in contact, and have built underground medical facilities.
Cape Wrath matters to this kind of training because it is the only place in Britain, and one of very few in Europe, where warships can fire live rounds at a land target. The range takes in Garvie Island off the headland, and the combination of the cliffs behind and the open Atlantic in front is what allows observation parties to work close to live naval gunfire.
The participation of a German boat and a Portuguese frigate alongside Dutch and Canadian ships reflects how the Commando Force now expects to operate, which is as the land element of a NATO maritime group rather than as a national force working alone. Norway and the United States also have personnel committed, and the stated purpose of the exercise is rehearsing allied crisis response in the High North and the North Atlantic.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones kill two in Moscow Region – officials
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones kill two in Moscow Region – officials
Two civilians have been killed and nine injured after Ukraine launched 650 drones toward Moscow and the surrounding region overnight, local officials have said.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said in the early hours of Tuesday that most of the UAVs were destroyed at “distant lines,” while 134 were intercepted on the approaches to Moscow itself.
In Moscow Region, air defenses neutralized 185 drones, Governor Andrey Vorobyov reported. A 20-year-old man was killed in the settlement of Radumlya, northwest of Moscow, while rescuers found a 71-year-old man dead beneath the rubble of a destroyed private home in Barybino, south of the capital, with a woman in the same building receiving injuries.
A man in Pokrovskoye, west of Moscow, was hospitalized with shrapnel wounds, while two residents of the Istra area, also west of the capital, were taken to hospital. Three people in Lyakhovo, south of Moscow, received medical care but declined hospitalization, Vorobyov added.
Vorobyov said a total of 47 private homes were damaged across the region. In Lobanovo, south of the capital, windows and balcony glazing were blown out in four apartments, while a nearby boiler house was also damaged. Three cars were hit, and a small fire at a warehouse in Litvinovo, northwest of Moscow, was extinguished, according to the governor.
According to the Russian Defense Ministry, a total of 868 Ukrainian drones were intercepted across the country overnight.
On Tuesday, Rodion Miroshnik, the head of the Russian Foreign Ministry mission tracking alleged Ukrainian war crimes, told TASS that 29 civilians, including two children, were killed and 206 injured in Ukrainian attacks on Russian regions over the past week alone. He added that 98% were victims of drone strikes.
Ukraine has ramped up attacks deep into Russia in recent weeks, targeting oil refineries and civilian infrastructure. After Vladimir Zelensky pledged to escalate the strikes even further, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Sunday that it had “taken note” of the statement, vowing to intensify attacks on Ukrainian military and defense industrial facilities as well as related infrastructure. Moscow maintains it never targets civilians.

articles.title: Russia Says Ukraine Just Launched Its Biggest Strike of the War—1,750 Drones and 17 Flamingo Missiles

Russia Says Ukraine Just Launched Its Biggest Strike of the War—1,750 Drones and 17 Flamingo Missiles
Ukraine launched what Russia described as the largest combined drone and missile strike of the war, with 1,750 fixed-wing UAVs and 17 Flamingo cruise missiles allegedly used against targets across Russia over the past 24 hours, the Russian Defense Ministry claimed on October 6.
Moscow also said its air defenses intercepted two guided aerial bombs and one HIMARS rocket during the same period. The figures have not been independently verified.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
If accurate, the drone count would exceed Ukraine’s previous reported record from August 18, when Russian authorities said 1,671 UAVs were detected over 15 regions, occupied Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas.
The reported use of 17 Flamingo cruise missiles would also represent a major jump from earlier strikes, when launches were generally reported in groups of three to six.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said 11 regions, occupied Crimea, and targets over the Azov Sea came under attack overnight.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 650 drones were flying toward the Russian capital during the attack. He initially reported 105 intercepted on approach to Moscow and later said another 68 had been destroyed.
Moscow region Governor Andrei Vorobyov said 185 UAVs were intercepted across 16 municipalities.
Russian authorities also reported damage to 47 private homes in Volokolamsk, Stupino, Dmitrov, Naro-Fominsk, Serpukhov, Domodedovo and Istra, as well as damage to an apartment building in the village of Lobanovo.
The scale of the overnight attack also caused major disruption at Moscow’s airports, where more than 200 flights were delayed or canceled after midnight.
Sheremetyevo saw the largest impact, with about 47 departing flights and 106 arrivals affected. Another 28 departures and 23 arrivals were disrupted at Vnukovo, while Domodedovo reported changes to four flights.
Previous reports indicated that Ukrainian forces recorded more than 11,000 confirmed strikes against Russian targets located over 20 kilometers (12 miles) from the front line in September, while also hitting a record number of Russian air defense systems.
September marked the first time the number of confirmed strikes beyond 20 kilometers exceeded 11,000 in a single month. Ukrainian forces also recorded their highest number of strikes against targets located more than 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the front.

articles.title: Putin’s Family War Games Are Now in Full Swing
articles.body:
- Category

Putin’s Family War Games Are Now in Full Swing
What began as a Kremlin-backed “patriotic” family initiative has grown into nationwide military-style competitions where children as young as 11 train alongside their parents, handle weapons, practice battlefield skills, and are coached by veterans of Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Russia has expanded its military-style youth training into entire households, bringing parents and children together for nationwide war games that include shooting, grenade throwing, drone operations, and tactical exercises.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Barents Observer on October 6, families from nearly every Russian region are taking part in the “Family Zarnitsa” competition, a Kremlin-backed initiative promoted as a way to strengthen “traditional values” and ties between generations.
Teams consist of two adults and two children aged 11 or older. Participants wear military-style uniforms and compete in exercises including grenade throwing, dismantling and reassembling Kalashnikov assault rifles, marksmanship, tactical field operations, first aid, and evacuating simulated casualties.
The training grounds are designed to resemble combat environments, while each family is assigned a coach who is a veteran of Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The project was formally presented in early 2025 by Russian Deputy Defense Minister Anna Tsivilova and was later backed by Vladimir Putin.
“Today, the ‘Family Zarnitsa’ project brings families together, strengthens the bond between generations, and integrates veterans of the Special Military Operation into a system of mentoring and patriotic education for young people,” Tsivilova said, using Russia’s official term for its war against Ukraine.
The competition is organized by several Kremlin-linked groups involved in the militarization of Russian youth, including Yunarmiya, VOIN, and Movement of the First, alongside the state-run Defenders of the Fatherland fund.
Russia has spent years expanding military and patriotic education among children and teenagers through organizations such as Yunarmiya and VOIN, whose combined membership now reaches hundreds of thousands of young Russians.
After regional qualification rounds, successful families advance to a national final. One of this year’s participants was the Maksimenko family from Zaozersk, a closed naval town on Russia’s Kola Peninsula.
The family defeated teams from Pechenga, Lovozero, and Murmansk before reaching the national final in Volgograd, where it finished 10th among 89 teams.
Yevgeniya Maksimenko, the family’s mother, said the competition included drones, mines, shooting, grenades, radio communications, and first aid, but described teamwork as its main lesson.
“We’ve become a REAL team. There are no ‘mums,’ ‘dads,’ or ‘kids’ here,” she wrote on social media.
Maksimenko has also been active in Russia’s ruling United Russia party. In 2025, she received an award from former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev for her work with the party’s women’s movement. Her eldest daughter, Liza, is a member of the VOIN military youth organization in Murmansk.
Earlier, in March 2025, Putin ordered the nationwide launch of “Family Zarnitsa,” a military-patriotic competition for parents and children proposed by Deputy Defense Minister Anna Tsivilyova. The initiative was designed to combine physical challenges with patriotic education and activities focused on Russian history and culture.

Ukraine Records 11,000+ Deep Strikes in September, Hits More Russian Air Defenses Than Ever
Ukrainian forces recorded more than 11,000 confirmed strikes against Russian targets located over 20 kilometers (12 miles) from the front line in September, while also hitting a record number of Russian air defense systems, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense reported on October 6.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the ministry, September marked the first time the number of confirmed strikes beyond 20 kilometers exceeded 11,000 in a single month. Ukrainian forces also recorded their highest number of strikes against targets located more than 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the front.
The largest concentration of these longer-range strikes occurred along the Russian military logistics route linking temporarily occupied Mariupol with Crimea, the ministry said.
September also saw the highest number of Russian air defense assets hit since the launch of Ukraine’s ePoints battlefield performance program. The targets included radar systems, with one Russian air defense asset struck at a distance of 552 kilometers (343 miles).
In total, Ukrainian units recorded 33,087 confirmed strikes against Russian personnel during September. Only March and April saw higher monthly figures in 2026 under the ePoints program.
The Defense Ministry said all results counted by the program are supported by video recorded in Ukraine’s DELTA battlefield management system and subsequently verified by the Brave1 defense innovation cluster.
Ukraine also reported increased effectiveness against Russian Shahed-type attack drones. Ukrainian forces downed 28% more Shahed-type UAVs in September than in August, despite Russia changing its aerial attack tactics and deploying a growing number of jet-powered drones.
The ePoints program tracks battlefield results across Ukrainian military units, allowing defense officials to compare the effectiveness of different weapons and tactics and expand successful approaches across the Defense Forces.
Earlier, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces reported hitting or destroying 300 Russian air defense assets in the first 261 days of 2026, including 162 air defense systems, 124 radar complexes, and 14 electronic warfare systems.

articles.title: India expands Navy’s BrahMos strike capability
articles.body:
India expands Navy’s BrahMos strike capability
India has contracted for more BrahMos missile launchers and fire-control systems for its Navy warships, expanding deployment of its primary maritime-strike weapon across the fleet.
The Defense Ministry signed the roughly $69 million contract with BrahMos Aerospace Private Limited in New Delhi on Tuesday. The order covers fire-control systems and launchers for Indian Navy ships and was made under a scheme to buy items that are indigenously designed and manufactured.
Several frontline Indian warships including destroyers and frigates already are armed with BrahMos missiles. New ships commissioned in recent years have received the system as standard equipment, while older vessels are being retrofitted in phases as part of a wider push to expand BrahMos deployment across the fleet by 2030, reports said.
BrahMos can be launched vertically or at an incline from naval platforms and is capable of striking both ships and land targets at extended ranges at supersonic speed.
The Indian Navy has operated BrahMos since 2005, when its anti-ship variant was integrated onto Rajput-class destroyers. The system has since become the service’s principal surface-to-surface weapon.
The latest purchase follows much larger contracts signed in 2024 when the missiles were ordered for the Navy’s combat and training requirements, along with additional shipborne BrahMos systems.
BrahMos Aerospace is a joint venture between India’s Defense Research and Development Organization and Russia’s NPO Mashinostroyenia. The program has produced ship-, land-, and air-launched versions of the supersonic cruise missile.
The new project will have at least 68% indigenous content and involve Indian companies, including micro, small, and medium enterprises. The ministry said the program is expected to generate employment over three years while increasing domestic participation in advanced military technology.

articles.title: Seoul backs Ukraine, but sanctioned tankers carried fuel from South Korea to Russia
articles.body:
Seven tankers made 14 trips from South Korea to Russia's Far East in July and August, carrying more than 176,000 metric tons of fuel, most of it diesel, the Guardian found in a 6 October analysis of port records and ship-tracking data. The UK and EU have sanctioned three of the ships, and one loaded its fuel from another tanker at sea off South Korea instead of at a terminal.
Ukrainian strikes have cut Russia's fuel output as Moscow scrambles for supplies, while fuel loaded at South Korean ports has flowed to Russia. Loadings began to surge in July, the same month South Korean President Lee Jae-myung pledged $100 million for Ukraine's reconstruction, the Guardian reported. That creates a tension in Seoul's policy toward the war: South Korea has provided Ukraine with humanitarian and non-lethal aid but ruled out sending weapons directly, while the fuel trade appears legal under South Korean law even though three of the tankers are under UK and EU sanctions.
Russia imported 368,000 metric tons of oil products by sea in August, 112,000 of them from South Korea, according to Kpler data analyzed by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) and cited by the Guardian. CREA's own August report gives 172,000 metric tons in total, including 18,000 from South Korea. Neither explains the gap.
Where the tankers said they were going
The Layla, a tanker under UK and EU sanctions, made two voyages from Ulsan to Vladivostok, carrying a total of 57,000 metric tons of diesel. It left South Korea on 19 July and 10 August. On the first trip, it told South Korean authorities it was bound for Vladivostok; on the second, it declared Niigata, Japan, but sailed to Vladivostok again.
The Astoria, a Russian-flagged tanker under UK, EU, and Australian sanctions, loaded nearly 11,000 metric tons of fuel at Ulsan on 1 August. It declared Japan as its destination but sailed to Vladivostok.
The Chongchon did not berth at a South Korean port. Instead, it took about 26,000 metric tons of fuel from the unsanctioned Celeste I at an anchorage off Yeosu in early August. It declared Singapore as its destination but headed to Vladivostok. The owners and managers of the four tankers did not respond to the Guardian's requests for comment.
Why Russia needs the fuel
Ukrainian drone strikes have severely disrupted Russia's refining capacity, the Guardian reported. In July, Ukraine's General Staff said the strikes had knocked out 42% of Russia's refining capacity, costing the industry billions of dollars.
Russian refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% from a year earlier, the International Energy Agency said, according to the Guardian.
Russia has also restricted fuel exports to protect domestic supplies, extending its diesel export ban until the end of October; on 2 October, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Moscow could consider partially lifting the ban if there was overproduction, according to the Moscow Times.
Responses to the shipments
Seoul's non-lethal aid has included helmets, body armor, and demining vehicles, and in 2023 it pledged $2.3 billion in support, mostly in loans.
Isaac Levi, an analyst at CREA, told the Guardian:
"It is shocking that EU-sanctioned tankers loaded fuel at South Korean ports and carried it to Russia. This undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea's support for Ukraine."
South Korea's Foreign Ministry did not address the shipments or the sanctioned tankers. In a statement, it said the government supports international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery. The ministry said it was strictly enforcing its export controls and had expanded them to cover 1,402 non-strategic items with high potential for diversion to military use. The UK Foreign Office did not answer the Guardian's questions about UK-sanctioned tankers using South Korean ports, saying only that it remains committed to monitoring its sanctions.
Ties between Kyiv and Seoul are also strained over Ukraine's disclosure of its transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, which Seoul said should have remained private.

articles.title: Iran’s defense industry reaches new capacity as army chief warns enemies of ‘Historic Confusion’
articles.body:
Iran’s defense industry reaches new capacity as army chief warns enemies of ‘Historic Confusion’
TEHRAN — Iran’s indigenous defense industry has maintained uninterrupted production through the recent US-Israeli war and expanded its weapons production capacity to 2.5 times its pre-war level, senior Iranian military officials said, stressing that any renewed aggression would face a stronger response with more advanced weapons.
Army Commander Major General Amir Hatami said Iran’s adversaries were facing “historic confusion” in the face of the power and resilience of the Iranian nation.
Hatami made the remarks during a meeting with Mehrdad Akhlaqi, the nominee for Iran’s Minister of Defense and the current managing director of the Defense Industries Organization.
The Army chief commended the efforts of specialized, committed, and revolutionary personnel in Iran’s defense industry during the wars of aggression imposed by the United States and the Zionist regime, saying enemy attempts to disrupt the production chain for military equipment and weapons had failed.
He said defense-industry production lines “did not stop serving and working for a moment” even during the most critical circumstances of the aggression, enabling Iran’s Armed Forces to maintain their capabilities and preventing the enemy from achieving its objectives.
Hatami said the recent war demonstrated that Iran’s indigenous defense industry had become a strong and reliable support for the country’s combat forces and would continue to fulfill that role.
He added that, under the guidance of the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, and through the vigilant presence of the Iranian people and the efforts of the Armed Forces, “all the enemy’s calculations and objectives have been defeated.”
“The sworn enemies of the Islamic Republic are facing historic confusion in the face of the power of the great Iranian nation and engage in empty rhetoric every day,” Hatami said.
Akhlaqi, for his part, expressed hope that Iran’s Armed Forces would continue their achievements and secure the “final victory,” namely the expulsion of the United States from the region.
Iran’s weapons production capacity rises 2.5-fold
Separately, Defense Ministry spokesman Brigadier General Reza Talaei-Nik said Iran’s weapons production capacity has increased to 2.5 times its level before the war, stressing that any new aggression would be met with a more powerful response and more advanced weapons.
Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Talaei-Nik said enemy psychological operations and moves suggesting the possibility of renewed aggression would be met with a decisive response and heavier defeats for the adversary.
He described the removal of the United States from the region and the suppression of the Zionist regime’s acts of aggression as achievements of Iran’s defense during the recent US-Israeli war.
“The punishment of the American and Zionist murderers is the firm resolve of the Islamic Republic and will never be forgotten,” he said.
Talaei-Nik attributed the sharp rise in production capacity to the full mobilization of Iran’s defense-industrial capabilities, saying the country’s strategic depth in defense production had become an important component of national power and had strengthened Iran’s resilience in confronting its adversaries.
He said Iran’s production plans for offensive equipment were being continuously updated in accordance with developments in warfare and under the direction of the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters and the General Staff of the Armed Forces, based on requirements identified by military commanders.
According to the Defense Ministry spokesman, Iran has the capacity to produce more than 1,000 weapons systems and military equipment, with some systems capable of being upgraded and manufactured in larger quantities in accordance with operational requirements.
“If the enemy makes a wrong calculation, it will definitely face more advanced weapons and a heavy response from the Armed Forces,” Talaei-Nik warned.
Iran, Russia and China deepen defense consultations
Talaei-Nik also pointed to the longstanding cooperation and convergence among Iran, Russia and China, saying active relations among the three countries have been supported by all sides.
He said defense-related exchanges of views with Russia and China were on Iran’s agenda, underlining Tehran’s continued engagement with the two countries in the defense field.

articles.body:

Lithuania Moves to Lift Constitutional Ban on Nuclear Weapons on Its Territory
Lithuania’s parliament has backed a constitutional amendment that would remove the country’s ban on weapons of mass destruction, including nuclear weapons, being stationed on Lithuanian territory, LRT reported on October 6.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The proposed amendment would remove part of Article 137 of Lithuania’s Constitution, which currently prohibits weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases from being located on the country’s territory. The proposal under consideration concerns the provision on weapons of mass destruction.
Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said removing the restriction would strengthen Lithuania’s resilience and deterrence capabilities while eliminating legal differences between Lithuania and other EU and NATO members.
Opposition Conservative leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas, who supported the amendment, said Lithuania’s existing restrictions prevent allied aircraft or ships carrying nuclear weapons from entering the country for deterrence purposes.
“With the current restriction, we cannot fully participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence plans. Since nuclear deterrence is the queen of all deterrence, this decision is strategically important,” Kasčiūnas said.
Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas also supported the change, linking the initiative to the security environment created by Russia’s war against Ukraine and the presence of strategic weapons in Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad region.
“We are responding to Russia’s aggression. If Russia had not started the war in Ukraine, we probably would not be having the discussions that we are having today,” Kaunas said.
The debate over Lithuania’s constitutional restrictions also follows recent Russian nuclear threats involving Kaliningrad, the heavily militarized Russian exclave bordering Poland and Lithuania. On September 30, Reuters reported that Moscow had privately warned NATO it could resort to nuclear weapons if the alliance sought to isolate the region.
In a diplomatic note sent to NATO and reviewed by Reuters, Russia accused the alliance of pursuing a “dangerous and reckless course” that posed “high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict.”

articles.title: Air Force deputy commander: F-16s actively used against jet UAVs, require constant technical support
articles.body:
The Air Force is actively using F-16 fighter jets to counter the enemy, particularly against jet-powered UAVs, Deputy Commander of the Air Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Yuriy Cherevashenko has reported.
"F-16s are one of the most effective means of countering jet UAVs. Any aviation equipment has a limited resource, and we are using it at an extremely high rate. Therefore, keeping the aircraft in a state of constant readiness is a very difficult job. And here, the help of partners is critically important to us," Cherevashenko said on Tuesday in the Verkhovna Rada at a meeting of the Temporary Commission of Inquiry (TCI) investigating potential violations of Ukrainian legislation in the sphere of defense, anti-corruption legislation, and compliance with human rights and freedoms under martial law.
Cherevashenko reported that the delivery of jet drone interceptors in the necessary quantities is expected in about two months—"no earlier than the end of November."
According to him, the best option for destroying Russian jet drones is to strike them at their deployment and launch sites, the so-called drone ports. "Several such strikes have already been carried out. But these are heavily fortified objects reinforced with concrete, so hitting them is not easy. This is one of the important components of countering jet UAVs."

articles.title: Ukraine’s civilian casualties 55% higher in first eight months than in the same period in 2025, UN says
articles.body:
The UN Human Rights Office verified some 15,280 civilian casualties in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026, 55% more than in the same period last year, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said on 2 October.
Türk's statement comes as Russia has begun its Winter 2026-2027 campaign of long-range strikes against Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said Russian forces began the campaign in late September. Damage to energy infrastructure disrupt electricity, heating, and water supplies during the winter, increasing the risks to civilians.
Russian glide bombs killed and injured nearly 2,500 civilians in Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts during the first eight months of the year, 62% more than in the same period last year, according to UN figures.
"As winter approaches, Ukrainians fear the worst is yet to come," Türk said.
On 4 October, Russia's Defense Ministry announced that it was intensifying strikes on infrastructure in Kyiv City and Oblast and across Ukraine, according to ISW.
Why Russia is turning to long-range strikes
ISW said Ukraine's 2026 battlefield successes "appear to be forcing" Russian President Vladimir Putin to shift focus from advances on the battlefield toward a winter campaign intended to compel Ukraine to surrender.
A week earlier, ISW assessed that Putin was likely attempting to force Ukraine to capitulate before spring 2027, with his theory of victory heavily relying on cheap, jet-powered Geran-type drones.
A toll rising all year
The 15,280 figure extends a trend the UN has tracked all year. Over the first seven months of 2026, its monitoring mission verified 1,839 civilians killed and 10,638 injured. In September, UN Under-Secretary-General Rosemary DiCarlo told the Security Council that more civilians were killed or injured in the first eight months of 2026 than in all of 2025.

articles.title: Objections to conscription triple in Germany – media
articles.body:
Objections to conscription triple in Germany – media
The number of Germans seeking conscientious objector status has risen sharply amid Berlin’s military buildup and debate over reinstating conscription, the RedaktionsNetzwerk Deutschland (RND) reported on Tuesday.
According to RND, whose parent company is partly owned by the ruling coalition’s Social Democratic Party (SPD), Germany’s Federal Office for Family Affairs and Civil Society Functions received 12,102 conscientious objection applications between January and August, compared with 3,879 in all of 2025 and 2,249 in 2024. Applicants include reservists, active-duty troops and people who have never served in the military.
Germany suspended the draft in 2011. Following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, Berlin announced plans to expand the Bundeswehr from around 186,000 active-duty troops to more than 260,000 by 2035, backed by 200,000 reservists. Senior German officials have cited the country’s NATO commitments and a perceived threat from Russia to justify the military buildup. Moscow has repeatedly dismissed claims that it intends to attack NATO as “nonsense.”
Several politicians in Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s ruling coalition have argued that conscription may have to be reinstated if voluntary recruitment falls short.
A new military service system introduced this year requires all 18-year-old men to register for potential service. Enlistment remains voluntary, but parliament can activate compulsory service if recruitment targets are not met or the security situation deteriorates.
Such a prospect has fueled student protests across Germany. In late September, organizers of the so-called School Strike Against Conscription said around 45,000 demonstrators took to the streets in some 100 cities and towns.
Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has warned that Russia could attack a NATO member as early as 2028 and suggested compulsory service may be necessary to boost Germany’s preparedness.
Last May, Merz pledged to turn the Bundeswehr into the strongest conventional military force in the EU.
Moscow has sharply criticized Germany’s military buildup. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov warned earlier this year that Germany and the EU risked evolving into a “Fourth Reich.”

articles.title: Russia warns Lithuania against possible NATO base, nuclear weapons deployment
articles.body:
MOSCOW, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- The possible deployment of a NATO military base and nuclear weapons in Lithuania would further escalate tensions, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday.
"Both of these things will not contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent. On the contrary, they will become another significant round in the escalation of tensions," Peskov said.
A constitutional amendment to lift a ban on weapons of mass destruction, potentially opening the way for stationing NATO nuclear weapons in Lithuania, passed the first reading in the Lithuanian parliament earlier Tuesday. A final vote on the amendment has been scheduled for Jan. 12, 2027.
Peskov added that if such deployment occurs, Russia would be forced to take retaliatory measures to ensure its national security. ■

articles.title: Russians use AI to plan attacks on cities – Air Force deputy commander
articles.body:
Russians are using artificial intelligence to plan attack routes and identify targets, and the Air Force is acting similarly, Deputy Commander of the Air Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Yuriy Cherevashenko has reported.
"It is difficult to accurately assess the scale [of Russia's use of artificial intelligence], but we see elements of AI in their work. In particular – in strike planning. There were attacks on Odesa that lasted a long time, in waves, with very short pauses. In my opinion, without AI, this would be extremely difficult," Cherevashenko said on Tuesday in the Verkhovna Rada at a meeting of the Temporary Commission of Inquiry (TCI) investigating potential violations of Ukrainian legislation in the sphere of defense, anti-corruption legislation, and compliance with human rights and freedoms under martial law.
He expressed confidence that Russians are already planning at least attack routes and target recognition with the help of AI.
To the question of what the Armed Forces of Ukraine can counter this with, Cherevashenko said: "The same thing. We are also introducing artificial intelligence. For example, in automated turrets."
Cherevashenko also noted that the most difficult situation for air defense forces is in the Black Sea. From there, it is significantly easier for Russians to attack Ukraine. "It is much harder to control the sky over the sea. Some of our capabilities simply cannot be used there as effectively as over land. We can often only operate on a head-on course," he said, noting that an additional negative factor is the weather. "Storms, fog, difficult weather conditions—all of this seriously complicates the work. And the Russians, conversely, find that the sea gives them more freedom for routes and launches."
According to Cherevashenko, to protect ports and the coastline, so-called "drone motherships"—platforms that carry other drones—are used, among other things. This makes it possible to increase their operating time in the air and effectively organize a constant patrol of drones in the required areas.
He also added that defense at sea and along the coast "has its own specifics, which is why we combine various available means."

articles.title: Germany arrests former intelligence chief over alleged spying
articles.body:
A former head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service has been arrested on suspicion of treason and spying on behalf of an overseas intelligence agency, in what prosecutors suspect could be the most egregious national security breach since the cold war.
August Hanning, 80, was head of the federal intelligence service (BND) – which operates outside Germany to gather information across the fields of political, economic and military intelligence – between 1998 and 2005.
He was arrested at his home in Nordwalde near Münster early on Tuesday. His former chief of staff, identified only as Manfred D, was arrested at the same time in Bavaria, on suspicion of “aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage”, according to a prosecutor’s statement. Media pictures showed Hanning, dressed in an open-necked white shirt, being taken from his redbrick house to a bullet-proof vehicle by masked officers.
Manfred D, who continued to work for Hanning’s successors at the BND after Hanning’s departure until the present day, is accused of using his role to gain access to classified information which he then handed to Hanning “in exchange for payment”, the prosecutors’ statement continued.
“The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings,” the statement said.
Prosecutors believe that Hanning intended to resell the documents as part of a paid consulting role he had built up after leaving the BND, prosecutors added. To what extent and to whom he disseminated them remains part of an ongoing investigation.
He is accused of using the information to “draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service”, prosecutors said. It was unclear if this information had reached its intended recipient, they added.
Over several years, Hanning is also believed to have passed on potentially sensitive political information, in part based on information passed to him by Manfred D, to a close contact representing a separate foreign intelligence service.
Hanning and his legal team denied the allegations following his arrest. There was no immediate response from Manfred D. or his legal representatives.
Several properties connected to both men were searched simultaneously on Tuesday, including in Berlin.
Manfred D is due to appear before judges at the federal court of justice in Karlsruhe later on Tuesday, while Hanning is scheduled to appear on Wednesday.
The allegations prompted shock in German political and intelligence circles, where memories resurfaced of historic espionage scandals. Hanning is thought to be the most prominent person to be accused of treason in Germany since Günter Guillaume, one of Willy Brandt’s personal aides, was exposed as a long-term Stasi agent in 1974. The “Guillaume affair” brought an abrupt end to Nobel peace prize-winning Brandt’s career, as he swiftly resigned as chancellor of West Germany.
Marc Henrichmann, chair of the Bundestag’s intelligence oversight committee, said in a statement to AFP: “Whoever allies themselves with the enemies of our liberal democracy will be found out.” If proven to be true, Hanning’s alleged behaviour would represent “trampling his official duties underfoot”, he added.
Konstantin von Notz of the Greens, a prominent member of the same committee, urged the federal government to establish as soon as possible the “potential intelligence-related damage” that might have been done by Hanning’s alleged betrayal of Germany’s official secrets.
“This is a truly outrageous and deeply disturbing story,” he told Der Spiegel.
Suspicions over Hanning’s activities emerged as a result of an investigation into the kidnappings of the children from a prominent Hamburg business family, which is the focus of a major trial in the north German port city.
Investigators were led to Hanning over allegations, which he denies, that he helped Christina Block, the heiress of a steak restaurant dynasty, to organise the violent cross-border seizure in Denmark of her children from her estranged husband who has custody of two of their children. Block denies the charges.
After he left the BND, Hanning worked as a global consultant in the fields of security and business, based on his credentials as former intelligence chief. He is considered to have been well connected with government and business sectors in Russia and China, and also had contacts with top-ranking intelligence authorities in Israel.
Hanning was an officer stationed at the embassy-equivalent organisation for West Germany in communist East Berlin. After his role as president of the BND ended in 2005, he became the highest-ranking official in Germany’s security sector as the head of all security agencies under the federal interior minister Wolfgang Schäuble.

articles.title: Trump blames Ukraine for US fuel price surge (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Trump blames Ukraine for US fuel price surge (VIDEO)
US President Donald Trump has blamed Kiev for record-high fuel prices in the US, saying they are no longer driven by the Iran war but by Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries. He also pointed to policies pursued by Democrat-led states as a contributing factor.
In a Truth Social post on Monday, Trump said: “What’s driving up gasoline is no longer the Strait of Hormuz, because record numbers of barrels are coming out now on an almost daily basis, but the word, ‘refineries,’” adding that Russian refineries “are being blown up by Ukraine.”
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian refineries and other petroleum-linked facilities in recent months, disrupting production and contributing to fuel shortages and price hikes.
Moscow responded by restricting exports of gasoline, diesel, and other petroleum products. The diesel ban is currently in effect until the end of October. Russian President Vladimir Putin acknowledged that the strikes cost around 1% of GDP, but said damaged facilities are being quickly restored and the country’s energy system has significant reserve capacity.
https://t.co/FuWlIHEEeZ
— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) October 5, 2026
This is not the first time Trump has lashed out at Kiev over the strikes. During a visit to Ireland last month, he blamed Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky directly, saying: “Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia… Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world.”
Earlier, Trump said Ukrainian attacks caused Russia to lose “control of its diesel oil industry,” calling for and end to “this ridiculous and never-ending war,” as “the whole world suffers.” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also said Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy assets and refined products are contributing to a wider “energy shock.”
Despite repeated warnings about the global fallout, Zelensky vowed over the weekend to intensify strikes on Russian oil facilities. The Ukrainian Defense Ministry also claimed that its long-range attacks have disabled 51% of Russia’s refining capacity, though Moscow has not corroborated the figure.
Russia, which has retaliated by expanding strikes on Ukraine’s military-industrial facilities and severely disrupting Ukrainian logistics and Black Sea shipping, pledged on Sunday to step up its campaign.
Can Trump blame his way out of the fuel crisis?
With the midterm election just weeks away, Trump also blamed high fuel prices on the Democrats, lashing out at the “Dumocrats” for jeopardizing supplies “in Blue States, like California” through refinery closures.
California has lost around 17% of its refining capacity following the closure of two major facilities. The US Energy Information Administration warned that this could tighten supplies and increase price volatility. State officials reject claims that policy alone drove the closures, citing broader industry changes, although refiners have pointed to pressures linked to California’s regulatory environment.
Trump has also sought to play down the impact of the Iran war. The months-long disruption of the Strait of Hormuz – which once handled around 20% of global oil supplies – earlier pushed crude oil above $100 per barrel. Crude oil flows have since largely recovered through pipelines and ship-to-ship transfers, but refined oil supplies, particularly diesel, remain constrained. US diesel prices hit a record $6.52-$6.53 a gallon on September 22 and remain near historic highs, with prices in states such as California exceeding $8.21 a gallon, while regular gasoline stood at around $4.36 as of October 5.
The price surge has prompted emergency measures. In Texas, Governor Greg Abbott declared a disaster over record diesel costs, temporarily allowing truckers to use cheaper red-dyed diesel, normally reserved for agricultural and off-road equipment, and raising truck weight limits to 95,000 pounds to reduce trips and fuel use. Nine other states have since temporarily allowed dyed diesel for some on-road use.
Trump signed an executive order on Monday expanding the measure nationwide and deferring the federal fuel tax through the end of the year. However, an AP-NORC poll found that 65% of Americans blame Trump’s policies for the high prices, and 69% said the economy is worse off now than when he returned to office.
With fuel costs squeezing truckers, farmers, and consumers, the issue has become a political liability for Republicans heading into the midterms. RT’s Caleb Maupin reports on the mounting pressure – and whether voters will make Trump pay at the ballot box.

articles.title: At ruined Donetsk’s airport, three Russians snap selfies and ready jet-powered Geran-4. Ukrainian drone slips in unseen and rams their launcher
articles.body:
Russian troops were taking selfies beside a jet-powered Shahed launcher when a Ukrainian drone hit them. A Ukrainian drone attacked a pickup truck converted to launch Russian Shahed drones in the Donetsk airport area while its crew prepared to fire a jet-powered Geran-4, according to video from the Cursed Empire drone unit of the 100th Separate Mechanized Brigade that volunteer Serhii Sternenko published on 6 October.
Russia launches Shahed drones, including jet-powered ones, from pickup trucks and fixed launchers, and the ruined Donetsk airport, about 50 kilometers from the front line, is one of its drone bases. In September, Oboronka outlet counted that in general, Russia has at least 63 launchers at its drone bases, which are built to survive strikes.
The video shows three carefree Russian soldiers next to a pickup fitted with a launch frame.
"That was their last photo shoot," Sternenko noted, commenting on the hit on the soldiers.
The primary target
Earlier, an officer of the 1st Separate Center of the Unmanned Systems Forces, call sign “Falco,” explained that the primary goal of strikes on drone bases is to disrupt Russia's ability to launch drones.
This is done by destroying launchers and storage facilities, as well as creating an aerial threat over the drone base. Such attacks can delay drone launches indefinitely, while the destruction of infrastructure can reduce the overall number of drones launched.
But the "jewel" of anti-drone port operations is the military staff
Although these facilities are important targets, the Unmanned Systems Forces have another priority: drone operators.
“The most difficult and, at the same time, the most valuable target is the operator. They don’t stay near the launchers for long,” Falco said.
By taking out drone operators, Ukraine inflicts losses on a scarce resource. There are already relatively few of them, and Russia will have to spend additional money and time training new crews.
